News.title: Cause of Ann Widdecombe's death not yet established, inquest hears
News.content:
The cause of Ann Widdecombe's death is yet to be established, the opening of an inquest into her death has heard.

The 78-year-old former MP and MEP was found dead at her home in Devon on 9 July with "visible injuries" Exeter Corner's Court heard.

Senior coroner Philip Spinney said a post-mortem examination had taken place and "at this stage the precise medical cause of death has yet to be established".

Joshua Kerry, 28, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, has arrived at Westminister Magistrates' Court where he is due to appear charged with her murder.

Spinney, senior coroner for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay, said the inquest was now adjourned "until the conclusion of the criminal proceedings".

Widdecombe was found unresponsive in her home by an employee who carried out a welfare check due to her being "uncontactable", the hearing heard.

Emergency services were called, but she was pronounced dead at 12:20 BST on Thursday, 9 July.

Kerry was first arrested on suspicion of murder two days after former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, Widdecombe, 78, was found with serious injuries at her home in Haytor, Devon.

He was later re-arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

The investigation, which remains ongoing, has been led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East, supported by Devon and Cornwall Police.

News.title: Parts of the UK move closer to drought
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all.

For central England it has been the longest dry spell since 1995. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

News.title: Watch: 'My flat was turned into a brothel,' landlord tells BBC Panorama
News.content:
A BBC Panorama investigation has uncovered how organised crime gangs are exploiting the UK's private rental market - targeting properties to take over and use for their operations.

Among those featured in a new documentary is landlord and property developer Craig Shepheard, who discovered his flat was being used by a prostitution ring, run by a network in Brazil.

BBC Panorama reporter Hazel Martin also found that criminals are using fake IDs to get rental agreements.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
A Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 40 nautical miles south of Plymouth on Monday.

The Royal Navy monitored the exercise and is continuing to "track the vessel's activity closely", a Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said.

The Russian frigate, Neustrashimy, was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

Prior to opening fire, the BBC was also told that the Russian warship informed the Royal Navy Offshore Patrol Vessel, HMS Tyne, of its intention to conduct gunnery activity.

The Russian warship requested that that HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did. The Russian live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months. UK defence sources would not comment on whether the incident might have been timed to coincide with the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles (37km) off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they were "not on a collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

Additional reporting by Ella Kipling

News.title: Thames Water lenders offer 'golden share' to head off nationalisation
News.content:
Thames Water's main lenders are offering the government a "golden share" and more control for local authorities in a bid to stop the troubled supplier from being nationalised.

The government recently rejected a previous rescue proposal, and the BBC understands the lenders are preparing a legal challenge in case the new Andy Burnham-led government takes the firm into public hands.

The "golden share" would give the government veto powers over major decisions such as mergers.

The lenders are also proposing giving local authorities greater involvement in the firm, similar to the relationship between United Utilities and Greater Manchester agreed when Burnham was the city's mayor.

In his first speech as prime minister on Monday, Burnham said he wanted to see greater public control of "life's essentials".

Sources close to the creditors have told the BBC that in the event of full nationalisation they would pursue payment in full of the outstanding debts, as has happened in previous cases, which could leave the government with a multi-billion-pound bill.

The London & Valley Water (L&VW ) consortium of lenders had already proposed a Â£10bn deal to prevent Thames Water from entering administration. It would involve writing off nearly half of its debt and injecting new cash in return for leniency on future pollution fines.

The deal was rejected by the government in June, with then-environment secretary Emma Reynolds saying it did not do enough for consumers or the environment.

Sources close to the new deal said the creditors had sweetened it with hundreds of millions in new money on top of the existing offer.

A golden share would give the government veto power over major decisions such as mergers and acquisitions. Golden shares are seen as a way for the government to retain a stake in companies of national significance or importance, such as Royal Mail or Rolls Royce.

Any new proposals would have to be reviewed by Ofwat, the regulator.

A government spokesperson said Thames Water "remains financially stable, but we stand ready for all eventualities, including applying for a Special Administration Regime [SAR] if that were to become necessary".

"The government will always act in the national interest on these issues," they added.

An SAR is a form of temporary nationalisation which would allow the government to recoup some taxpayer cash if Thames was sold again to a private buyer.

L&VW said on Tuesday that the new offer had "material improvements" on the old one, and would benefit customers.

A spokesperson said: "We continue to believe that the L&VW plan is by far the fastest and most reliable route to solving Thames Water's complex problems and improving outcomes for customers and the environment."

They said the new deal "achieves this without any government funding or cost to taxpayers".

Fears first emerged three years ago that Thames Water could collapse and it has recently warned it could run out of cash by November.

If the company does go bust, households will still have drinking water and sewerage services.

Thames Water announced a hosepipe ban for all of its customers on Tuesday morning, citing the UK's "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The company, which supplies water and wastewater services for 16 million people across London and parts of southern England, was handed a Â£122.7m fine last year, the biggest ever issued by the industry regulator Ofwat, for breaching rules on sewage spills and shareholder payouts.

Sources close to the creditors have previously told the BBC that in the event of full nationalisation, they would pursue payment in full of the outstanding debts as has happened in previous cases, which could leave the government with a multi-billion-pound bill.

News.title: Fifa opens investigation into Argentina post-final trouble
News.content:
Argentina will face an investigation into the ugly scenes at the end of the World Cup final, Fifa has confirmed.

Fifa's disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened after the final whistle at MetLife stadium.

Any player or coach involved in the fracas could face suspension, while the Argentine Football Association (AFA) may also be fined.

Following their 1-0 defeat on Sunday, members of the Argentina team and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain players as they began to celebrate their World Cup success.

Nahuel Molina, Leandro Paredes, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala all appeared to be involved.

It was incorrectly reported on Fifa's commentator information system that Paredes had been sent off by referee Slavko Vincic for pushing Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat.

Paredes' red card was deleted shortly afterwards and Fifa has confirmed to BBC Sport that no disciplinary action was taken at the time.

Argentina had already had one player dismissed, with Enzo Fernandez receiving a second yellow card in second-half stoppage time.

Fifa had already begun the process of potential disciplinary action against Argentina after their players held a banner in support of their country's claims to the Falkland Islands following the 2-1 semi-final win against England.

News.title: Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for millions
News.content:
Thames Water has announced a hosepipe ban affecting 16 million people after an "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The restrictions mean, from Thursday, hosepipes should not be used for watering gardens or allotments, cleaning cars, filling paddling pools or swimming pools, or cleaning windows.

The water company said its region had seen 40% of average rainfall and more days at or above 34C this year than ever recorded before.

Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources, said: "We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment."

The ban applies to all customers that Thames Water supplies with drinking water and comes into effect on Thursday.

The company provides water for 16 million customers across parts of Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Kent, Surrey, the Thames Valley, Greater London, and the surrounding areas, external.

It said water use was currently 10% above normal in the Thames Valley and Home Counties and 7% above normal in London, which amounted to an extra 100 million litres of water every day.

Muncaster added: "Recent heatwaves and a very dry spring and summer have led to sustained high demand. While there is enough water for essential use, we need to reduce non-essential outdoor demand to keep taps flowing.

"Many customers have already reduced their water use and that support has made a difference. Thank you to everyone who has already changed their daily habits.

"Our teams are working 24/7 to keep water moving, fix leaks and support customers. We will keep the situation under close review and lift restrictions as soon as it is safe to do so."

News.title: Monkey abandoned in laundry bag on London bus
News.content:
A marmoset monkey has been rescued by animal welfare officers after being found abandoned inside a laundry bag on a bus in north-west London.

The female primate was discovered by a driver on the route 302 bus when it arrived at Kensal Rise on Friday morning, the RSPCA said.

A passenger with a buggy had been unable to move down the bus because the bag was blocking the luggage bay. When the driver moved it, the monkey began chirping and jumping inside.

A spokesperson for the charity said the marmoset was trapped inside a small, metal bird cage wrapped in a chequered plastic bag. She was left with a piece of apple but was stressed and dehydrated.

News.title: UK borrows less than expected in June but public finances remain a challenge
News.content:
The government borrowed slightly less than expected in June, according to figures published as new Prime Minister Andy Burnham began setting out measures to cut living costs for households.

Borrowing - the difference between spending and income from taxes - was Â£16bn, about Â£7.9bn lower than a year earlier, although analysts said challenges remained over the UK's public finances.

Other data showed the unemployment rate was unchanged, with the Office for National Statistics (ONS) saying the labour market was "relatively steady".

However, while the borrowing figure was less than forecast, the ONS said total debt was high by historical standards and close to the annual value of the UK economy.

Borrowing for June was slightly below the Â£16.3bn that had been predicted by the government's official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said June's figure was "a rare piece of good news" for the new prime minister and his new Chancellor, John Healey.

However, she added: "Overall, there's no escaping the fact that the public finances are fragile and that there is limited scope for extra borrowing."

So far in the current financial year, borrowing has reached a total of Â£57.6bn, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). While this is down Â£3.7bn from the same period last year, it is Â£2.7bn above the OBR's forecast.

James Smith, chief UK economist at ING, told the BBC's Today programme the fact that borrowing was still running ahead of the OBR's projections was "a reminder of the challenges that the new chancellor and the new prime minister face".

He added they would face a "difficult picture" at the autumn Budget, with "lots of tough choices to be made".

Burnham and Healey have both pledged to stick to former chancellor Rachel Reeves' fiscal rules on spending and borrowing. although the new prime minister said on Monday he would use "any flexibility within them" to help with policy changes.

Shortly after Burnham's comments were made public, the yield on 10-year government bonds - effectively the interest rate charged to the UK government for a 10-year loan - rose above 5%.

The yield hit 5.03% late on Monday afternoon. However, when trading began on Tuesday the rate slipped back slightly to 5.01%.

In a statement released on Monday, Healey said "fiscal credibility is the bedrock for economic stability and for national security".

The new leadership's first major policy announcement was to cut VAT on household electricity bills from 5% to zero from the beginning of October.

Ministers said it would be funded by savings from the cancellation of the digital ID programme, but Labour's Darren Jones, who was sacked as chief secretary to the prime minister on Monday, accused the government of announcing an unfunded tax cut.

News.title: Does Scotland have the 'game changer' helicopters it needs to fight wildfires?
News.content:
A devastating wildfire burning in the Cairngorms has entered its seventh day, as helicopters battle to stop the spread of the flames.

Two specialist helicopters have been "invaluable" for waterbombing hard-to-reach areas, the Cairngorms National Park Authority says.

But the flames were allowed to torch the landscape for nearly two days before they arrived on the scene around Glenmore Forest Park.

There's been vocal frustration from some local people, who believe the wildfire might have been brought under control if specialist air support had been called in sooner.

Why the delay? Do Scotland's firefighters have the aerial resources they need to tackle the growing threat of wildfires?

News.title: Owners of viral TikTok blue lagoon warn people to stay away
News.content:
Owners of a "blue lagoon" that went viral on TikTok during the Covid pandemic have warned people not to enter the site, particularly during the current hot weather.

Brombil Reservoir in Margam in Neath Port Talbot attracted thousands of visitors, which caused traffic problems and littering.

To reach the 30m-deep (100ft) reservoir, visitors must walk up a steep 900m (2,953ft) public footpath.

Leisure Estate Investments Ltd, which bought the secluded site at auction for Â£20,000 in 2024, are now charging Â£2 a visit as "a temporary deterrent" and have installed barriers on its dam face.

It is concerned about people swimming, paddleboarding, littering and damaging structures around the site.

Although the reservoir can be accessed via public footpaths, the barriers were installed to stop people from walking on the dam face - but these have since been removed by trespassers.

The owners said the Â£2 levy was introduced in an effort to manage unauthorised visits and help fund clean-up operations, as part of its efforts to discourage public access because of "inherent safety risks".

A spokesperson for the company said: "We have strictly banned [people] from going there and walking on the face of the dam.

"Our long-term vision has always been to build a sustainable public-private framework so the community can safely enjoy this asset.

"However, managing a critical piece of infrastructure presents immense structural, environmental, and financial challenges that cannot be indefinitely sustained by a private entity alone."

News.title: Tributes to Kevin Keegan 'will never be enough'
News.content:
Fans around Newcastle have paid tribute to Kevin Keegan after news broke of the former footballer's death at age 75.

Although not from the city, Geordies claim Keegan as one of their own thanks to the influential stints he had as both player and manager.

Even Sunderland fan, Eddie, whose wife Brenda supports Newcastle, said: "He's a legend isn't he? Red and white, black and white it doesn't matter."

Newcastle United manager Eddie Howe said Keegan had been an "inspiration" and "a friend whose guidance and support meant a great deal in recent years".

"He was always willing to share his wisdom, offer encouragement and provide support, and I will always be grateful for that," he said.

"Every conversation with Kevin left you feeling better. He had remarkable warmth and humour and also a love for football that touched everyone around him."

Flowers have been laid at St James' Park as supporters flock to the ground to pay their respects.

Former Newcastle player and boyhood fan Shola Ameobi was also seen paying his respects at the stadium on Tuesday.

News.title: Northern Ireland's deputy first minster was 'floored' by news of Donaldson arrest
News.content:
Northern Ireland's deputy first minster says she was "completely floored" when she first heard of the arrest and charges of former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson over historical sex abuse.

In June, he was convicted of 18 counts of sex abuse, including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

Emma Little-Pengelly said that people who worked alongside Donaldson over the past 20 years are "floored, shocked and utterly repulsed".

On Friday, it emerged Donaldson is to appeal his conviction.

After the former DUP leader was found guilty, a BBC Spotlight investigation reported on the double life of Donaldson.

The programme heard from former senior police officers and politicians who spoke about behaviour they described as hypocritical and which put Donaldson in danger of being compromised by his political opponents.

Speaking to the BBC's Red Lines podcast, Little-Pengelly said those reports should not take away from the scale of the crimes that he has been found guilty of.

"He's been convicted of being a paedophile and a rapist, and yes, there's all of these other allegations, but they absolutely pale into insignificance of that," she said.

"The focus should always be on the fact that he's been convicted of being a rapist and a paedophile, and that the victims of that have gone through a terrible ordeal to get justice."

News.title: 'Treasured' teen, 18, died after cardiac arrest at festival
News.content:
A teenager who died at a music festival suffered a cardiac arrest, an inquest opening has heard.

Lucy Ellen Halpin, 18, died on 11 July after going to the Tonnau festival near Llanfaethlu on Anglesey.

Opening the inquest, coroner Kate Robertson said she had reason to suspect the cause of death was unnatural.

A post-mortem examination was being carried out but the cause of death was not confirmed.

Emergency services were called to the Carreglwyd estate, Llanfaethlu at 01:45 BST on 11 July following reports of a medical emergency.

Halpin, from Bangor, Gwynedd, was taken to hospital, where she later died at 03:18.

At the time, organisers of Tonnau festival confirmed that the festival had been cancelled to enable the authorities to carry out their inquiries.

Opening and adjourning the inquest on Tuesday, the coroner said she extended her deepest sympathies to Lucy's family.

In a tribute on its Facebook page, Breeze Hill Bar, Eatery and Hotel, where Lucy worked, said she was "exceptionally good at looking after our customers, many of whom will miss her lots".

"Lucy wasn't just staff, Lucy was a member of our extended family and was treasured by us, our customers and her colleagues, many of whom became her close friends.

"Lucy was caring, funny, clever and always smiling," they said in a statement, adding it was "a pub full of broken hearts".

Her friends said she "lit up every room she walked into and put a smile on everyone's face without fail".

In a tribute accompanying a fundraiser for Lucy's family to help with funeral and other costs, they said she would be "carried in all our lives with love" and "deeply missed".

News.title: Andy Burnham’s cabinet – who’s in and who’s out as Healey becomes chancellor and Rayner returns
News.content:

John Healey has been appointed chancellor and Ed Miliband has become the new foreign secretary as new prime minister Andy Burnham finalises his new cabinet appointments.

Shabana Mahmood will remain home secretary after she and Mr Miliband had been tipped as the leading candidates for the Treasury.

These ministers will make up the top team in his new government, helping to deliver the policy agenda that Mr Burnham sets out.

Louise Haigh, who managed Mr Burnham’s Makerfield campaign, will be first secretary of state, chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and minister for the cabinet office.

Meanwhile, Rachel Reeves and David Lammy are among several senior ministers leaving government after Sir Keir Starmer tendered his resignation to the King earlier on Monday.

Ahead of the major reshuffle, business secretary Peter Kyle, and housing secretary Steve Reed also resigned from government.

Here are the Labour MPs who have taken the top jobs in Mr Burnham’s new cabinet:

Who’s in?

John Healey

open image in gallery John Healey ( PA )

Chancellor

In a move that has surprised many, John Healey has been appointed as chancellor by Andy Burnham. The MP for Wentworth since Labour’s landslide 1997 general election victory, the Treasury appointment is the most senior in a long line of ministerial positions for the veteran politician.

His tenure as defence secretary lasted from July 2024 to June 2026, when he dramatically quit over disagreements with the government’s defence spending plans.

Mr Healey’s decision to resign came at an incredibly bruising time for Sir Keir Starmer, who had already faced calls from several resigning ministers to go over Labour’s disastrous local election results.

Mr Healey and Mr Burnham share a long professional history dating back to their days as cabinet colleagues under Gordon Brown in the late 2000s. He is thought to have been picked by former Manchester mayor for Number 11 for his national security credibility and popularity amongst MPs on Labour’s right.

Angela Rayner

open image in gallery Angela Rayner ( UK Parliament )

Housing secretary

Angela Rayner has regained the position of housing secretary just under a year after resigning from the role over issues around unpaid stamp duty.

The Ashton-under-Lyne MP has been a high-profile figure in British politics for most of her 11 years in the role after being appointed shadow secretary of state under Jeremy Corbyn just a year after her election.

In May this year, she was cleared of wrongdoing by HMRC over her tax affairs, clearing the path for her to rejoin the cabinet.

Following Labour’s disastrous local election results in May, she issued a “last chance” warning to Sir Keir, telling him that blocking Mr Burnham from standing in the by-election in Gorton and Denton was a “mistake”.

Jonathan Reynolds

open image in gallery Jonathan Reynolds ( PA )

Business secretary

Jonathan Reynolds has been appointed as business secretary in Andy Burnham’s cabinet, taking over from Peter Kyle.

The Stalybridge MP initially held the role form July 2024 to September 2025, when he was shifted to chief whip by Sir Keir.

He now returns to the expanded role of secretary of state for business, innovation, science and trade following the abolition of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) by Mr Burnham.

Ed Miliband

open image in gallery Ed Miliband ( PA )

Foreign secretary

Former Labour leader Ed Miliband has been promoted to foreign secretary.

Energy secretary since 2024, his recent focus has been on green initiatives and energy independence, especially in light of price shocks like those caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

His approach is characterised by the establishment of ‘Great British Energy’ last year, publicly owned energy investment company which works with the private sector to fund clean energy and community projects.

Mr Miliband and Mr Burnham have a long-standing political relationship, both sitting in Gordon Brown’s cabinet in the late 2000s, and running against each other in the 2010 Labour leadership election.

Shabana Mahmood

open image in gallery Shabana Mahmood ( UK Parliament )

Home secretary

Shabana Mahmood retains the position of home secretary despite strong briefings that she was bound for the Treasury.

The Birmingham MP has risen quickly through the Labour party ranks since her election in 2010, holding several shadow front bench positions from the early days of her time in Parliament.

Ms Mahmood was appointed shadow justice secretary and lord chancellor by Sir Keir Starmer in 2023, taking up both of these positions in government before being appointed home secretary in 2025.

Her tenure in the role has seen Labour tack further to the right on issues like immigration and policing. Shortly before becoming prime minister, Mr Burnham voted in favour of the government’s immigration and asylum bill in defiance of 80 backbench Labour MPs who urged him against it.

Keeping her on as home secretary is perhaps a signal that the former Manchester mayor’s intends to maintain some continuity with the previous Labour government on the issue of immigration and policing.

Wes Streeting

open image in gallery Wes Streeting ( PA )

Defence secretary

Former health secretary Wes Streeting has been appointed defence secretary by Mr Burnham in his new cabinet.

Elected as the MP for Ilford North in 2015, Mr Streeting served in the health brief from July 2024 to May 2026. His resignation served a major blow to Sir Keir Starmer, delivered in response to Labour’s disastrous local election results.

Upon his resignation, he said he was proud of his work on reducing NHS waiting times during his time in the post, alongside improving ambulance response times and recruiting 2,000 GPs.

Mr Streeting is often credited as one of Labour’s most able media performers, and has long been linked to ambitions for the top job. It is understood that he had intended to challenge Mr Burnham for leadership before it became clear he could not gather required 81 Labour MPs to support his bid.

Yvette Cooper

open image in gallery Yvette Cooper ( UK Parliament )

Health secretary

A mainstay in the Labour Party for nearly three decades, Yvette Cooper will now become health secretary, moving from the position of foreign secretary.

Ms Cooper was then appointed foreign secretary by Sir Keir in his 2025 cabinet reshuffle, becoming the first woman in history to serve in both this role and as home secretary.

Her political relationship to Mr Burnham spans back nearly as long as her time in Westminster, with the new prime minister becoming an MP just a few years after her.

Both served in the cabinet of former prime minister Gordon Brown, with Ms Cooper serving as work and pensions secretary while Mr Burnham held the health brief.

Ms Cooper delivered a major boost for Mr Burnham’s leadership bid at the end of June, telling reporters that he is “the right person” for the job.

Lucy Powell

open image in gallery Lucy Powell ( UK Parliament )

Education secretary

Elected as the MP for Manchester Central in a 2012 by-election, Lucy Powell became a natural ally for Mr Burnham during his time as the city’s mayor – and this partnership will continue in Westminster.

The deputy Labour leader has been appointed education secretary by Mr Burnham, taking over from Bridget Phillipson.

During Sir Keir Starmer’s time as leader of the opposition, he appointed Ms Powell to several shadow ministerial roles. She would ultimately hold the brief as leader of the House of Commons for a year, before being dismissed by Sir Keir in the 2025 cabinet reshuffle.

Mr Burnham backed Ms Powell as deputy leader of the Labour party, to take over from Angela Rayner who was forced to resign over an issue with her tax affairs.

Her victory over then-education secretary Bridget Phillipson was seen as a decisive moment in Mr Burnham’s rise to power, giving the former mayor yet another powerful ally in Westminster.

Her longstanding support for Mr Burnham makes her a natural ally as he builds his top team, and her appointment as education secretary little surprise.

Bridget Phillipson

open image in gallery Bridget Phillipson ( UK Parliament )

Equalities minister

Bridget Phillipson remains a member of the cabinet reshuffle, albeit in a reduced role.

The Sunderland MP retains her position as equalities minister, but has handed the education brief over to Lucy Powell.

In the education brief, she oversaw initiatives such as expanding free breakfast clubs, overhauling school inspections, and addressing rising school absenteeism.

Pat McFadden

open image in gallery Pat McFadden ( UK Parliament )

Work and pensions secretary

Pat McFadden is one of the few ministers to hold on to his job from the Starmer cabinet, staying on as work and pension secretary.

First elected as the MP for Wolverhampton South East in 2005, Mr McFadden has held several ministerial roles during his time in parliament.

He was appointed to the DWP brief in Sir Keir’s 2025 reshuffle, tasked with focusing on structural welfare reforms and getting young people into work.

Louise Haigh

open image in gallery Louise Haigh ( Getty )

Cabinet Office

Former transport secretary Louise Haigh was manager of Mr Burnham’s campaign in Makerfield, and a key proponent in Westminster of his return to parliament.

She has been appointed first secretary of state, chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and minister for the cabinet office.

Ms Haigh resigned as transport secretary in November 2024 after it emerged she had pleaded guilty to a fraud offence a decade ago, telling police she had her work mobile taken in a mugging, but later finding it had not been taken.

In the time since, the Sheffield MP is understood to have become a “right-hand” to Mr Burnham, credited with elevating his campaign to return to parliament as leader.

Anneliese Midgley

open image in gallery Anneliese Midgley ( UK Parliament )

Chief secretary

Elected in 2024 for the Merseyside seat of Knowsley, Anneliese Midgley was a political director for Unite and the Trade Union Congress earlier in her political career, before going on to advise both Jeremy Corbyn and Sir Keir in opposition.

The Knowsley-born politician worked as the “political lead” on Mr Burnham’s campaign in Makerfield, and is understood to be a close ally.

Her extensive trade union experience and connections makes her a potentially wise choice for a top job in Mr Burnham’s cabinet, following from union backlash towards the end of Sir Keir’s tenure.

In May, 11 unions which help fund the Labour Party, including Unite, Unison and GMB, called on the outgoing prime minister to resign over disastrous local election results.

Ms Midgely has taken over as chief whip under Mr Burnham, in a role which may help the new prime minister forge deeper ties with essential backers.

Miatta Fahnbulleh

open image in gallery Miatta Fahnbulleh ( PA )

Energy secretary

Miatta Fahnbulleh, who resigned as a housing minister in protest at Sir Keir’s leadership earlier this year, has been advising Mr Burnham and fleshing out his policy plans.

Ms Fahnbulleh, the new Energy Secretary, is considered to be a member of Mr Burnham’s inner circle.

She previously served as a parliamentary under-secretary of state in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and is also considered to be a close ally of Ed Miliband.

Alex Norris

open image in gallery ( PA )

Justice Secretary

Alex Norris, who has been appointed as justice secretary, previously served as minister of state for border security and asylum.

Earlier this month, Mr Norris said “all options are on the table” regarding the deportation of Rochdale grooming gang leader Shabir Ahmed who was released from prison.

Who’s out?

Astronomers are perplexed to find signs of the same as-yet-undiscovered molecule on the surfaces of both Pluto and Saturn’s moon Titan, pointing to a unique shared chemistry between the two worlds billions of miles apart.

Titan is Saturn’s biggest moon, and one of the only worlds with clear evidence of stable surface liquid in the Solar System.

In complete contrast, Pluto is a frozen dwarf planet at the edge of the solar system, far colder and about half the size of Titan.

Now, researchers analysing data from Titan and Pluto recorded by Nasa’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have found that the atmospheres of both these worlds share a unique common feature.

“We have found an unidentified absorption feature in JWST spectra of Titan and of Pluto,” scientists wrote in the yet-to-be-published study posted on arXiv.

open image in gallery Composite image shows an infrared view of Saturn's moon Titan ( Nasa )

In both data sets, scientists have identified a common light absorption feature, which is known to be caused by certain molecules.

But what exactly this molecule is remains a mystery.

Researchers assessed past studies on light absorption bands by molecules, and could not find a match for the feature found on Pluto and Titan anywhere else, they say.

"We did not find any band referenced in these publications that corresponds to the location of the observed absorption in Titan and Pluto,” scientists wrote.

"It's rather mysterious...We cannot say what it is,” said study co-author Bruno Bézard told Space.com.

Experts theorised that acetylene ice and benzene mixed with other molecules could cause the effect, but additional tests are needed to verify whether these chemicals can cause the kind of absorption seen.

“We searched for possible simple ice and organic candidates in the literature and found that only a few of them are plausible: the group of allenes and, if mixed with other species, benzene, ketene or less likely acetylene,” scientists wrote.

open image in gallery Enhanced colour global view of Pluto ( Nasa )

There is also some evidence from the data that the molecule is prevalent on the surfaces of both Titan and Pluto, but not their atmospheres.

Both the worlds are known to have methane–nitrogen environments, so scientists now suspect this unique chemistry could be playing a big role in producing this shared molecule.

Researchers hope to assess further JWST observations to map exactly where on Titan signs of the molecule are strongest and narrow down its source.

But the thick atmosphere of Titan makes it difficult to study its surface using telescopes.

Nasa’s Dragonfly spacecraft may help narrow down the list of candidate molecules on Titan's surface, researchers say.

“Dragonfly, the next mission to Titan scheduled to arrive in the mid-2030s, will conduct in situ studies of the surface composition and chemical complexity at various geological sites,” they wrote.

It began as a satirical movement online, embracing the humble cockroach as a way to voice the frustrations of young people in India after a series of scandals rocking the education sector.

Now, the so-called “Cockroach Janta (People’s) Party” has captured the attention of the nation, with a weeks-long sit-in protest in the capital culminating in a march on parliament that was met by tear gas and baton charges from the police.

Dubbing itself the “voice of the lazy and unemployed” as a response to criticism of Gen Z workers from India’s most senior judge, the CJP was founded on 16 May by Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old public relations graduate at Boston University and former social media strategist for the Aam Aadmi party (AAP).

Within a week, it amassed nearly 20.5 million followers on Instagram, while its official X account – which was temporarily blocked in India due to a legal demand from the government – now has over 300,000 followers.

open image in gallery A supporter of CJP wears a cockroach mask during a protest demanding the resignation of the Education Minister over alleged examination paper leaks ( Getty Images )

With the social media accounts came a website complete with a manifesto, membership guidelines, and a sign-up form inviting users to join “a political party for the people the system forgot to count”.

The party’s name parodies Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), in power since 2014.

The movement traces its origins to comments from India’s chief justice Surya Kant, who said during a Supreme Court hearing on 15 May that there were “youngsters like cockroaches” who, unable to find employment or “any place in the profession”, turned to media, social media, and activism to “start attacking everyone”.

The comments, made while criticising what he described as “parasites” attacking Indian institutions, spread rapidly across Indian social media and struck a nerve among younger users.

The following day, Mr Dipke responded with a post on X asking: “What if all cockroaches come together?” alongside a Google form inviting users to join “a new platform for all the cockroaches”.

Mr Kant later clarified that he had been referring specifically to people entering professions using “fake and bogus degrees”, not unemployed young people broadly, who were “the pillars of a developed India”.

But the seed of an idea had already been sown. “Those in power think citizens are cockroaches and parasites,” Mr Dipke told Al Jazeera. “They should know that cockroaches breed in rotten places. That’s what India is today.”

open image in gallery A supporter of Cockroach Janta Party seen through a torn CJP banner at a protest site ( REUTERS )

Unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 stood at 9.9 per cent in 2025, rising to 13.6 per cent in urban areas, according to the Indian government’s Periodic Labour Force Survey. The 2026 State of Working India report by Azim Premji University also found unemployment among graduates aged 15 to 25 was close to 40 per cent.

Mr Kant’s remarks came amid nationwide anger after authorities cancelled India’s competitive medical entrance examination following a paper leak scandal. At least 2.3 million students sat the test on 3 May. The controversy followed similar scandals elsewhere, including the cancellation of Uttar Pradesh’s police recruitment exam in 2024, affecting 4.8 million applicants, and the scrapping of the UGC-NET examination the same year over leak allegations.

The controversy has since become a rallying point for the CJP, which has broadened its campaign to demand greater accountability in education, employment and governance. The group launched an indefinite sit-in protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar site on 20 June, making the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan its central demand.

open image in gallery ( AP )

The movement drew support from renowned activist Sonam Wangchuk, who launched a hunger strike in solidarity with the CJP’s campaign. Mr Wangchuk was later forcibly moved to hospital by police after three weeks of fasting.

Established political parties have been wary of how to handle the CJP’s sudden rise to the centre of public discourse, with few big-name politicians engaging with the group’s Delhi sit-in.

“The youth of India has largely vanished from the mainstream political discourse,” Mr Dipke told Reuters. “Nobody is talking about us. Nobody is listening to our issues or even trying to acknowledge our existence.”

That appeared to shift on 21 June when the Leader of the Opposition in parliament, Rahul Gandhi, spoke out in the CJP’s defence after protesters were tear-gassed the day before.

open image in gallery Delhi police officers armed with batons confront protesters during a march organised by CJP on July 20 ( Getty )

open image in gallery Protesters run as police use tear gas during clashes at a demonstration organised by CJP ( Getty )

Other opposition politicians, including Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Trinamool Congress MP Kirti Azad and Aam Aadmi party leader Manish Sisodia, have voiced support for the CJP publicly.

The CJP’s manifesto channels frustration into a mix of satire and direct political demands. One proposal calls for retired chief justices to be barred from receiving seats in parliament’s upper house as a “post-retirement reward”, while another proposes a 20-year ban on politicians who defect between parties.

The manifesto also calls for 50 per cent of seats in parliament and cabinet positions to be reserved for women, and demands that media outlets owned by the billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, whose business groups control Network18 and NDTV respectively, have their licences revoked “to make way for truly independent media”.

Membership requirements listed on the website include being “unemployed, lazy, chronically online, and able to rant professionally”.

Supporters have described the CJP as a “breath of fresh air” and “completely unafraid to ask uncomfortable questions that mainstream politicians keep dodging”.

Critics have dismissed the movement as hidden arm of a major opposition party, pointing to Mr Dipke’s previous work with AAP between 2020-2023. Mr Dipke has denied allegations that the movement was coordinated by any political party, and told India’s The Print website that the idea emerged “completely impromptu”.

“I read the CJI’s comment – that everybody is a cockroach – and I tweeted from my personal account,” he said.

Others have questioned if the movement represents meaningful political organising or simply internet spectacle. “I have realised most internet folks have no clue how politics really works. Real-life political work is a ball buster,” wrote one critic on X. The Quint website argued that the movement remained “performance theatre” unless it connected to “organised power”.

Mr Dipke has stopped short of saying whether the CJP will formally enter electoral politics, cautioning against comparisons with the Gen Z-led uprisings in Bangladesh and Nepal. “Whatever we do, we will do within the rights of the constitution. We will do it in a very democratic and peaceful way,” he said.

For now, Mr Dipke says he wants to build what he describes as an “online political party” that encourages younger Indians to become more politically active. He said he wanted the platform to “mobilise youth, encourage civic engagement, and even guide supporters toward activism through steps such as filing Right To Information applications to hold governments accountable”.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe’s cause of death yet to be established, inquest hears
News.content:

Ann Widdecombe’s cause of death is yet to be established, the opening of an inquest into her death has heard.

The former MP and MEP was found dead at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, on 9 July, having suffered “visible injuries”, a brief hearing at Exeter Coroner’s Court heard on Tuesday.

Philip Spinney, senior coroner for the county of Devon, Plymouth and Torbay, said Miss Widdecombe was found unresponsive in her home by an employee carrying out a welfare check after concerns were raised due to her being “uncontactable”.

Emergency services were called to her address in Haytor Vale but she was pronounced dead at 12.20pm on 9 July.

Mr Spinney said: “A post-mortem examination has taken place and at this stage the precise medical cause of death has yet to be established.

“Shortly after the conclusion of this hearing I shall be taking steps to formally suspend this inquest… Until the conclusion of the criminal proceedings.”

Whether you’re seasoning a dish mid-cooking or adding a final sprinkle before serving, a reliable salt and pepper grinder is a must-have for any kitchen. However, with countless styles available, finding the right one can be surprisingly difficult. Grinders differ in everything from their materials and appearance to how they work, with options ranging from classic manual designs to battery-powered models and features such as adjustable grind settings.

Peugeot introduced the first electric grinder in the 1990s, with brands such as Cuisinart following with their own models. While electric grinders offer speed and convenience, many home cooks still prefer manual designs for the satisfying feel, hands-on experience and greater control over the grind.

If you enjoy cooking, a grinder with adjustable settings is worth considering. The ability to change the coarseness means you can tailor your seasoning to the dish, from a chunky grind for steak to a finer texture for sauces.

Thames Water has become the latest company to announce a hosepipe ban, affecting its more than 10 million customers after the exceptionally dry hot heather and high demand.

The restriction, also known as a temporary use ban, will come into effect at 12.01am on Thursday 23 July. However, the utility firm is asking households to follow the ban immediately ahead of its official start date.

Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources at Thames Water, said: “We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment.

“While there is enough water for essential use, we need to reduce non-essential outdoor demand to keep taps flowing.”

It comes after South East Water extended its hosepipe ban over the weekend, from Kent-only to customers in Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.

The latest ban brings the total companies enforcing restrictions up to six, affecting at least 20 million customers across the regions they serve.

Water customers across central and south-east England remain banned from using hosepipes as back-to-back heatwaves have caused a spike in water demand and fears of droughts.

South East Water said it has seen a “decline in river levels” and needs to “protect some groundwater sources” after lower than average rainfall, hot weather and high demand for water.

The first hosepipe ban has also been announced in Wales by Welsh Water. It came into effect for around 33,000 customers in Ceredigion, Pembrokeshire and Carmarthenshire from Sunday 19 July.

The bans come as central and south-east England have seen the longest unbroken spell of no recorded rainfall this century, Met Office figures suggest.

An average of zero rainfall has been measured across the organisation’s weather stations in both regions for 14 days in a row, from July 2 to July 15, according to the latest available data.

This is the longest unbroken run of days with no rain for south-east England since a 15-day spell in April 1997. For central England, it is the longest period since a 14-day run of no recorded rainfall in June 1996.

Data for July 16 has yet to be published, but could show the rain-free spells in both regions extending for even longer.

UK households have been asked to be mindful of their water usage ( Getty )

June 2026 was also the hottest on record for England, the Met Office has said, with the highest temperature of 37.7C set in Lingwood, Norfolk, on 26 June. The previous record of 35.6C was set in Southampton in June 1976.

Anglian Water, which serves most of the East of England, brought in a ban on Saturday 11 July. The company has more than 5 million customers in the region, making it the UK’s largest.

Affinity Water has also introduced a hosepipe ban for most of its customers, which began Saturday 11 July. It covers large areas of Bedfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire and Surrey.

London and Essex, which are served by a number of different water companies, are also affected in some areas. Customers can check with their drinking water provider for exact details.

South East Water introduced the first official temporary hosepipe use ban to cover much of the Kent region from Friday 3 July. It came just a week after it put one in place in the county during June’s heatwave.

Southern Water has also confirmed that a hosepipe ban will be put in place for its customers in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight from Friday 10 July.

Cambridge Water announced a temporary hosepipe ban for its 350,000 customers, marking the first time in three decades that it has introduced the restriction.

Households across the country have been advised to limit their use, with some companies asking customers to pause hosepipe activity where possible, short of a full-on ban.

A hosepipe ban is different to an advisory notice. Anyone caught breaching an official ban can be issued a fine of up to £1,000.

Others have asked customers to limit their use during the heat spikes.

Thames Water, which serves Greater London, advises: “At times, we're using water faster than we can deliver it through our network.

“Reducing your use at home, especially outdoors, will make the biggest difference. So we're asking customers not to use hosepipes or sprinklers during heatwaves.”

While July temperatures been less severe than June’s heatwave, conditions continue to present health risks and challenges for water firms which are still recovering from the event.

All households have been urged to limit their water usage during the heatwaves. National Drought Group chair and director of water at the Environment Agency, Helen Wakeham, said in June: “We enter summer in a generally favourable position, but we can never be complacent ahead of those crucial drier months.

“Heatwaves will continue to be a concern as they can drive spikes in water demand, so we need to continue to work collaboratively to use our finite water wisely.

“While many of us enjoy the hot weather, we ask everyone to be mindful of their water use. Every drop saved leaves more available for farmers, our local rivers and wildlife.”

Homelessness charities have welcomed Andy Burnham’s vow to end rough sleeping but warned that the new prime minister cannot afford to ignore the growing ‘hidden homelessness’ crisis in the UK.

Speaking outside Downing Street for the first time as prime minister, Andy Burnham said that his first instruction to his government would be to “end rough sleeping” and that he will put “the care of people at the heart of everything I do.”

The prime minister added: “For too long, we’ve been told that ending rough sleeping will take decades or even that it’s impossible. I’m not having that. This is something a government can fix if it chooses to.

open image in gallery Burnham talks to a homeless person in London on Monday, hours before he became prime minister ( Reuters )

“We’ll get to work immediately, bringing together national and local government with the investment needed to get it done.”

The latest annual national statistics, published in February, showed an estimated 4,793 people were sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England, a new record high, marking the fourth annual increase in a row.

Speaking to The Independent following the prime minister’s speech, Helen MacNamara, the chair of trustees at homelessness charity Shelter, described the promise to end rough sleeping as “tremendous news”.

“It’s great to see a prime minister standing on the steps of Downing Street, and that the first thing he says is talking about ending rough sleeping and his commitment to building council housing.

“This is one of the pestilences of our age for sure, and Andy Burnham means what he says about rough sleeping. He did make a [similar] commitment in Manchester, and those numbers have started to come down, so I think we can be confident that he means it.”

She added: “There have been tried and tested ways of tackling rough sleeping, and it sounds like he’s going to go for a housing-first approach, and it can be done, governments could end rough sleeping if they need to.

“It’s fantastic to see a prime minister in this first intervention talk about the importance of housing and somebody with a very strong commitment to getting rid of the kind of shame on us as a society of rough sleeping. We shouldn’t have people sleeping on our streets.”

open image in gallery Burnham pledged millions in funding to help at least 3,000 rough sleepers ( PA )

However, Ms MacNamara warned about the “hidden homelessness” problem that Burnham also needs to solve.

“The bit of housing that I’m also extremely worried about is the hidden homelessness that you can’t see,” she said. “So, it’s not the people on the streets, that obviously really matters, but we’ve got 176,000 children who currently don’t have a permanent home.

“This hidden homelessness, it’s the families and the children, the kids in primary school that don’t have a permanent home, and you’ve got people living in hotels, in B&Bs, in HMOs where you’ve got a mum and their kids crammed into one bedroom or are not able to cook, and there’s no kitchen and the kids are doing their homework with no space and nothing of kind to call their own, and they’re not even sure if they’re going to be back to the same place after. It’s just so damaging.”

According to government figures, there were 134,210 households as part of the “hidden homelessness” issue at the end of December 2025, down from 134,700 at the end of September 2025.

According to figures from homelessness charity Crisis, there are around 208,600 households across the country experiencing “hidden homelessness” on any given night – a rise of almost a third (30 per cent) since 2020.

The number of children in temporary accommodation has also continued to rise, standing at 176,130 at the end of December, up from 175,930 at the end of September, according to government figures. The number was up 6 per cent year on year, from 165,450 at the end of December 2024.

Also praising the prime minister’s approach was Yvonne Hope, chief executive of Barnabus, a homelessness charity that operates in Manchester, where Mr Burnham was mayor between 2017 and 2026, who said that she is “over the moon” with the announcement.

“If anyone’s going to do it, it will be him,” she said. “He’s got the determination, he’s got the knowledge, but he’s also got the humility to understand this is a human story.”

In further details set out by No 10, £340 million funding was announced to go towards acquiring suitable homes, identifying those most in need and starting to provide housing and support “without delay”.

The funding will provide 1,200 homes and intensive support for at least 3,000 long-term rough sleepers over five years, the government said.

The money, said to be from within uncommitted Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government budgets, will be on top of the previously announced £3.6 billion funding under the National Plan to End Homelessness – which came under Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership – bringing the total to over £3.9 billion.

Andy Burnham – who took over as prime minister promising a “circuit-breaker” for British politics – has started in post with a bang.

The new PM conducted a brutal purge of Starmer loyalists within hours of moving into Downing Street, sacking more than nine ministers who had close ties with his predecessor.

David Lammy, Darren Jones, Rachel Reeves and Peter Kyle all left the government, while senior party figures including Angela Rayner, Wes Streeting and John Healey have returned.

Here, The Independent looks at the key winners and losers of the new prime minister’s reshuffle.

Winners

open image in gallery Andy Burnham became prime minister on Monday ( AP )

John Healey

John Healey is the big winner from the reshuffle, taking arguably the most important job in government, bar prime minister. The former defence secretary’s appointment as chancellor is a hugely surprising move, and follows weeks of speculation that either Shabana Mahmood or Ed Miliband could be Mr Burnham’s chancellor.

Mr Healey quit Sir Keir Starmer’s government amid a row over defence spending, but he now has the keys to the Treasury, a department he so viciously criticised for standing in the way of more funding for Britain’s military. The move signals that Mr Burnham’s government will prioritise Britain’s military, and suggests that No 10 will fall in line with Mr Healey’s vision for defence spending.

open image in gallery John Healey is the new chancellor ( Getty )

Ed Miliband

Mr Burnham has appointed Ed Miliband as foreign secretary, making him another key winner of Monday’s reshuffle. While it is not quite chancellor – a role that he missed out on amid speculation that appointing him to the Treasury could spook the markets – it is one of the four great offices of state and is a clear promotion for the left-wing energy secretary.

Earlier this week, The Independent reported that Mr Burnham is planning a major shake-up of the Foreign Office, which is expected to include a roadmap to return the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of GDP on international aid and giving Mr Miliband explicit permission to prioritise tackling climate goals through the department.

open image in gallery Ed Miliband has been appointed to the Foreign Office ( Reuters )

Louise Haigh

Louise Haigh, who was forced to resign as transport secretary after it emerged she pleaded guilty to a fraud offence a decade ago, has been brought back into government as First Secretary of State, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster and minister for the Cabinet Office. The role puts her at the heart of Mr Burnham’s government, a move which comes as no surprise given she has been planning Mr Burnham’s ascent to power since last year.

For the latest political headlines delivered straight to your inbox, 

Angela Rayner

Nearly one year after she was forced to resign over her tax affairs, Angela Rayner has returned to the frontline of government as housing secretary. In the role, she will champion two of Andy Burnham’s key missions – devolution and building more council houses.

Once dubbed Labour’s Red Queen, she had left the same role in Sir Keir Starmer’s cabinet last September, as well as stepping down from her jobs as Labour’s deputy leader and deputy prime minister. The Ashton-under-Lyne MP has since been cleared of any wrongdoing by HMRC.

open image in gallery Angela Rayner has returned to her role as housing secretary ( PA )

She was spotted meeting with Mr Burnham in Greater Manchester earlier this year, in a sign she was willing to back his bid for No 10. A socialist, Ms Rayner championed Labour’s workers’ rights package in her previous cabinet role.

Alex Norris

Alex Norris, a fairly unknown face in the Labour government, has been promoted to justice secretary, replacing David Lammy. He was previously a junior minister in the Home Office and has not held a cabinet position before.

Losers

Rachel Reeves

Rachel Reeves is a key loser of Monday’s reshuffle, announcing in the afternoon that she will be leaving government. Posting to social media, Ms Reeves said it was the "privilege of my life to serve as the chancellor”.

While allies of the former chancellor have claimed she was offered a “big job” in government but decided to decline it, rather than being sacked, it is highly unlikely she would have been offered a role as significant as chancellor.

However, there was some good news for the Reeves family, with her sister Ellie Reeves being promoted to Attorney General – the chief legal adviser to the government.

open image in gallery David Lammy and Rachel Reeves have left the cabinet ( PA )

Lord Hermer

Sir Keir Starmer’s attorney general Lord Richard Hermer – a key ally of the former PM – confirmed he is leaving the cabinet, saying he will support Andy Burnham’s Labour government from the backbenches.

Lord Hermer has a long-standing personal relationship with Sir Keir, with the pair working together at Doughty Street Chambers together from 1996.

But he became a lightning rod for criticism during the Starmer government, with the Tories accusing him of conflicts of interest as a result of some of the clients he represented during his 20-year career as a barrister. He was also criticised by those within Labour for supposedly blocking legislative progress.

Yvette Cooper

Yvette Cooper has lost out in Mr Burnham’s reshuffle, being moved from the Foreign Office to the Department for Health and Social Care, meaning she is no longer in one of the great offices of state, having been both home secretary and foreign secretary under Sir Keir.

David Lammy

As Sir Keir’s deputy prime minister, David Lammy was, unsurprisingly, closely bound up with the last government. He has now paid the price for it, becoming another casualty of Mr Burnham’s purge of Starmer loyalists.

Darren Jones

Likewise, Starmer ally Darren Jones confirmed on Monday afternoon that Mr Burnham had called to tell him he “won’t be a part of his new cabinet”.

Mr Jones’s sacking came as no surprise given he was closely linked to Sir Keir, and – as chief secretary to the prime minister – was so often sent out to defend the government's mistakes.

open image in gallery Darren Jones was often sent out to defend the government’s mistakes ( Getty )

Steve Reed

Housing secretary Steve Reed was one of the first to announce his plans to leave the government, taking a swipe at disloyalty in the Starmer administration.

“Keir Starmer showed me loyalty by appointing me to his cabinet. I make no apology for returning that loyalty. It’s what is expected of functioning teams, and I hope those who did not show loyalty to Keir will now show it to you”, he said.

“I’m proud I acted with integrity at every step over the turbulent last few months.”

Peter Kyle

Peter Kyle, the former business secretary, is understood to have been sacked by Mr Burnham, leaving government on Monday. While he was loyal to the former prime minister, he was also seen as a strong performer in government, meaning his sacking came as somewhat of a surprise.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

News.title: How to have the perfect holiday in France’s gastronomic capital
News.content:
Calling all bon vivants. This is your city. Within seconds of tucking into a traditional andouillette (tripe sausage) or modern vegetarian cuisine in a jam-packed bistro, admiring fine art in a Renaissance abbey, or getting delightfully lost in a traboule (secret passageway) used by 19th-century silk weavers, you’ll quickly realise that Lyon is a city that knows how to live well.

Enthralling, cinematic and richly storied, after living here for 10 years, I still find myself being surprised by a walled garden I never knew, a fresque (wall mural) suddenly popping up on a riverfront wall, a new museum or river boat route.

Street-smart Romans first spotted the city’s extraordinary topography, founding Lugdunum (Lyon’s predecessor) in 43BC on the sunny slopes of Fourvière. And to this day, this basilica-crowned hill above Lyon’s quaint Unesco-listed Old Town (Vieux Lyon) is the perfect perch for clocking the mighty Rhône and Saône rivers that wend their way so gracefully through the centre.

The city’s quays, landscaped with peaceful water gardens and floating bars, buzz night and day – while culture lovers can explore a bounty of museums. Then there’s the gastronomy: among France’s finest, thanks to the unfaltering creativity and sass of city chefs, both past and present.

News.title: The 16 best things to do in Lyon
News.content:
Few dedicated foodies make the pilgrimage to Lyon without dining once chez Paul Bocuse, be it at the late chef’s mythical, out-of-town gastronomic temple in Collonges-au-Mont d’Or (which lost one of its three stars in 2020, having held three since 1965) or at the more affordable Comptoir Paul Bocuse inside landmark covered market Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse. Across the street, admire a larger-than-life portrait of the iconic chef, frescoed onto the side of a building. Inside the market, the moules glacées (cold mussel ‘soup’) at oyster and shellfish specialist Maison Merle and a gooey round of Saint Marcellin cheese from Fromagerie La Mère Richard are other local legends. Avoid buying fruit and veg here unless you have to – weekly outdoor food markets elsewhere in the city are cheaper.

To sample future talent in the Lyonnais kitchen, mingle with students over lunch, dinner or drinks and live music at La Commune – an innovative food court that hosts chefs aspiring to open their own restaurant in Lyon. Resident chefs cook up a storm at La Commune for maximum six months, meaning an ever-changing rollcall of epicurean excitement at this unique culinary incubator.

To extend the experience further afield, consider a road trip along a section of the Vallée de la Gastronomie, stretching 620km (385 miles). In Lyon, the gourmet route delves into the secrets behind chef Joseph Viola’s award-winning duck foie gras and sweetbread pâté en croûte (think French-posh pork pie) and the city’s distinctive offal-based bouchon (Lyonnais bistro) cuisine.
