Sports.title: JEFF POWELL MBE: Why unapologetic imposter Lionel Messi is now not even in the top five players of all time - and will forever be tainted as the leader of Argentina's brutes in ugliest World Cup final ever
Sports.content:
An image of the real greatest footballer of all time flickered briefly across the stadium with no proper name before the team captained by the imposter to that throne desecrated his beautiful game. Pele, from wherever he was watching, will have been as tortured as the rest of us by the ghastly possibility of Argentina slithering to World Cup victory on penalties after kicking more Spaniards than they did footballs. Brazil’s maestro of the most glorious football ever played, along with hundreds of millions of us who love this game, was spared that obscenity by a solitary goal scored by a Spanish substitute in extra time. Nor will Pele have been as forgiving of Lionel Messi’s part in that looming travesty as all those who have casually mis-proclaimed their darling little Leo as the most talented player ever to walk God’s hallowed turf. With the emphasis on walk. And neither will he have been impressed by the armbanded standard-bearer for the ugliest losers in World Cup history. Especially not as Messi sat shedding tears for his men’s brutish failure to defend their championship. Instead of crying for Argentina and himself, he should have wept for the infamy of the team under his charge. From Messi there has not been one syllable of apology for the thuggery which ruined the principal showpiece for the game which has enriched him beyond Croesus. Not one word of regret for his disgruntled brethren instigating the brawl which disgraced their hour of defeat. No hint of recognition for reducing this nasty, tedious game to the bottom of the list of the 13 World Cup finals which have come under my scrutiny. Lionel Messi shed tears for his men’s brutish failure to defend their championship. Instead of crying for Argentina and himself, he should have wept for the infamy of the team under his charge, writes Jeff Powell There was no hint of recognition for reducing this nasty, tedious game to the bottom of the list of the 13 World Cup finals which have come under my scrutiny MY UPDATED TOP 10 FOOTBALLERS OF ALL TIME 1. Pele Brazil 2. Diego Maradona Argentina 3. Garrincha Brazil 4. Johan Cruyff Netherlands 5. Alfredo Di Stefano Spain 6. Lionel Messi Argentina 7. Ferenc Puskas Hungary 8. Cristiano Ronaldo Portugal 9. John Charles Wales 10. George Best Northern Ireland To think, furthermore, that I was once seduced by his natural-born skills into elevating Messi to third in my ranking of the best in the anthology of football. We all make mistakes. Those revised rankings accompany this verdict on FIFA’s elongated tournament of mixed blessings. Along with little Leo clinging on to a place in my forever best world Xl. Just about. Although he was on the brink of deletion at the end of Sunday’s final to which his only contribution was to lob a hopeful cross-cum-shot onto the roof of the Spanish goal netting. That carefully curated image was not helped, either, by Messi doing precious little in the semi-final before Thomas Tuchel sounded England’s retreat into suicidal defence of a one-goal lead. A lot of reputations were damaged in this ever-lasting tournament. To suggest that Tuchel should escape the hardest judgement because England won a ten-goal so-called thriller against France in that spurious run-out for third place only handicaps any hope of recovery. That was a Mickey Mouse coconut shy of a match which France threw away by not turning up for the first half, although they partially redeemed themselves by running riot through Tuchel’s wonky England defence after the interval. Also exposed was this manager’s stubbornness in not selecting England’s most exciting player, Bukayo Saka, before they were knocked out. Even though the Arsenal forward had declared himself fully fit. With the FA further hog-tied after rushing an extension of Tuchel’s contract to the home Euros two years from now, they are condemning England to stagnation. As Brazil, Germany, France, Argentina, especially Italy and Spain as well as Argentina begin a four-year recycling programme of head coaches as well as players towards the next World Cup, so England will lag two years behind. Trapped in their Tuchel syndrome. If it carries on like this, stand by for another 60 years of depression. Ominously, also, the gap is closing fast between the old-guard masters of Europe and South America and the uprising of African, Asian and Caribbean football. Witness Morocco, Egypt, Cape Verde, Senegal, Ivory Coast, DR Congo and Curacao coming close to springing a mass upset here. To think that I was once seduced by his natural-born skills into elevating Messi to third in my ranking of the best in the anthology of football. We all make mistakes DR Congo came ever so close to causing a huge upset against England in the last 32

Your browser does not support iframes.

Pele had predicted the time was fast approaching when an African team would win the World Cup. This is coming closer and closer as more and more talents from the continent garner experience in the major European leagues. The greatest one’s forecast is not beyond realisation in 2030, even though Spain in their dedicated and organised development of a winning style of football will again be the team to beat. Especially since they will be co-hosts. Meanwhile this country of ours which gave the greatest of all games to the world trundles along, with the blinkered moguls of the Premier League at the wheel. Even as their clubs splurge hundreds of millions of pounds on domestic players of limited promise. If England learned one thing from this tournament, it is that the likes of Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice are not worth nine-figure fees. Not close. If the Premier League was taught one lesson, it is that the UFC cage-wrestling with which Arsenal won the title last season will no longer be tolerated by referees. It is an ill World Cup wind which brings no such consolations. Although 2026 in all its expansionist corporate greed, half-time grovelling to yawn-inducing musical celebrities and suspicions of favouritism has come close to bringing down the Infantino empire. As well as England.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson recalls spending 'a night on the piano' with Kevin Keegan just weeks after his infamous 'I would love it if we beat them' rant - when he bumped into his old rival at a bar
Sports.content:
Sir Alex Ferguson recalls spending 'a night on the piano' with Kevin Keegan just weeks after his infamous 'I would love it if we beat them' rant - when he bumped into his old rival at a bar

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Sir Alex Ferguson has revealed he enjoyed a 'great night' with his old rival Kevin Keegan shortly after the former Newcastle manager's infamous 'I would love it if we beat them' outburst during the 1996 Premier League title race.

Newcastle and England legend Keegan passed away aged 75 on Monday after a short battle with illness, having been diagnosed with stage four stomach cancer in January and admitted to hospital with abdominal problems.

Bryan Robson, Graeme Souness and Michael Owen are among those who have written heartfelt tributes about Keegan for Daily Mail Sport, paying homage to the warm, kind and immensely talented former player and manager whose passing has left the football world in mourning.

And even Ferguson, whose fierce rivalry with Keegan defined the dramatic 1995-96 Premier League title race, had only warm words for his old adversary as he fondly recalled the 'great night' they shared just weeks after Manchester United pipped Newcastle to the crown.

Keegan and Ferguson's rivalry reached its defining moment in April 1996, when Newcastle's then manager delivered one of the most iconic post-match interviews in Premier League history, emotionally shouting down the microphone: 'I would love it if we beat them. Love it.'

Sir Alex Ferguson has revealed he had a 'great night' with Newcastle legend Kevin Keegan (left) shortly after their rivalry reached boiling point during the 1996 Premier League title race

Keegan delivered the infamous 'I would love it if we beat them' rant in response to Ferguson's mind games - but just weeks later enjoyed a 'night on the piano' with the ex-Man United boss

Speaking on Track Radio on Tuesday, Ferguson said: 'That was Kevin's emotions. He was all emotion in a lot of his job and he brought that emotion to the team too. They played for Kevin Keegan, there's no question about that.

'The interesting thing about that outburst from Kevin, about two weeks after the season had finished I was playing at Wentworth golf club with two of my friends and the barman said there was a great bar up the road with nice food.

'So we went up there and who walks in, Kevin Keegan. And we spent the rest of the night on the piano. The great thing about him - he held no grudges. That was a fantastic quality he had. We had a great night.

'You would always find whatever happened previous weeks, that was soon forgotten. I really respected him for that.'

Keegan's 'love it' explosion occurred after Newcastle triumphed 1-0 over Leeds to keep their fading title hopes alive, having previously held a 12-point advantage over Manchester United at one stage in the season.

In the build-up to the game, Ferguson suggested that other teams played harder against the Red Devils than they did against Newcastle, prompting Keegan - who had spent months trying to ignore the Scot's psychological tactics - to snap during a live Sky Sports interview.

Visibly angry, he stared into the camera and launched into his famous rant, insisting Newcastle would fight until the end before delivering the iconic line.

Although Newcastle won their remaining games, Manchester United held their nerve to clinch the Premier League title, and the speech became one of the defining moments of the decade.

Sports.title: MICHAEL OWEN: Why Argentina's awful World Cup final performance fills me with England regret - we DO have the players to win a major tournament
Sports.content:
MICHAEL OWEN: Why Argentina's awful World Cup final performance fills me with England regret - we DO have the players to win a major tournament

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Not many would have thought Spain would win the World Cup without Lamine Yamal being the star of the tournament. That they did shows exactly why they are the right champions.

Spain don’t have the depth of superstar talent of some other countries. The best collection of players belongs to France. I’d say England have just as good as, if not better than Spain.

But Spain were by miles the best team. Everything you are coached as a player, they execute that as individuals and then collectively. The movement, the one-touch football, the courage to play through pressure, the calmness in possession. It was a masterclass.

I know some will look at the final being goalless after 90 minutes and feel short-changed, especially with expectation high on the back of the last World Cup final. But from a performance perspective, Spain were outstanding. They barely gave Argentina a kick and did not concede a shot in 90 minutes. If you’re a Spanish supporter, at no stage did you think you were not going to win.

It’s the mark of a great team when you do not have to rely on one or two players, and you can make six substitutions and it feels like you are watching the same side that started the game.

Spain had identity. They had class. They had total confidence in what they were doing. I’m happy we got the deserved winners.

Spain showed throughout the World Cup why they were exactly the right team to win it

AND THE RIGHT PLAYER OF THE TOURNAMENT

My player of the World Cup was Rodri - and the organisers agreed. I think we can safely say he's back to his absolute best.

It's taken him a while after such a serious knee injury, but over the last few weeks he's looked like the Rodri we've come to expect. For me, he's head and shoulders above every other holding midfielder in world football.

People talk about his passing and vision, but it's his bravery that really stands out. He always wants the ball, even in tight areas, and he has the quality to dictate the game. He's not just a sitting midfielder, either. Spain trust him to get forward, influence attacks and play higher up the pitch when the game demands it.

Wherever he is, Rodri makes everyone around him better. Only the very, very best can do that.

MY ENGLAND REGRET

Argentina’s awful performance in the final was a frustrating reminder that it should have been England. They did not beat us in the semi-final, we beat ourselves.

If you go back to the start of tournament, I was very positive about England’s chances. I thought we had the players in attack to hurt teams. Everything I saw of us in North America reinforced that. Jude Bellingham was sensational.

What concerned me was Mexico and the euphoric reaction to what was, in reality, a fortunate escape against an average team. That set the players’ mindset to survival and, when England went 1-0 up against Argentina, they reverted to it. It was a disaster. It was a waste.

That half hour apart, this was a positive tournament for England. There was nothing to stop us getting to the final other than our own misplaced belief of what was needed to see out that game. Would we have beaten Spain? I still think they would have edged it. But we would have given them a better game than Argentina, if we played with the right approach and trusted our ability, like we saw against France in the third-place match.

That is the regret, but it should also give us encouragement. We have the players to win major tournaments, I am convinced of that.

Argentina's awful performance in the final reminded us that it should have been England there

Argentina did not beat England in the semi-finals, but the Three Lions rather beat themselves

VAR…

Without VAR, Argentina would be uncontrollable!

The technology took its usual bashing during the tournament, and much of the criticism was over the top and short-sighted.

But the one thing this World Cup should remind everyone is that the presence of VAR is the unseen deterrent, a policing mechanism that is invaluable, if under-appreciated.

Imagine the tricks Argentina would pull if they thought there was a chance of getting away with more. They already constantly push the boundaries. It would be absolute carnage and the cheats would look to prosper.

Yes, we can work to improve the processes around it, and that is what we have to do, because the alternative is a scary thought. It would be chaos. Not convinced? Think Argentina!

FIFA…

The delayed kick-off for the final was unacceptable and spoke to a lot of my gripes with changes FIFA have made to the World Cup.

Then we had the half-time interval, which felt like it went on forever. As a former player, I know that would disrupt your rhythm. Footballers have routines for refuelling, receiving information and preparing mentally to go again. Stretch that break out to 30 minutes and you're changing the nature of the contest.

I understand the final is a global event and fans have paid a fortune to be there, but the football has to come first. Everything else should work around the game, not the other way round.

The same goes for the water breaks we've seen throughout the tournament. Dealing with difficult conditions has always been part of elite football. It’s a challenge you have to overcome and the fitter teams thrive.

But if a drinks break has to happen, make it 30 seconds. Keep everyone on the pitch, get some kids to run on and hand out bottles and get on with the game. What I don't like is players wandering to the touchline, managers delivering team-talks and the entire flow of the match being interrupted. For me, it changes the game too much, and not for the better.

The half-time show felt like it went on forever and football has to come first at the World Cup

THE FUTURE OF THE WORLD CUP

The biggest success of this World Cup was also its biggest flaw.

I loved seeing new nations on the biggest stage. Countries like Cape Verde have captured the imagination and delivered new heroes. Those players will return home as legends. Football has reached more people than ever before and that's something to celebrate.

But it has come at a cost. I said before the tournament that the group stage would be pointless, and it was. The jeopardy just was not there. None of the teams eliminated were a shock. I was bored with a lot of it until we got to the knockout rounds.

My other frustration is what this expansion has done to the history books. Part of the fascination of the World Cup has always been comparing generations. Now, players have more games and, in many cases, against weaker opposition. Take Michael Olise breaking Pele's assist record. Olise had a brilliant tournament and deserves credit, but it's simply impossible to compare those achievements fairly anymore.

Now that FIFA has opened the door, I'd actually go one step further and expand to 64 nations. We need to remove the safety net of third-placed teams getting out of the group. It’s ridiculous.

When the jeopardy did return in the knockout rounds, we saw what a magnificent spectacle World Cup matches really are. We need to protect that.

Sports.title: Madeleine McCann’s brother Sean, 21, competing for Scotland in Commonwealth Games
Sports.content:
Madeleine McCann’s brother Sean, 21, competing for Scotland in Commonwealth Games

The Games, which take place in Glasgow from this Thursday until 2 August 2026, will mark Sean McCann's Commonwealth debut for Scotland

View Image (Image: Getty Images for Commonwealth Sport)

Madeleine McCann’s brother will take part in the Commonwealth Games after being selected to swim for Scotland. Sean McCann is getting ready to step out onto the global stage this week when the Games begin in Glasgow.

‌



Madeleine was three when she went missing from her family’s holiday apartment in Praia da Luz in southern Portugal on May 3 2007, shortly before her birthday. Sean was only two at the time, and his twin sister Amelie is also part of the team selected for the rescheduled and slimmed-down Games.

‌



According to Scottish Swimming, Sean will compete in the freestyle disciplines as he looks to qualify for Team GB and swim at the LA Olympics in 2028. Sean began competing aged eight and previously raced for Scotland at the Commonwealth Youth Games in Trinidad and Tobago in 2023 in the 400m and 1500m freestyle.

‌



And peaking about his competitive journey a few years ago on the Joe Humphries Memorial Trust website, he revealed “I started competitive sport when I was eight, joining Charnwood triathlon club.

“It was here that I discovered my passion for swimming and I joined Loughborough Town swimming club to increase the number of swim sessions I did per week. At the age of ten, I was selected to swim at City of Leicester and I have since gone on to win multiple county titles as well as becoming regional and National champion in my age group.

Article continues below

Josh Kerr slams 'appalling' prize money he receives for running the fastest mile ever READ MORE :

“In order to have achieved this, I have had to remain extremely dedicated, getting up at 4am multiple mornings each week to train, since the age of 11. I train nine times a week in the pool, as well as three gym sessions, totalling over 20 hours of training per week.

“I’m aiming to compete at the 2026 Commonwealth Games and also the 2028 Olympics in LA.”

It is not known if his parents Kate and Gerry McCann will be in attendance at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre during the 11-day event, which begins on Thursday.

Sports.title: Conor McGregor backed to fight again after latest injury setback
Sports.content:
Conor McGregor backed to fight again after latest injury setback

The former two-division UFC champion tore his ACL against Max Holloway at UFC 329, but a UFC legend has backed McGregor to make yet another return

View Image Conor McGregor after his loss to Max Holloway at UFC 329 (Image: Cooper Neill)

Conor McGregor has been backed to fight again despite tearing his ACL against Max Holloway.

‌



The 38-year-old ended a five-year hiatus at UFC 329 against the former featherweight champion, but his comeback ended in defeat after he injured his knee just seconds into the contest in Las Vegas. The bout was waved off after just 69 seconds, handing McGregor yet another loss.

‌



He has since revealed he tore his ACL and damaged his meniscus, but is targeting a return to action next summer. Former UFC bantamweight champion Dominick Cruz is adamant the Dublin scrapper has both the resources and motivation necessary to make another comeback.

‌



"He has the physical therapy at the performance institute, he has all the best doctors and money in the world now,” Cruz said during a recent appearance on the Ariel Helwani Show. “I think he's going to stay in the testing pool this time. I don't know, last time he didn't. I had to stay, I chose to stay in, we'll see what he does with that. But with all the access to the things he has, he absolutely can come back.”

FOLLOW OUR FIGHTING FB PAGE! Latest boxing and MMA news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Conor McGregor demands Max Holloway fight result is changed READ MORE :

Conor McGregor secures new role days after UFC disaster READ MORE :

McGregor has been heavily criticised by fans since UFC 329, but the Irishman is convinced of another comeback - as is Cruz. “And I think that he definitely will be back. I really do because of the injury and because everybody got that taste and that feeling of showing up, and everybody doubts him right now, and everybody's kind of upset,” he said. “A lot of people are upset.

“Everybody wants a comeback story so no matter what anybody says they're going to watch because everybody loves a comeback story and he's entertaining so the build-up to that will be great.” The American added: “But I think he'll definitely do it. I think that feeling he had that night (at UFC 329) will resonate with him, he's going to hold on to it tight and get through and use it to get through this rehab. He has all the access he needs.”

Conor McGregor issues three-word update on career after injury nightmare READ MORE :

Conor McGregor's wife breaks silence after injury wrecked comeback READ MORE :

In a recent post uploaded to social media, the former two-division UFC champion provided a major update regarding his injury, stating: "It was the ACL and meniscus. It is the same injury as the first Holloway fight, only this time the opposite leg. Quite shocking. I returned to competition within nine months to fight Diego Brandao back then.

Article continues below

"With today’s regenerative medicine advancements and improved training methods it is well within my realm to return by next summer. I am walking without a crutch. I did leg extension machine work the other day to no issue. So I can walk without aid, and activate my quad under resistance. All very positive.

"I am at maximum discipline and have maintained it fully since the bout. I wonder was I saved from something worse here. I believe so. I would have attended the after party as “the man” and who knows then. I believe I was saved."

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua sent brutal warning ahead of boxing comeback
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua sent brutal warning ahead of boxing comeback

Anthony Joshua will make a stunning return to the ring on Saturday night, but a heavyweight rival has sent a vicious warning ahead of the Brit's meeting with Kristian Prenga

View Image Joshua will face Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia on July 25 (Image: Getty Images)

Kristian Prenga has been backed to repeat what Andy Ruiz did and shock the world by beating Anthony Joshua on Saturday night.

‌



That is according to Prenga's sparring partner, Brandon Moore - who envisions a stunning upset in Saudi Arabia. Joshua and Prenga will meet in a heavyweight showdown this weekend, and providing 'AJ' comes away unscathed - he will then take on long-time rival Tyson Fury later this year.

‌



Joshua, 36, was last seen in the ring back in December when he knocked out Jake Paul in a rather uninspiring Miami melee. Just days on from his win over the YouTuber-turned-boxer, 'AJ' was involved in a tragic car crash which claimed the lives of close friends Latif Ayodele and Sina Ghami.

‌



Many wondered whether the Brit would fight again, but it was not long before he got the itch to return to the squared-circle. While several are expecting an easy night at the office for the Brit this weekend, Moore believes that might not necessarily be the case.

FOLLOW OUR FIGHTING FB PAGE! Latest boxing and MMA news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

Barry Hearn gives clear verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight collapsing READ MORE :

Professional heavyweight brawler Moore can see a major shock, similar to the Ruiz fight. Joshua's first defeat came against Ruiz back in 2019 in a huge upset in New York that saw him lose his world titles. But just a few months later, 'AJ' would go on to get his revenge.

‌



"[Prenga] looks really, really, really good in sparring right now. It's going to be a pretty entertaining fight," Moore told Sky Sports. "I think that he has a pretty good shot of beating him, and I think he's bigger than Joshua. Joshua just has a muscular physique, but Prenga's a bigger man.

"It's going to be a tough fight, but I think he can catch [Joshua] the same way Andy Ruiz did. This is AJ's first fight back. AJ's had a lot of stuff going on in his life - nothing but respect to AJ, but when you're getting back into the ring, you haven't fought in a while, that ring rust is real. This is not a small thing - everybody's going to be watching."

Oleksandr Usyk branded 'average' after retirement decision READ MORE :

He added: "I told [Prenga] that he has the opportunity of a lifetime. He has the opportunity that I would wish for. AJ is a great fighter, and he's done amazing things in the sport of boxing.

‌



"But [Prenga] has the opportunity, you know, to be in the names of people that have beaten future Hall of Famers. Everything has to be aligned. He has to do everything perfectly."

Joshua, though, is hoping to avoid a seismic upset and book himself a date with Fury before the end of the year. "I know exactly what I need to do. I’m not worried about respecting this particular opponent, but when I look at myself, I know I’m going to deliver," he said ahead of the fight.

"This is my division. On July 25 in Jeddah, the best man will win. I’m going to go in there and show how good I am. I’m going to show him my class, my skill and my boxing IQ and see if he can survive my power as well."

Sports.title: Jockey William Buick banned for eight days after being blamed for causing horse stumble
Sports.content:
Jockey William Buick banned for eight days after being blamed for causing horse stumble

The Godolphin stable jockey was found guilty of careless riding after finishing second in the fifth race during the evening meeting at Windsor on Monday

View Image William Buick: suspended at Windsor (Image: PA)

Star jockey William Buick has been banned for eight days after he was blamed for causing another horse to stumble.

‌



The Godolphin stable jockey is rarely in trouble with the stewards but he was called to inquiry on Monday after an incident during the fifth race on the Windsor card.

‌



Buick rode the winner of the third race when the Charlie Appleby-trained Castlemont captured the 1m2f maiden race at odds of 15-8. In race five he was riding the John & Thady Gosden-trained Sunshine Star, a 5-2 chance for the 1m2f fillies’ handicap. The pair finished second, beaten three quarters of a length behind the Oisin Murphy-ridden Dream Camp, trained by Andrew Balding.

‌



But the stewards quizzed Buick about his riding of his filly with the Racing Post close-up commenting stating, “Prominent, waiting for room and lost position over 2f out, switched left and hampered rival over 1f out, ran on inside final furlong, no extra towards finish, did well in the circumstances.”

The analysis said Sunshine Star “could have won on another day”, adding, “She’s well up to winning something similar”.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

The inquiry considered the incident of interference around the one furlong pole which involved Sunshine Star, the unplaced Crystal Pier, ridden by Rossa Ryan. Saffie Osborne was also interviewed but found not to be involved.

The report concluded: “Buick was suspended for 8 days for careless riding as he angled his mount left-handed to continue his run when insufficiently clear of CRYSTAL PIER (IRE), causing Ryan to clip heels and stumble badly.”

Article continues below

The suspension will run from August 3 to 10 inclusive and fortunately for Buick falls either side of Glorious Goodwood and the York Ebor Festival. He would miss the Shergar Cup meeting at Ascot had he been involved.

Sports.title: Beverley race meeting abandoned after becoming latest to find ‘hole in track’
Sports.content:
Beverley race meeting abandoned after becoming latest to find ‘hole in track’

After similar disruption at Cheltenham and Haydock this year, racing was halted after just three races when an inspection confirmed the ground was unsuitable to continue

View 2 Images A hole was discovered under the stalls at Beverley (Image: Racing TV)

Beverley has become the latest British racecourse forced to abandon racing after the discovery of a ‘hole in the track’.

‌



The popular Yorkshire course was in the midst of staging a six race evening meeting on Monday which had to be scrapped with only half the races having been run. The racecourse stewards called an inspection after the starters raised concerns about the state of the surface in the area of the 7f start.

‌



The stewards report said: “The inspection confirmed that unsuitable ground had been identified underneath the starting stalls and on the racing line. Riders, PJ McDonald, Barry McHugh and Cieren Fallon; trainers, Ruth Carr, Nigel Tinkler and Lawrence Mullaney; The Clerk of the Course and the Veterinary Officer were interviewed.

‌



Ascot makes King George the richest race in Britain by lifting 2027 value to £2.5 million READ MORE :

“Having considered the evidence, the Stewards ordered racing to be abandoned.”

Beverley is now the third racecourse to encounter problems with its track. Haydock has not staged any racing since May following the discovery of an elbow-deep hole in the surface at its Temple Stakes meeting while Cheltenham’s Festival Trials Day fixture in January was disrupted when a hole opened up in the straight. Both tracks subsequently cancelled fixtures to carry out remedial work.

View 2 Images Racing at Beverley was called off due to a hole in the track (Image: PA)

‌



At Beverley on Monday the horses for the next race were at the start when the meeting was called off.

Racing TV presenter Chris Dixon said: “That hole in the track which is right at the stalls position for the 7f races is significant and nothing can be done about it in the short term.”

Pundit Adele Mulrennan said: “I think they’ve thought of numerous ideas but couldn’t get anything to work. They can’t move the stalls because of the fence. They have a gap to get in for each start and you have the fact there is still a big hole there.

Article continues below

Content cannot be displayed without consent

“It’s lucky they’ve found it because it’s quite a big hole. It goes from as wide as two stalls. It’s stall three and stall four that it’s affecting. It’s just disappointing.”

Beverley said it would make a compensatory payment to owners of horses due to run in the last three races while also providing complimentary tickets to racegoers to its season finale on September 22.

Sports.title: Barry Hearn gives clear verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight collapsing
Sports.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Barry Hearn gives clear verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight collapsing

Barry Hearn has delivered his verdict on whether Anthony Joshua's proposed fight against Tyson Fury could collapse, with both boxers in action this weekend

View 3 Images Barry Hearn has delivered his verdict on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury collapsing (Image: Getty Images)

Anthony Joshua's proposed heavyweight fight against Tyson Fury is still expected to GO AHEAD later this year, according to Matchroom's Barry Hearn. Joshua and Fury are due to clash in an all-British boxing showdown in November, providing both win their warm-up bouts this weekend.

‌



Fury, 37, is scheduled to go up against Mariusz Wach on Friday, with Joshua, 36, facing Kristian Penga the following evening. Should both win - which is backed as short as 1/16 with the bookmakers – a mammoth multi-million pound fight is poised to take place, though a final venue is yet to be decided.

‌



Although there is still an outside chance of the fight collapsing, boxing promoter Hearn is confident that both Joshua and Fury will come through their warm-up bouts unscathed. This is despite Prenga's team claiming that Joshua has made a "big mistake" by fighting the Albanian in Saudi Arabia.

‌



Guide to the 2026 Commonwealth Games is on sale now READ MORE :

Anthony Joshua undercard finally revealed ahead of comeback fight READ MORE :

When asked if the fight might not go ahead, Hearn, 78, told Mirror Sport: "No. I don't know if you've ever been hit on the chin by someone who weighs 17st... I haven't, and I don't want to. There's always the potential of a banana skin in boxing. History tells us that. I think it's unlikely in both cases, of course.

"But Anthony Joshua, to his credit, he's not thinking beyond Saturday. He knows what's at stake here, a fight that he's wanted for 10 years has been signed for. All they have to do is deliver their respective victories, I believe that is a huge odds-on favourite.

"Kristian Prenga's team, of course, whilst they're entitled to their opinion, have absolutely no idea what they're talking about. They've never been in with an animal like Anthony Joshua, especially in his [Oleksandr] Usyk training regime that he's now adopted and embraced and realised that he thought he was doing the best training that he could ever do, and now he's seen another level, which has inspired him, which I like.

‌



View 3 Images Anthony Joshua is on "another level", according to Barry Hearn (Image: Getty Images)

"I like people that are ready to embrace something new. So no, if there's always a banana skin, it's unlikely, and I can't wait for Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua. It's been a long time in the making."

While the long-awaited mega-fight has been discussed for years, Joshua and Fury have never fought in a professional boxing match before. Should the clash go ahead as planned, it's poised to be one of the biggest boxing has EVER seen, according to Hearn, alongside the 'Rumble in the Jungle' and 'Thriller in Manila' where both were won by the legendary late Muhammed Ali.

‌



Hearn added: "Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua would be... I'm trying to think what would be bigger. You're at Muhammad Ali, the Rumble in the Jungle. You're at the thriller in Manila with Frazier and Ali. You're at that level, that sort of marketplace. It's creme de la creme, but in today's world, it's on Netflix, the Tyson Fury fight.

View 3 Images Tyson Fury is set to go up against Anthony Joshua later this year (Image: Richard Pelham/Getty Images for Netflix)

"It's just a massive global event. I mean, the big global events get bigger and bigger. We've just seen the World Cup possibly. Forget Argentina because they weren't my favourite team there. But there's a massive, massive commercial enterprise beyond their normal imagination, and Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua is exactly the same."

Article continues below

Watford-born Joshua, who last fought against YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul in December 2025, has an imperious record of 29 wins and four losses across his professional. Meanwhile, Fury's most recent fight was against Arslanbek Makhmudov in April 2026 and has lost just ONCE across his 38 professional bouts.

Both Joshua and Fury as seen as two of Britain's greatest-ever heavyweight fighters, with both former world champions, making November's proposed fight a must-not-miss should it go ahead as scheduled.

Sports.title: Three things the Premier League must steal from World Cup 2026 and four things it must ditch
Sports.content:
The 2026 World Cup will go down in history as football's ultimate petri dish. With 48 teams scattered across three time zones, FIFA treated the tournament as a grand laboratory for new rules, hyper-commercialised entertainment and ground-breaking broadcast technology.

Some of it was an absolute triumph that enhanced the viewing experience immensely. Other elements were bloated, plastic and fundamentally detached from what makes football the beautiful game.

With the World Cup now in the rear-view mirror and the domestic season approaching, Mirror Football chief writer John Cross has sifted through the wreckage of the summer's experiments to highlight four things we must throw straight into the bin, and three things the Premier League needs to steal immediately.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



All 37 World Cup pundits ranked as BBC vs ITV winner decided and unexpected star emerges READ MORE :

John Cross’ alternative World Cup awards as FIFA bosses called out for huge mistake READ MORE :

THINGS THAT MUST BE DITCHED

Hydration breaks

What started as a genuine medical necessity in extreme climates has officially mutated into an unwanted tactical timeout. Cross is entirely clear: the corporate-friendly pauses have no place in a sport that relies on continuous momentum.

"Ditch them," says Cross on the final episode of the Make Football Great Again podcast. "They're just not for me." While stopping the clock might make sense in the scorching summer heat of Texas, trying to translate it to the domestic game is a laughable concept. Can you imagine trying to enforce a mandatory fluid break during a freezing, wind-swept January Monday night fixture in the north of England? Get rid of it.

View 6 Images Hydration breaks were unpopular with fans, but many teams used them to their advantage throughout the tournament (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Half time shows

Football is a sport rooted in subculture and raw terrace passion, not heavily choreographed corporate pop music. The attempt to inject American-style stadium entertainment into the intermission of the world's biggest match fell entirely flat for traditionalists.

‌



Cross was left thoroughly unimpressed by the plastic spectacle: "Ditch it. I'm kind of a bit meh. I don't care, but then basically, personally, I would ditch it... Those bizarre choreographed shows didn't really work for me, so generally ditch."

Football fans use halftime to dissect tactics, complain about the referee, and queue for a pie - not to watch a Hollywood stage production.

View 6 Images The World Cup half time show was a big bust (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

The 48-team format

The maths simply didn't work. By expanding the tournament to 48 teams, the opening round felt less like an elite global showcase and more like an endless, low-stakes warm-up where practically everyone qualified for the knockout rounds.

‌



"I hate the group stage and the lack of jeopardy," Cross explains. "It's embarrassing and it's just silly and it's just not what we want. You've got to go back to kind of 32 or the whole hog can go 64."

If the tournament is going to expand, it needs a format that creates immediate drama, rather than a endless safety net that dilutes the opening weeks.

The 'Snicko' ball sensor

Technology is supposed to eliminate controversy, but the microchip sensors embedded inside the tournament match balls only succeeded in muddying the waters, leaving fans and pundits entirely unconvinced by the digital readouts.

"Well, I didn't like it," Cross admits, recalling the highly contentious decision to rule Croatia's goal against Portugal out. "Because basically, you cannot tell me that it helped... No chance. Absolutely no chance."

‌



When technology starts contradicting the plain evidence of the human eye, it creates confusion rather than clarity. Hoof it into Row Z.

View 6 Images 'Snicko' technology failed to impress - and work properly! (Image: BBC)

THINGS THE PREMIER LEAGUE MUST ADOPT

Momentum graphics

Television coverage took a massive leap forward this summer with data overlays that actually added context to the unfolding match, tracking the shifting tides of dominance in real-time.

"I loved [the momentum graphics]. Absolutely loved them," Cross enthuses. "Keep, love that. I think it was a genuine, interesting stat that did generate, and it was fascinating."

‌



In a league as frantic and unpredictable as the Premier League, giving viewers at home a visual representation of which team is building sustained pressure would be an incredible addition to standard punditry.

View 6 Images Momentum graphics were a big hit with viewers

The Mistaken Identity rule

VAR protocol remains a constant source of frustration in England, but the World Cup proved that safety-net rules can be introduced effectively to prevent catastrophic officiating blunders without slowing the game down.

"Yeah, I liked it," says Cross. "And I think that, yeah, there were a few bits and pieces that I quite liked on the VAR thing. You know, I think that I was positive about various bits and pieces that they've done. So I think generally, yes, keep."

‌



The Premier League desperately needs to streamline its video review processes, and adopting this common-sense approach would erase a major refereeing headache.

View 6 Images VAR intervened for mistaken identity for the first time in history following a recent FIFA rule change (Image: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images))

The ban on covering the mouth

The modern habit of players shielding their lips with their hands whenever they speak to an official or an opponent has long driven fans crazy. The tournament's attempt to clamp down on this insincere behaviour was a breath of fresh air.

"I'd like to keep that rule that you can't, but you have to do it across the board," Cross argues, insisting that domestic football must enforce it strictly to break the habit. "Look, we'd have a couple of early scares, but then basically, they'd soon learn. We all know why it was brought in. It was brought in for the very best and most important reasons... The players will quickly learn."

‌

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan

Semi-final: Italy vs Northern Ireland

Semi-final: Wales vs Bosnia and Herzegovina

Final: Wales/Bosnia and Herzegovina vs Italy/Northern Ireland - Tuesday, 7.45pm kick-off
