World.title: MORNING GLORY: America is winning its battle with Iran. It’s only a matter of time
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In the four months and three weeks since combat began with Iran, the United States has lost 17 or 18 of its warriors (with three or four killed over last weekend), with more than 420 others wounded.

Sixty Israelis have been killed. More than 100 Iraqis have died as a result of the conflict. Our allies in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have all suffered civilian deaths and every country in the region has taken significant damage to its infrastructure.

Iran has suffered military deaths in the thousands with many hundreds of civilians killed as well. The toll on the country’s infrastructure is massive — exponentially larger than that which it has inflicted on its neighbors in the region — with the highest estimates in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Iran’s conventional military has been shattered. Its missile and drone forces have been significantly damaged or expended. It is far, however, from being out of ordnance with which to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz or its neighbors.

US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM

Iran has avoided striking Israel during the most recent 10 days of combat as it fears the response of the Israeli Defense Forces. That is deterrence restored. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard is afraid to strike the Jewish State. Now it must be made afraid to shoot at Americans or at its Arab neighbors or international shipping.

The rump regime that remains appears to be a military dictatorship led by the 68-year-old commander-in-chief of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, Ahmad Vahidi, who came out of retirement to lead the military dictatorship after the opening strike on Iranian leaders killed scores of leading officials in the country.

The "official" successor to the killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei is his son Mostafa Khomeini, who has not been seen in public since the conflict began. Khamenei 2.0 is widely believed to have been seriously wounded in the opening strikes of the battle and has recently been reported to have been moved out of the country.

'WE WANT LAND INVASION': IRAN MOUTHPIECE TOUTS NEW MISSILE, BOASTS DECADES OF WAR PREP

The economy of Iran is in a shambles with the exchange rate of Iranian rials for U.S. dollars approaching 2 million to one. The United States Navy’s blockade of Iranian shipping is completely effective as to shipping, so Iran is again denied the most basic and essential revenue stream from the sale of oil via the oceans. Its imports must come from land or air.

The conflict could extend for months or even years as America’s blockade drives the Iranian economy deeper into the hole out of which it will take decades to climb once combat ends. The country’s nuclear program is indeed obliterated, and while the deep tunnels and caverns of Pickaxe Mountain remain a mystery to the U.S. the IRGC’s ability to "break out" to a nuclear weapon has been crushed. (The U.S. has not yet targeted Pickaxe, and may not be able to damage its deepest reaches.)

Once measured in weeks, Iran is now years and years away from a nuclear weapon, even if oil exports resumed in the future and the rump regime dedicated all of that revenue from the sale of oil to again pursue nuclear weapons.

STEVE FORBES URGES TRUMP TO KEEP THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ OPEN AT ALL COSTS

The cost of oil hovers above $80 a barrel across the world, 30% higher than when the battle began but significantly lower than the $126 a barrel cost reached in April. Workarounds via pipelines and the use of the southern shipping route through the Strait near Oman have kept the cost of oil from skyrocketing, and production worldwide has also stepped up in response to the off-and-on closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Whether President Donald Trump decides to escalate the strikes on Iran to include destruction of power plants and bridges that serve dual uses that include the Iranian military and the IRGC (legitimate targets under the laws of war) will be revealed in the days ahead.

Every lethal attack on Americans elicits from the United States extraordinary punishment on Iran. The cost to the American families bearing those losses of family is immeasurable and the U.S. is extracting a price after every deadly blow delivered by the Iranians in the ongoing effort to deter the fanatics.

The economy of Iran is in a shambles with the exchange rate of Iranian rials for U.S. dollars approaching 2 million to one.

That may be an unrealistic goal given the martyrdom ideology of the theocracy, but the original dictator of the Islamic Republic, Ayatollah Khomeini, drank "from the cup of poison" in 1988 and accepted what was essentially a defeat in the Iran-Iraq War of 1980-1988.

Vahidi is a veteran of that war. Perhaps the dictator will follow the original supreme leader’s example, and the advice of his civilian advisers, and the public faces of Iran who are believed by some to have grasped the scale of the defeat inflicted on Iran. The President of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, and its Foreign Minister, Seyed Abbas Araghchi, have almost no power over the dictator and his legions with the guns who murdered tens of thousands of Iranian citizens in January. But the civilians have hinted at the reality of a shattered country, and the crushed proxy armies in Gaza and Lebanon should also weigh on Vahidi. Does he want the IRGC to go the way of Hamas and Hezbollah?

Iran can have a ceasefire in hours if it stops firing on shipping and agrees to minimal steps like comprehensive inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency of its known nuclear weapons development sites plus Pickaxe Mountain.

It is irrational for the regime to continue to take the pounding it is receiving, and the fact that Israel has not been targeted in these past 10 days suggests that Vahidi has grasped the reality of his situation. He has been deterred from ordering strikes on Israel. The nightly pummeling by the United States presents Vahidi with only terrible choices aimed at deterring him from his current course.

Whatever he calculated about the cost to the world in oil prices or to Trump in political damage in November, he was not just wrong, but very wrong. Does he have the ability to see that as clearly as Khomeini did in 1988?

About 7.5 million Americans saw Christopher Nolan’s "The Odyssey" this weekend. The monumental cinematic reflection on the cost of war — the retelling of a story that has resonated down more than 2,700 years — still has the power to remind every viewer of the infinite price of battle for those who lose loved ones in the conflict.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

No American should want this combat to continue a day longer than it must. Trump certainly does not. The destruction of Iran’s military capabilities and its military-industrial complex is near complete. Its nuclear program is in ruins. The Iranian people will face a much weaker regime when next they rise up to demand freedom from the fanatics.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But as every member of the military will tell you, the enemy gets a say in when the fighting ends. The decisive victory of the American military won’t be concluded until Iran stops its aggression on international shipping. It may not do so for a long while yet. The "cup of poison" isn’t anything Vahidi wants to accept or the regime mouthpieces want to acknowledge. But President Trump is pursuing the right strategy to make its sipping inevitable.

America must honor its fallen and care for their families as well as the wounded and their families. But we pray for this spring and summer of war to end before the fall arrives. It was a necessary battle, and further devastation of Iran is not something the president or any American should want, but that choice is with Vahidi.

Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of " The Hugh Hewitt Show " heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. World.title: MIKE PENCE: Here's where we should look for the leadership America needs now more than ever
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One year ago, America lost one of the architects of the modern conservative movement. But if the past 12 months have taught us anything, it is that America needs Ed Feulner’s example now more than ever.

Dr. Ed Feulner never confused winning momentary political battles with securing long-term victory. While others chased headlines, Ed built institutions. While others measured success by the next election, Ed invested in the next generation. While others sought influence, Ed cultivated leaders who would carry the cause of freedom long after he was gone.

He understood that political victories come and go, but a movement grounded in principle can shape history for generations. That conviction transformed the conservative movement and our country.

MAJORITY LEADER THUNE: LINDSEY GRAHAM WAS THE GOP’S GLUE, BINDING US TOGETHER WITH COURAGE AND GRACE

As the founding president of the Heritage Foundation, Ed helped create an institution that brought conservative ideas out of the academy and into the halls of government. Years later, we were deeply honored when he joined the board of Advancing American Freedom to continue the principled fight for timeless conservative values. As always, Ed’s concern was preparing the next generation to stand up for freedom with courage and conviction.

One year later, his life offers a blueprint for the challenges we face today.

America stands at an extraordinary moment in history. As we celebrate our nation’s 250th anniversary, we also face profound challenges: restoring confidence in constitutional government, confronting the growing threat posed by Communist China, taming a runaway national debt, defending free enterprise from government encroachment and ensuring that America continues to lead the free world with confidence and strength.

These challenges require the same enduring truths that guided Ed throughout his remarkable life.

HERITAGE FOUNDATION FOUNDER EDWIN J. FEULNER DIES AT 83

In an age consumed by personalities, Ed reminded us that principles matter more. In a culture driven by instant gratification, he taught that lasting victories require patience and perseverance.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The greatest tribute we can pay Ed Feulner is not merely to remember him, but to emulate him. Let us recommit ourselves to the principles he championed. Let us strengthen the institutions that defend liberty. Let us raise up a new generation of courageous conservative leaders. And let us never lose confidence in the goodness of America or the timeless truths that have sustained our nation from the beginning.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

One year after his passing, America needs more leaders like Ed Feulner who believe that principles endure, institutions matter and freedom is always worth defending. If we carry that work forward with the same humility, courage and faith, then Ed’s greatest legacy will not simply be what he built in the past, but what we build tomorrow because of him.

AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US

The Bible tells us, "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Ed Feulner devoted his life to advancing that cause. One year after his passing, we honor his memory best not with our words alone, but with our resolve to continue the work to which he devoted his life, and which has helped preserve the liberty we so cherish.

World.title: U.S. military identifies soldiers killed in Iranian attack in Jordan
World.content:
The Defense Department on Monday released the names of two soldiers killed in Iranian strikes in Jordan, identifying them as 25-year-old Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii and 19-year-old Isabella Gonzales of Texas.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Gonzales was killed Friday and Feehan on Saturday. The Pentagon did not provide details on the exact circumstances of their deaths.

Feehan and Gonzales had been assigned to Army missile defense commands in Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and Ansbach, Germany, respectively, it said.

The Pentagon said the two U.S. troops were part of a longtime, ongoing mission to counter ISIS, Operation Inherent Resolve, that began in 2014.

The troops were not technically part of the war with Iran, dubbed Operation Epic Fury by the Pentagon, despite President Donald Trump saying on Sunday that the troops were killed while ensuring Iran does not get a nuclear weapon.

“Those great patriots were out there fighting that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters.

In addition, another U.S. service member was killed in a separate incident in Iraq.

Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas, and 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii. U.S. Army

The release of the two soldiers’ identities comes after the U.S. military announced Sunday that it had recovered unidentified human remains while searching for an American service member reported missing following an Iranian missile and drone attack in Jordan.

U.S. Central Command said military personnel found the remains Sunday at the site of Friday’s attack in Jordan. Officials said an examination is underway to determine whether they belong to the missing service member.

Central Command said Saturday that two service members were killed and a third was missing following Iran’s attack Friday on U.S. and partner forces in Jordan.

Separately, a U.S. service member was killed Saturday in northern Iraq during the controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian one-way attack drone, the combatant command said. A second service member suffered a minor injury and remains under medical care.

“Our hearts go out to these families,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Sunday. “These are heroes that pay the ultimate price.”

In a social media post Monday, Trump said U.S. military leaders had been given the directive to make Iran pay “many times over” for the killing of U.S. soldiers. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Monday afternoon in a post on X that the president would attend the transfer of the remains of killed service members at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on Tuesday night.

Leavitt later posted on X that the transfer of remains would not take place on Tuesday. “The exact day and time are still being finalized,” she wrote.

Fifteen U.S. service members have been killed in combat since military operations against Iran began, while two more service members died from noncombat-related causes. American military members who have been wounded since the start of the conflict now number 140, including eight who were wounded severely.

The discrepancy in the naming of the conflict reflects an ongoing confusion about the war with Iran — specifically about whether Operation Epic Fury continues.

NBC News previously reported that the Trump administration was considering re-naming the start of combat operations in Iran to circumvent the 1973 War Powers Resolution, which requires troops to be withdrawn within 60 days of starting combat operations if Congress was not notified beforehand.

In May, Trump notified Congress that Operation Epic Fury had ended. Since then, the Pentagon has not said what the ongoing military operation in Iran is named.

The military says Operation Inherent Resolve is the Combined Joint Task Force that works with partner forces to ensure the defeat of ISIS. Asked about the discrepancy in the mission the fallen service members were on, Acting Pentagon Press Secretary Joel Valdez said in a statement, “They were deployed on orders to support Operation Inherent Resolve.”

There are more than 50,000 troops in the region, according to U.S. Central Command. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine last gave a briefing at the Pentagon on the war in Iran in May.

At least 3,375 people have been killed in Iran since military operations began, according to the country’s state-affiliated news media, citing a senior judicial official.

The mounting death toll has effectively ended the interim ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran negotiated last month. After weeks of trading accusations that each side has violated the agreement, the two countries resumed attacks, with U.S. forces striking Iranian military targets and Tehran launching missiles and drones at U.S. allies in the region.

Rubio said that the U.S. remained open to diplomacy with Iran, but that “even within their own system, there’s a growing split.”

“They continue to send signals that they want to talk, that they want to negotiate,” he said. “But their behavior is what we’re responding to, and their behavior is they’re launching missiles and drones against ships, including tonight.”

“Their behavior has to change in order for ours to change,” Rubio added.

On Sunday evening, Central Command said it conducted a ninth consecutive night of attacks on Iran starting at 7 p.m. ET. It said in a subsequent statement shortly after 10 p.m. ET that the strikes had concluded.

“CENTCOM assets targeted Iranian military command centers, air defense and coastal surveillance sites, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites, and communications networks to further diminish Iran’s ability to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” it said.

On Saturday, the command said U.S. forces completed the eighth night of launching munitions against Iran when it targeted Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces believed to have been involved in Friday’s attack on U.S. service members in Jordan.

The military said the two service members died defending against an Iranian ballistic missile and drone attack. Four other U.S. service members were medically evacuated to hospitals in Jordan and have since been discharged.

World.title: FDA says it’s still investigating Taylor Farms in cyclosporiasis outbreak
World.content:
Taylor Farms continues to be the subject of a Food and Drug Administration investigation into the growing cyclosporiasis outbreak, despite a false positive test result, the agency said Monday.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Late Sunday, the FDA said that a lettuce sample from the company had falsely tested positive for cyclospora, the parasite that causes the illness. That sample, however, did not come from lettuce already implicated in the outbreak and recall. Instead, it came from a separate shipment the agency collected during routine import inspections.

“To clarify, this false-positive lab sample DOES NOT change the basis for FDA’s ongoing outbreak investigation or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the current voluntary recall by Taylor Farms,” the FDA said Monday on X.

The company’s voluntary recall of shredded iceberg lettuce to 27 states is still in effect.

On Sunday, Taylor Farms said in a statement that the FDA had “apologized” about the false positive test results. On a call Monday, an FDA official disputed Taylor Farms’ claim that the agency had issued an official apology.

Taylor Farms did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Determining the source of an outbreak goes beyond finding a positive sample.

Public health officials don’t rely solely on laboratory tests to identify the source of a foodborne outbreak, said Donald Schaffner, a food microbiology professor and chair of the food science department at Rutgers University.

Instead, investigators look at patient samples and interviews, food receipts and information from the food supply chain to determine where the contaminated food likely came from.

In the ongoing outbreak, investigators found that many people who got sick had eaten at Taco Bell restaurants supplied with Taylor Farms lettuce. As of Saturday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had confirmed more than 1,600 cases in people in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia.

“Taylor Farms is still implicated because of the epidemiology,” Schaffner wrote in an email. “This means that people that ate at Taco Bell, and ate Taylor Farm lettuce, are sick with the parasite. It’s important to realize that this is only a statistical correlation. Correlation is not causation, but it was strong enough evidence that FDA and CDC believe that this is the cause.”

On Saturday, Taco Bell said it had removed all Taylor Farms lettuce from its U.S. restaurants.

Schaffner said it’s unusual for investigators to be able to detect the cyclospora parasite in a food sample.

“Almost always it’s too late because the food has already spoiled or has been eaten,” he said.

A positive result for the parasite would have been a strong piece of confirmatory data, said Don Stoeckel, an environmental microbiologist and associate at the Produce Safety Alliance, a food safety training group.

The lack of a positive result, however, “does not reduce the importance of following the CDC’s recommendation to avoid consumption of the product named on the CDC investigations page,” Stoeckel said.

World.title: Tropical Storm Bertha strengthens, threatening Gulf Coast. See its path.
World.content:
Tropical Storm Bertha was getting stronger early Tuesday, threatening the Gulf Coast with heavy rain as its projected path sparked watches and warnings along the coastal the region.

Bertha was in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico as of 5 a.m. ET, heading northwest at 5 mph with maximum sustained winds of 50 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center. It is the second named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season.

Maps show projected path

Bertha could strengthen more later today, followed by gradual weakening through the middle of the week, forecasters said.

"A slow northwestward to west-northwestward motion is expected today followed by a turn westward by the middle part of this week," the hurricane center said. "On the forecast track, Bertha will move near or along the northern Gulf Coast during the next several days."

Map shows the forecast path for Tropical Storm Bertha. CBS News

NOAA

NOAA

Warnings and watches in effect

A Tropical Storm Warning was in effect Tuesday from the Alabama-Florida border to the Jefferson-Plaquemines Parish border in Louisiana.

Tropical Storm Watches were posted for the area stretching from the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida westward to the Florida/Alabama border, from west of the Jefferson-Plaquemines Parish border to Morgan City, Louisiana, and for the New Orleans metro area, Lake Pontchartrain and Lake Maurepas.

A Storm Surge Watch was in effect for the Alabama-Florida border to the mouth of the Mississippi River.

"Tropical storm conditions are expected within the warning area along the northern Gulf Coast by late today into Wednesday," the hurricane center said. "Tropical storm conditions are possible in the watch area in the Florida Panhandle later today. Tropical storm conditions are possible within the watch area in Louisiana by late tonight into Wednesday."

Forecasters warned of rainfall up to 6 inches in some areas. Rain was expected through the week and along the Gulf Coast and in adjacent inland areas from western Florida to the Texas coast. Parts of Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana will also be affected and the rainfall could bring flash flooding.

The system could also produce storm surge, raising waters up to 4 feet in some locations along the coast.

Bertha comes weeks after the 2026 hurricane season's first named storm, Tropical Storm Arthur, which made landfall in June along the Gulf Coast of Texas.

World.title: Supreme Court will review Alaska's bid to seize plane over 6-pack of beer
World.content:
The Supreme Court agreed Monday to review an Alaska bush pilot's claims that state authorities have tried to illegally seize his $95,000 airplane after a passenger brought a six-pack of beer on a flight bound for a dry village.

The pilot, Kenneth Jouppi, sued to block his plane's seizure after he was convicted of an alcohol-related misdemeanor charge. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in the state's favor that Jouppi's plane was subject to criminal forfeiture laws.

On Monday, however, the nation's highest court agreed to hear Jouppi's case. He argues that taking his 1969 Cessna would violate the Eighth Amendment's "Excessive Fines Clause." Arguments are expected in the fall. Under Supreme court rules, four justices must vote to take up an appeal in order for it to appear before the court.



"I'm thrilled that the U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to hear this case, because this case isn't just about me or my airplane anymore," Jouppi said in a statement released by his attorneys at the Institute for Justice. "I'm in my 80s now, and I've been fighting this for over a decade because I see it as my duty to ensure that the Bill of Rights actually means something in protecting against government overreach."

In April 2012, Jouppi was preparing to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to a remote village, Beaver, where alcohol was banned. The passenger had packed beer with other groceries in her luggage. State Police troopers searched Jouppi's plane before it departed and spotted a six-pack of Budweiser in a shopping bag.

In this Aug. 2025 photo provided by James Wilson, Ken Jouppi sits in a hanger at the Shoshone County Airport in Shoshone County, Idaho. James Wilson via AP

Jouppi, his company and the passenger were charged with a misdemeanor offense of knowingly transporting an alcoholic beverage into a dry community. The passenger pleaded guilty. A jury convicted Jouppi and the company after a trial. A judge sentenced him to three days in jail.

According to the Fairbanks Daily-News Miner, Judge Patrick Hammers hinted that a message needed to be sent to other pilots. "A message that if you do it (help alcohol smugglers) and get caught, you lose your airplane," Hammers said. "A message that it's not worth it."

The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in 2025

that the state's seizure of Jouppi's plane was not an excessive fine.

Jouppi's attorneys say Alaska's high court examined his conduct "purely in abstract terms" and didn't evaluate whether it was part of a broader pattern of criminal activity. And they say it wasn't.

"Few excessive fines cases will present the issue so sharply; a decision upholding the forfeiture of an airplane for a six-pack is a self-recommending candidate for review," lawyers from the Institute for Justice wrote in their appeal.

In response, lawyers from the Alaska Attorney General's office argued that the state Supreme Court's "fact-bound decision" should be allowed to stand.

"Courts across the country apply a multi-factor test to determine whether a fine or forfeiture is grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense," they wrote. "Jouppi does not claim that the four-part standard applied by the Alaska Supreme Court is wrong, only that the court misapplied settled law by giving too much weight to some factors and not enough weight to others."

Jouppi's attorneys argue that the ruling from the state's highest court conflicts with case law established in other courts, including U.S. Supreme Court precedent.

"The Excessive Fines Clause was built for cases like this," they said.

Alaska's attorneys said Jouppi hasn't shown how punishing him with forfeiture of his plane is "grossly disproportional to the gravity of his offense."

"Alcohol abuse is a serious problem in rural Alaska, and airplanes are sometimes the only realistic means to commit the crime of alcohol importation," they wrote.

World.title: Key Arizona primaries to watch today
World.content:
Arizona voters will go to the polls Tuesday to choose who will take on Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, and key congressional districts are also holding primaries as the heated battle to control the House continues.

Arizona has traditionally been a heavily Republican state, and six of its nine House representatives are Republicans. But the state currently has a Democratic governor, and both U.S. senators are Democrats. The state voted for former President Joe Biden in 2020, but flipped back in 2024 for President Trump.

After the 2020 election, Arizona was one of the states Mr. Trump targeted for his baseless claims of voter fraud — and those claims have continued to reverberate throughout Arizona's politics.

Here are the races to watch:

Arizona Republican primary for governor

Hobbs is running unopposed for the Democratic nomination, and there are four Republicans on the ballot to take her on in November. The two leading candidates are Reps. Andy Biggs and David Schweikert, and Biggs has the president's endorsement.

Biggs is leading in early polls, and Francisco Pedraza, the head of Arizona State University's Center for Latina/os and American Politics Research, told CBS News that he could see a Biggs-Hobbs matchup as a "tight race."

In 2022, Hobbs narrowly defeated Trump ally Kari Lake in the governor's race. Lake, who backed Mr. Trump's false claims about the 2020 election, has since been tapped by the president to lead the U.S. Agency for Global Media, which oversees Voice of America and other services like Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. The Senate has not yet voted to confirm her nomination.

Biggs has represented Arizona's 5th District for five terms and is the former chair of the House Freedom Caucus. Biggs, who has been one of the top proponents of Mr. Trump's election fraud claims, was subpoenaed by the now-defunct Jan. 6 select committee over his alleged involvement in plans to bring protesters to Washington on that day, as well as his efforts to convince state officials that the 2020 election had been stolen from Mr. Trump. His name appeared frequently in the final report.

Pedraza said the 2020 election claims and "whether we can trust our election systems" will be a central theme in the race, though Hobbs has been focusing on affordability and curbing school vouchers. He cited ASU's research on the 2024 election that found that one in three Arizona voters are "not that confident" or "not at all confident" that absentee or mail-in ballots will be fairly counted and free of fraud.

"That is some evidence that when thought leaders — and especially elected officials, public officials, including the president of the United States — when they continue to bang on this drum that there's fraud happening despite no evidence that that is the case, it sticks, and so people's beliefs are really tainted," he said.

Arizona 1st Congressional District

Schweikert was first elected to Congress in 2010 as part of the Tea Party wave to represent the Scottsdale area, but he told the Arizona Republic last year that he wanted to run for governor because he was frustrated with gridlock in Congress. "We have a body that can't even pass its appropriation bills," he said.

Schweikert won by only 3.8 points in 2024 over former state legislator Amish Shah, and the district is ranked as a toss-up by Sabato's Crystal Ball rankings by the UVA Center for Politics. Several Republicans are vying for the GOP nomination, including former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik, former Arizona Cardinals kicker Jay Feely and businessman John Trobough. Mr. Trump has backed Feely.

On the Democratic side, several candidates are seeking the nomination, including Shah and Marlene Galán-Woods, who was defeated by Shah in the 2024 primary. The Democrats' House campaign arm is backing Galán-Woods, a former broadcast journalist.

Galán-Woods has been criticized for being a Republican until 2018 and supporting GOP politicians in the past. She told the Arizona Republic that the party has changed: "The Republican Party has been driven off a cliff by Donald Trump and people like (incumbent U.S. Rep.) David Schweikert."

Arizona 5th Congressional District

With Biggs' entry into the governor's race, his congressional seat is left open in the safe Republican district.

Mr. Trump has backed former Pinal County Sheriff Mark Lamb, who has branded himself "America's Sheriff" and told the Arizona Republic when he launched his campaign he was focused on "faith in God, Jesus Christ, my family." Lamb led early in the race, but the Arizona Republic published a multi-part investigation in May alleging that Lamb engaged for years in sexual misconduct, explicit messages and abuse of power, and was investigated by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

CBS News has reached out to Lamb's campaign.

Lamb's campaign has denied allegations of misconduct. In a Facebook post in May, Lamb's wife said "after all we've been through, a massive smear campaign is certainly not going to stop us from doing what's right."

Last week, Mr. Trump reaffirmed his support for Lamb, who is being challenged by wealthy construction owner Daniel Keenan. Keenan has poured in $1.6 million of his own money into his campaign, and a poll by a GOP polling firm and backed by his campaign recently showed him with a slim lead.

Biggs won by over 20 points in 2024, and the district is ranked Safe Republican by UVA's Sabato's Crystal Ball, so Tuesday's winner will likely be favored to win in November.

There are three Democrats running to take on the winner of the Republican primary.

World.title: Tourists stabbed near famed Acropolis in Athens, Greece
World.content:
Athens, Greece — A man stabbed two tourists Tuesday morning near the ancient Acropolis in Athens, Greece's top tourist attraction, police said.

The assailant attacked a man and woman, both Greek Americans, with a knife near the entrance of the Acropolis Museum, which lies at the foot of the Acropolis hill. The woman suffered light injuries to a leg, while the man was more seriously hurt with wounds to an arm, police said.

The attacker was detained, while the two victims were transported to a hospital by ambulance, authorities said.

The iconic Parthenon at the Acropolis, Athens, Greece is seen in an undated photo. Joe Daniel Price / Getty Images

The attacker's identity wasn't immediately clear, but police said he appeared to have been suffering from psychological problems.

The attack didn't lead to any closure to the sites, which continued operating as usual. Greek media reported that the assailant had allegedly been randomly threatening passers-by with a knife, and that police had been alerted by a member of the public.

Violent street attacks are rare in Greece. In April, authorities arrested an 89-year-old man who allegedly opened fire with a shotgun in a social security office and a courthouse in central Athens, wounding at least four people, reportedly over social security grievances.

The Acropolis hill in Athens hosts the nearly 2,500-year-old Parthenon temple as well as other monuments, and attracts millions of tourists. Last year, about 4.6 million people visited the site.

World.title: Army veteran sets off fireworks, starts fire outside NYC federal building, FBI says
World.content:
A man was arrested after the FBI and New York City Police Department said he ignited fireworks and started a fire outside a federal building in Lower Manhattan on Monday morning.

The incident happened at 8:20 a.m. outside 26 Federal Plaza, a building that houses dozens of agencies including the FBI, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Officials identified the suspect as Andrew Arrabaca, 43, a U.S. Army veteran from Poughkeepsie with an address in Harlem.

According to a U.S. Army spokesperson, Arrabaca served in the regular Army from July 2001 to July 2004 and in the Army National Guard-New York from July 2004 to July 2005. He had no deployments and left the Army in the rank of specialist.

"He came armed with bad intentions"

FBI New York Assistant Director James Barnacle said Arrabaca was armed with two axes, a machete, three knives, fireworks and other destructive devices.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the suspect ignited a bundle of fireworks before dumping flammable liquid outside the building and setting it on fire.

Heavy smoke was seen outside 26 Federal Plaza after an explosion caused by fireworks, sources said. CBS News New York

Federal agents ran up to the suspect and tackled him, and the fire department quickly put out the blaze.

"He came armed with bad intentions," Barnacle said. "Looking to injure people and harm people."

He described Arrabaca as an anti-ICE activist who had a small cart with him with the slogan "ICE off our streets" written on it.

"He is an anti-American, anti-government extremist," Barnacle said.

Police sources said Arrabaca has had a previous encounter with federal agents for acting as an emotionally disturbed person but was not arrested.

The FBI New York Joint Terrorism Task Force is investigating the incident.

Airsoft guns, commercial-grade fireworks found

The suspect was carrying two airsoft guns, according to Tisch.

CBS News law enforcement analyst Richard Esposito described the materials as "things you might use in paintball-type events."

Tisch said he fired several pellets into the air before he doused parts of the building in flammable liquid.

The DHS spokesperson said the man's bag also contained a manifesto.

An airsoft rifle, carbon dioxide cartridges, halogen lighting and a helmet were among the items found at 26 Federal Plaza after an explosion. CBS News New York

Law enforcement has seized Arrabaca's car and is working to obtain a search warrant for it.

3 minor injuries at 26 Federal Plaza, FBI says

Barnacle said three people were hurt, two of whom were government employees.

One person was grazed by the fireworks, a DHS spokesperson said. A security officer also had minor injuries after tackling the suspect.

Video from the scene showed heavy smoke in front of the building and law enforcement arresting a man.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident "deeply disturbing."

"My team is in touch with the NYPD, and we will support the federal investigation. Our administration will continue to ensure that every New Yorker is safe in their city — and hold accountable any who threaten that," he wrote, in part, on social media.

World.title: FBI agents told to stand down on ICE assault probes; DOJ denies policy shift
World.content:
FBI agents around the country received guidance last week that they will no longer participate in investigations of assaults on immigration agents, including incidents that culminate in an immigration agent opening fire, emails reviewed by CBS News show.

Instead, an arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement called Homeland Security Investigations will handle the probes.

Justice Department and Homeland Security Department officials deny such a policy change is taking place.

But in the emails reviewed by CBS News, FBI officials and HSI special agents in field offices were advised that the FBI would be deferring on all assault on federal officer inquiries involving DHS agents to HSI. In one email sent to FBI field offices, agents in each office were asked to compile a list of existing investigations involving assaults on federal officers from DHS.

HSI and ICE are overseen by the Department of Homeland Security, meaning the immigration enforcement agency would effectively be investigating incidents involving its own agents.

The FBI has historically served as the lead law enforcement agency to investigate assaults against federal agents. The bureau also handles highly specialized color-of-law civil rights investigations, such as when civilians are killed by police. Several high-profile fatal shootings by immigration agents over the last 18 months have involved elements of both, with DHS alleging agents were assaulted before they discharged their firearms.

Unlike the FBI, HSI is not typically tasked with investigating officer-involved shootings and is not structured or equipped to handle core elements of such cases, including ballistics analysis, forensic processing, firearm examinations, video review and large-scale witness canvassing, CBS News has previously reported. HSI typically handles a wide variety of cross-border crimes, ranging from human trafficking and cybercrime to art smuggling.

The change was first reported by The New York Times.

Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News that the directive was issued on Thursday to leaders in various FBI field offices.

Both DHS and the Justice Department publicly have denied that any such change is taking place, with each agency posting on X that the changes reported in the media on how assault investigations involving DHS agents would be investigated were "false."

The FBI "will continue to investigate in accordance with agency policy," the Justice Department wrote on X. "This administration has been clear, anyone who assaults law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law."

A Justice Department official told CBS News on Monday morning that the FBI was unaware of any such guidance being distributed to field offices.

Later on Monday evening, however, CBS News reviewed an additional email that was addressed on Thursday to HSI agents in one of its field offices, one source with knowledge of the matter said.

According to the email reviewed by CBS News, the new guidance will impact all assault investigations, from minor cases involving assaults on DHS employees, all the way up to agent-involved shootings. The abrupt shift prompted hours-long calls with FBI special agents in charge, U.S. Attorneys, HSI leaders, and the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general's office, the email shows.

In the email, a local HSI official also expressed concerns about the need for more training and resources to handle some of the serious cases.

The FBI will still provide resources and assistance upon request, according to both the email and a different source with direct knowledge of the new policy. The email said that HSI would still have strong support from its local partners to work through the policy changes being directed out of Washington.

Several sources familiar with the matter confirmed the policy shift was communicated to FBI field offices last week, with one source adding that the change was reiterated again on Monday — even after both DOJ and DHS publicly denied any such change was taking place.

Spokespeople for the Justice Department, the FBI and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to additional follow-up questions from CBS News.

The new policy shift comes on the heels of fatal shootings by federal immigration officers in Texas and Maine earlier this month, and raises questions about what role the FBI will play — if any — on color-of-law civil rights investigations.

On July 7, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed a Mexican national in Houston who had lived in the U.S. for decades. Days later, an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine.

The Justice Department, the FBI and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions from CBS News about how this policy shift may impact the investigations in Texas and Maine.

The FBI earlier this year surged resources in Minnesota to investigate alleged assaults on immigration officers who were carrying out enforcement operations in Minneapolis. Some of those cases were later dismissed after prosecutors reviewed the evidence.

The issue became a flash point after a fatal encounter between an ICE officer and Renee Good. The Justice Department pressured the FBI and prosecutors to treat the investigation as an assault on a federal officer as opposed to a civil rights investigation into her killing, prompting several prosecutors and an FBI agent to resign.

When HSI was tasked with leading the federal investigation into the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January, with the help of the FBI, the decision raised questions among current and former federal law enforcement officials.

After concerns were raised, the FBI and the Civil Rights Division were ordered to take the lead on the probe. That investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Pentagon ID's 2 soldiers killed in Iran strike in Jordan; 1 still missing
World.content:
The Pentagon has identified two U.S. Army soldiers killed in an Iranian strike on a military base in Jordan over the weekend.

A third service member was also missing in action from the attack, U.S. Central Command said. Unidentified remains were later found in the area, the military said Sunday.

The Pentagon said Monday that 19-year-old Pvt. Isabella Gonzales of Carrollton, Texas, was killed in action on Friday during an attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, and that 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, was killed in action on Saturday.

The Pentagon said the soldiers were supporting Operation Inherent Resolve, the name for the U.S. mission against the Islamic State group. They were assigned to the Army Air Missile Defense Command.

Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas, and 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii, were killed in an Iranian attack at a base in Jordan. Department of Defense

Four other U.S. service members were medically evacuated to a hospital in Jordan and have since been discharged. Other service members were treated for minor injuries, according to the military.

A U.S. official had previously confirmed to CBS News that the attack occurred at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base. The location of the strike was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The Pentagon said Gonzales was assigned to the 1st Battalion, 57th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 52nd Air Defense Artillery Brigade, 10th Army Air Missile Defense Command, in Ansbach, Germany.

Gonzales' friends described her as outgoing, spontaneous, and someone who loved to dance. They told CBS News Texas she left for boot camp exactly one year ago.

"I think she really did want to make people proud of who she was," Zuleyka Acosta said. "She wanted to be very disciplined, and she wanted people to view her as someone who was very brave."

Feehan was assigned to the 2nd Battalion, 55th Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 32nd Army Air Missile Defense Command, Fort Bragg, North Carolina.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said President Trump will attend the dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base. Leavitt originally said the dignified transfer would take place Tuesday evening, but said later Monday it had been rescheduled, although the exact date and time were not yet known.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reacted to the deaths of the U.S. service members in a social media post saying, "Godspeed, heroes." "Their sacrifice only stiffens our resolve," Hegseth said on X.

Following that Iranian attack, U.S. forces launched a new round of airstrikes against Iran at the direction of President Trump, CENTCOM said Saturday evening.

It marked the eighth straight night of strikes on Iran since ceasefire talks broke down, and the strikes continued the following day as well.

"The strikes are designed to further degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and swiftly punish Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces who launched attacks against American service members in Jordan last night," CENTCOM said.

The deaths in the latest round of fighting mark the 15th and 16th among U.S. service members in the war with Iran. Prior to Saturday, the most recent death was that of a U.S. Navy pilot who died when his MH-60S helicopter made an emergency landing at sea last month, though the Navy said there was "no indication" of hostile action.

Six service members were killed in an Iranian attack on a base in Kuwait in March. Also in March, six were killed when a refueling plane crashed in Iraq, and one was killed in an Iranian strike on the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Trump imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
World.content:
Trump imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods

toggle caption Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Monday imposed 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, declaring that Canada has unfairly discriminated against American autos, alcohol and dairy products.

The move could unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between two nations that had been closely woven together before Trump's return to the White House. The administration official previewing the action said that Canada was one of the only nations other than China that retaliated against Trump's previous tariffs and must be held accountable.

The official insisted on anonymity on a call with reporters to preview the president's actions and said that Trump signed three proclamations to launch the tariffs under Section 338 of the 1930 Trade Act. Several Democratic lawmakers last year proposed repealing the section because they said Trump could use it to destabilize the economy.

Sponsor Message

The new 50% tariffs would exclude energy products, potash, fish and critical minerals, but they would include goods that had previously been protected from import taxes by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. That 2020 trade pact was not renewed by the U.S., triggering a new set of negotiations that could run until 2036.

The White House said in a fact sheet that the tariffs would go into effect in 30 days, meaning there is time for negotiations as Trump has not always followed through on his announced tax hikes on imports.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that his government believes in the "benefits of free and fair trade," having signed "more than 20 new economic and security partnerships." He said Canada is prepared to negotiate with the Trump administration.

"This trade dispute has raised costs for families, particularly in the U.S.," Carney said. "Canada stands ready to engage intensively to address outstanding issues with the U.S. to the mutual benefit of our citizens."

Canada faces the risk of a broader trade war

Still, the tariffs could escalate into a wider trade war as Canada seeks to defend its economy. Ontario Premier Doug Ford saw a possible showdown ahead.

Sponsor Message

"If these tariffs proceed, Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar," Ford posted on social media.

Candace Laing, CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, said the Trump administration's moves were "regrettable" but the two countries need to use the 30-day window before the tariffs start "to make meaningful progress in advancing formal talks."

Chris Swonger, CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, also called for a deal: "We encourage policymakers on both sides of the border to pursue a negotiated solution that restores market access for U.S. spirits and avoids further harm to the U.S. hospitality sector."

But the use of a Great Depression-era law to impose the tariffs broadens some of the risks, as those tariffs could be applied to other U.S. trading partners, not just Canada, and inject "massive uncertainty" into the global economy, said Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank.

"We crossed the Rubicon," Lincicome said. "The invocation of 338 is the nuclear option for Trump tariffs."

Tariffs are also a political challenge for Trump

The new tariffs carry serious political and economic risks for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections for control of Congress. His "Liberation Day" tariffs last year in April provoked a financial market meltdown over concerns about inflation and a recession, prompting him to walk back the rates for a period of negotiation.

The Supreme Court ruled this February that Trump had lacked the legal authority to impose the tariffs by declaring an economic emergency, causing the administration to find alternative ways to raise import taxes based on a series of legal authorities.

Tariffs are taxes on imports, which companies can then pass along to consumers in the form of higher prices. The president maintains that the costs created by tariffs will cause manufacturing to relocate to the U.S., though there is little evidence of that in the economic data.

Sponsor Message

"These new taxes will raise prices on American families and likely lead to retaliation against the very industries Trump purportedly wants to protect," said Rep. Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., who is chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

The latest import taxes could worsen Trump's weak ratings on the economy. He promised voters when running for the presidency that he would bring prices down, but the annual inflation rate has risen since he became president because the tariffs and the war in Iran are pushing up oil prices.

Trump has repeatedly targeted Canada on trade issues

The Trump administration official said the president had also requested that his aides look into additional tariffs on Canada because its wildfires hurt air quality in the U.S. He had publicly threatened to do so in social media posts.

At the World Cup final on Sunday, Trump watched the game with Carney. The Trump administration official said their time together at the game was not a working visit to discuss trade and tariffs.

Trump claims in the proclamations that Canada discriminates against American autos, alcohol and cheese relative to other nations, but his argument rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the U.S. president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.

Trump noted in his autos proclamation that Canada maintained, starting in April 2025, a 25% tariff on the imports of U.S. motor vehicles that did not qualify for preferential treatment under the USMCA.

The White House said that, regarding alcohol, all but two Canadian provinces and territories halted the purchase and retailing of American alcoholic beverages beginning last year, which was also a response to Trump's tariffs and taunts of making Canada the 51st state.

But Trump has long objected to Canada's treatment of U.S. cheese, saying in his proclamation that Canada discriminates against the U.S. compared to Europe on dairy products.

Sponsor Message

Trump and Carney have had a frosty relationship, with Carney, a former central banker, who pledged to go "elbows up" for Canada during his election campaign last year.

At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, Carney called out Trump — without naming him — by saying that the "most powerful" countries are using the economy to coerce less powerful nations.

Trump responded at the time by saying: "Canada lives because of the United States."

World.title: How soccer brings a Bhutanese community together in Harrisburg, Pa.
World.content:
How soccer brings a Bhutanese community together in Harrisburg, Pa.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

HARRISBURG, Pa. — At a park in the hills of central Pennsylvania, children in jerseys shout in a mix of English and Nepali, chasing a ball across the grass while their parents watch from the sidelines. A mother cheers on her son. For this community of Nepali-speaking Bhutanese refugees, the field is more than a field. It's where they've rebuilt a homeland that no longer exists.

Tens of thousands of Bhutanese refugees settled in Harrisburg starting in the late 2000s, after their families were forced out of Bhutan in an ethnic-cleansing campaign on the Lhotshampa people, as the country sought to modernize and unify and the government enacted policies in the 1980s that targeted ethnic Nepalis' legal status and culture. The refugees spent nearly two decades in camps in Nepal. It was there that soccer became a lifeline. Barred from work permits, families built farms and schools by day. At night, they turned to the sport to help cope with their traumas. One refugee, Kalu Singh Tamang, had been a national soccer star in Bhutan before the expulsion. In the Beldangi camps of Jhapa, Nepal, he coached thousands of fellow refugees on how to play. He died in the camp, never getting the chance to leave.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

That tradition crossed the ocean with the community that carried it. In 2007, the U.S., with the support of the U.N., initiated a program that resettled about 85,000 refugees. Each year, a memorial tournament bearing Tamang's name reunites refugees from across the country. Birkha Gurung, one of its co-founders, said he started it because, "When we were in Nepal, in the refugee camp, I played with [Tamang] and he coached so many of the refugee soccer fans. Our community, especially the adults, are having so many problems with mental health issues [since the camps], so I started this adults' tournament." Proceeds now fund Soccer for Success, a youth program serving over 50 kids a week — passing the game down to children who might never see the camps or the country their parents fled.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

Both programs run through Asian Refugees United (ARU), a Harrisburg nonprofit that also teaches cultural classes to refugee children. But the fields have become something else too: one of the few places this community still feels safe, as it faces a wave of deportations unlike anything it has seen before.

Sponsor Message

Under an intensified immigration crackdown, dozens of community members have been deported over the last 18 months. Before March 2025, the U.S. government did not deport these stateless refugees regardless of criminal history. Now they are being flown to Bhutan — a country that still refuses to recognize them as citizens and expels them on arrival to India or Nepal. Unable to repatriate to Bhutan, Nepal, or the U.S., they are left stateless twice over, with nowhere left to land.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to requests for comment.

ARU co-founder Robin Gurung has traded running soccer programs for full-time advocacy, spending evenings and weekends with immigration attorneys, training staff in civic engagement, and flying to Washington to meet lawmakers. "We were not prepared for this when we [built] the rapid response team. Our job now requires us to talk to the family members, folks who are in ICE detention. The immediate need is to stop the deportations. Folks who are deported, they are not safe," Gurung said.

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

toggle caption Maansi Srivastava/NPR

The fear has outrun the deportations themselves. Bhagawat Dulal, a Soccer for Success coach who now also translates for detainees, said even ordinary life has started to feel dangerous. "I had some people I was talking to ask, 'Can I go garden or should I not do that because of the [ICE] situation?' The one thing that has always been there through Bhutan, Nepal and to America: We found a way to garden, because that is what brought us joy — and now the same people are scared to go garden," Dulal said. "I'm so frustrated."

Sponsor Message

Even so, the fields fill every week with children learning the game from their elders. The community still gathers to mark their religious festivals. Their trades from life before the camps are flourishing through small businesses. On the soccer field, as everywhere else, they keep carrying forward what ARU staff member Manju Gurung called, ahead of a day of advocacy on Capitol Hill, "a future of hope, for our parents and all refugee parents around the globe."
