According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Petro to seek court order to annul election of De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro said Tuesday that he will seek a court order to annul the election of President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a post on social media platform X, Petro said he had gather enough evidence to prove that his successor “was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes.”

“Today we are presenting the body of evidence we have gathered to the representatives elected by the people, and we will file a lawsuit with the courts to annul the elections, as is our duty,” said the outgoing president.

We are not making things up when we say that Abelardo’s government was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes included in the percentage automatically adjusted by algorithms created by private Israeli companies with the endorsement of their genocidal government. President Gustavo Petro

“We are facing not only the imminent rise of fascism in Colombia but also what may be the greatest threat to global democracy since Hitler’s time,” said Petro.

In a response that was broadcast on his social media channels, De la Espriella reiterated that Petro was a “tyrant” who was trying to perpetuate power through a coup d’etat with the help of the leftist runner-up in the election, Senator Ivan Cepeda.

Even before becoming a candidate, I warned you: Petro is a tyrant in the making who seeks to perpetuate himself in power by any means necessary. And today, as the president-elect of all of you, I ratify what I have said for so many years. This is no longer an analysis or an opinion; it is a palpable reality. From the moment nearly 13 million Colombians stood by me to defeat him and his political frontman, Petro and Cepeda began their Plan B to stay in power, no matter what it takes. And they want to do so through a coup d’état. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

The president-elect asked the armed forces “to protect the Constitution and democracy, and to disobey any order that Petro may be giving to the contrary.”

Resistance, dear compatriots. We cannot allow them to snatch away what we achieved at the ballot box in an epic democratic battle this past June 21. Let us resist, for August 7 is near. God, the vote, and democracy have spoken; we are going to defend the Constitution and the rule of law as we must. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella has long claimed that he will extradite his predecessor to the United States.

World.title: De la Espriella suspends Colombia’s transfer of power
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella on Tuesday suspended the transfer of power after President Gustavo Petro accused him of fraud.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said he had “given instructions to the vice president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term.”

I have just given instructions to the president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term, a government that, with its decisions and its conduct, seeks to destroy Colombia. Abelardo de la Espriella

“My duty is to protect the interests of the Nation and guarantee a serious, transparent transition at the service of Colombians, never to legitimize the disaster or the disregard for the constitutional order,” said the president-elect.

In a press conference, Finance Minister German Avila said that he had also suspended cooperation with the transition process in response to comments made by a member of De la Espriella’s team, convicted fraudster Carlos ALonso Lucio, that “undermine the respect, dignity, and decency” of the transition process.

Recent statements by members of the incoming transition committee undermine the respect, dignity, and decency of a process such as the one we are carrying out. These statements were surely made intentionally to hinder the transition process. Accusations and insults have been leveled against the president and his administration, alleging that they are criminals, that they are manipulating the justice system, and that they are seeking to extradite us, among other blunders that have been made. German Avila

“All we have received are insults and disrespect, slander and offenses, and we will not tolerate a single further act of aggression or threat,” said the finance minister.

Avila asked Inspector General Gregorio Eljach to oversee the continuation of the process.

In a post on social media platform X, incoming vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo stressed that his team would continue going through the books to make sure that “those who have betrayed the trust of the Colombian people must answer to the institutions and to history.”

World.title: Colombia’s Petro refuses to recognize successor Abelardo de la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s outgoing President Gustavo Petro said Monday that he doesn’t recognize the outcome of the election that made the far-right Abelardo de la Espriella president-elect.

In a post on social media platform X, Petro said he saw “evidence of electoral fraud carried out through algorithms and with foreign funding, which is prohibited by our Constitution.”

The president called the alleged election fraud “the harshest blow to national sovereignty since the Spanish reconquest during the years of the Patria Boba.”

Colombia’s president, according to the decision of the Colombians, is the philosopher Iván Cepeda. We have suffered the harshest blow to national sovereignty since the Spanish reconquest during the years of the “Patria Boba.” President Gustavo Petro

According to Petro, he had “all the information about how, from an IP server located in Los Angeles, California, owned by the Bautista brothers, integrated into the scrutiny operation, algorithms were used that substantially varied the vote in favor of” De la Espriella.

Additionally, the president accused a close associate of US President Donald Trump, Florida attorney Dan Newlin, of paying a $1.8 million Facebook campaign for De la Espriella.

In a post that was published on Sunday, Petro asked De la Espriella of he had registered the alleged campaign contribution of Trump’s former ambassador pick.

In a response, Newlin said that “I have contributed zero dollars, not a single cent, directly or indirectly, to his campaign.”

“I challenge you to provide evidence to the Colombian people to support these demonstrably false accusations. You will not be able to do so, because no such contribution ever occurred,” said the Florida attorney.

Petro has been promoting conspiracy theories about alleged election fraud ever since the June 21 elections that were won by De la Espriella with a 250,000-vote difference.

World.title: Colombia’s land agency claims elections triggered surge in land theft
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s land agency ANT filed criminal complaints about at least eight attempts to steal land from beneficiaries of President Gustavo Petro’s land reform.

According to ANT director Harman Felipe, armed men associated with drug traffickers and paramilitary commanders intimidated the communities at six plots that had been given to victim of the armed conflict.

The incidents we have reported follow the same pattern of intimidation against families who have benefited from the Agrarian Reform. The threats are intended to force communities to leave so that land currently in the hands of small farmers can be reclaimed. What is at stake is not only the safety of these families, but also the defense of the Agrarian Reform and the right of small farmers to remain on their land. Harman Felipe

In one of the attempts, armed land thieves allegedly tortured members of a family that had been given land in Puerto Lopez, a municipality in the central Meta province.

This land used to belong to Ignacio Alvarez, a drug trafficker of the now-defunct Norte del Valle cartel.

Most incidents happened in the Magdalena Medio region, where the legal occupants of five plots were ordered to abandon their properties by armed men.

At one of the plots, which used to be of Daniel Barrera, the owners were told “these lands don’t belong to guerrillas.”

At another plot, a member of the Isaza Clan threatened a women’s association that was given control over land that used to belong to Maria Georgina Arango, the wife of a former commander of paramilitary organization AUC, Ovidio Isaza, a.k.a. “Roque.”

In Cordoba, a Caribbean province, the legal occupants of another one of Alvarez’s plots fled.

“We want the Attorney General’s Office to investigate these incidents, which are not minor matters and could even constitute crimes against humanity due to the displacement they have caused,” the ANT director told press.

Land thieves stole between 6.5 and 8 million hectares of land during the armed conflict between 1964 and 2016, often with the support of corrupt elements within the State.

World.title: Cepeda calls for civil disobedience if De la Espriella doesn’t renounce US citizenship
World.content:
Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda urged followers to exercise civil disobedience unless President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella does not renounce his US citizenship and ends the persecution of opponents in the US.

At a press conference, Cepeda announced the “civil disobedience against the violation of our national dignity” and called on the 12.7 million Colombians who voted for him to follow his lead.

The leftist opposition leader said that he would “not lend myself to this violation of our sovereignty and will embark on the path of peaceful civil disobedience”

“This implies refusing to recognize the authority of someone who does not answer to the defense of national sovereignty. Let it be very clear: peaceful civil disobedience,” said Cepeda.

I call upon and invite the millions of voters who placed their trust in me to do the same and, if what I demand is not met, to peacefully ignore any order, provision, or mandate from someone who does not fulfill the role of guardian and guarantor of our Political Constitution. As civil disobedience teaches us, when the law, institutions, or authority come into conflict with moral conscience, the citizen has not only the right but the duty to resist peacefully, refusing to collaborate with injustice, opprobrium, or oppression. Ivan Cepeda

In order to call off the civil disobedience, the opposition leader demanded that De la Espriella renounce his US citizenship and clarified whether or not he is an agent or an asset of US intelligence agencies like the DEA and CIA.

Additionally, Cepeda demanded that the president-elect “cease all persecution against President Gustavo Petro and drop any attempt to extradite him,” and end the persecution of political opponents.

De la Espriella announced on Sunday that he had called on his transition team to send evidence of alleged wrongdoing by the Petro administration to Colombian justice and the US Department of Justice “so that they can determine what their competitive processes are, because there’s an international conspiracy going on there.”

The president-elect has long vowed to extradite his predecessor.

World.title: PM Andy Burnham’s first conversation was with President Trump, whom he invited to visit Manchester
World.content:
PM Andy Burnham’s first conversation was with President Trump, whom he invited to visit Manchester

21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 07:16 UTC Full article

The Prime Minister also hoped that he would be able to show the President what Manchester had to offer during a visit in the future.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke to the President of the United States, Donald Trump, shortly after taking office Monday afternoon, 20th July 2026. According to 10 Downing Street, the Prime Minister began by congratulating the President on a successful World Cup and agreed that England had an excellent tournament.

The Prime Minister also hoped that he would be able to show the President what Manchester had to offer during a visit in the future.

Setting out his vision as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister said he would be focused on ensuring reindustrialization up and down the country to ensure good growth in every postcode.

The Prime Minister also underlined his commitment to defense and security and said ensuring the security of the UK and its Allies was at the top of his agenda.

The President then updated on the situation in the Middle East, and the Prime Minister outlined the UK’s commitment to securing the movement of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to support global supply chains and drive down costs for businesses and families across the country. They concluded looking forward to speaking again soon.

The report from Washington said the newly appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and US President Donald Trump held a phone call immediately following Burnham's inauguration.

The conversation was described by Trump as “interesting” and going “very well,” and covered the long-standing UK-US alliance, trade, North Sea oil and gas, and stability in the Middle East.

Details of the call indicate that Burnham assured the US President of London's continued commitment to defense, explicitly confirming UK support for securing shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz.

Likewise on the North Sea Oil, and energy policy, Trump expressed strong interest in expanding oil drilling in the North Sea.

Finally Burnham used the introductory call to officially invite President Trump to visit Manchester, England, an offer Trump reportedly accepted. The visit may coincide with the 2027 G20 summit, which is rumored to be hosted in Manchester.

Other phone calls by PM Burnham on Monday afternoon included, Chancellor Merz. Germany; President Antonio Costa of the European Council; NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte; President of France, Emmanuel Macron; President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen, and Ukraine’ president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

World.title: The Falklands, FIFA and the Future of the British Overseas Territories
World.content:
The Falklands, FIFA and the Future of the British Overseas Territories 21st Tuesday, July 2026 - 07:10 UTC Full article Members of the Argentine team held up a banner exclaiming ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’ (‘The Falklands are Argentine’). By Peter Clegg (*)

I have been researching the British Overseas Territories (BOTs) and their geopolitical relationships for over twenty years, and I cannot remember so much focus on them as there has been in recent days. The FIFA World Cup match between England and Argentina provoked heated discussions over the future of the Falkland Islands (or Malvinas if you are Argentine). Gibraltar has received significant media coverage with the removal of the border infrastructure with Spain. The Caricom Reparations Committee has called for the British Virgin Islands (BVI) to be decolonized by the UK, and new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will likely retain the government’s commitment to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius. So, are we witnessing centrifugal forces that could fracture the BOTs’ relationship with the ‘UK family’? Let us start with the Falkland Islands. It is not unusual for the Falklands to be the source of heated debate when England play Argentina, but there has certainly been a lot of rhetorical exchanges. Before the game, Argentina’s vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, called England ‘usurping pirates’, which The Sun newspaper called ‘a hate-filled tirade’. Then, after Argentina’s win, members of the team held up a banner exclaiming ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’ (‘The Falklands are Argentine’). The response from the UK was swift, the government said: ‘The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands definitely are’, while Conservative Party leader, Kemi Badenoch declared: ‘The Conservatives fought for them before; we will do so again if necessary’. And Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, called for the capacity of the Royal Navy to be boosted. So, what can be discerned from all of this? First, nothing will change in the foreseeable future, but arguably the extent of diplomatic support for UK sovereignty is fraying. The Trump administration has hinted a more sympathetic position towards Argentina’s claim, and it defended the Argentina team’s right to unfurl the banner, while since Brexit the European Union has used ‘Malvinas’ in official communiqués. However, there is not a clear view at the United Nations or in international courts in relation to who has the strongest territorial claim, and the view of Falkland Islanders themselves is important when it comes to self-determination. It is also worth remembering that the Falklands has over 60 nationalities living there and should no longer be considered as a ‘white British’ population. Second, although it is highly unlikely that there will a repeat of the 1982 military conflict, concerns have been raised over the UK’s capability to defend the Falklands, however, the UK government is confident defenses are adequate. Gibraltar was the focus of media attention on 15th July when the border infrastructure with Spain was removed—the last frontier fence in Western Europe. This was the culmination of protracted negotiations to avoid a hard border, which was a possibility after Brexit. The deal eliminates controls and customs checks at the border and gives Spain responsibility for Schengen controls at Gibraltar’s airport and port. In a related development, Spain removed Gibraltar from its blacklist of tax havens; Gibraltar had been on the list since 1991. Gibraltar Chief Minister Fabian Picardo said: ‘The frontier that has so often divided and constrained our region will now become a place of cooperation and shared opportunity’, while Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, stated that an ‘open wound’ was finally being closed. Commentary in sections of the UK’s right-wing media was highly critical. For example, Stephen Glover in the Daily Mail, claimed that Gibraltar ‘has virtually been handed to Spain’. Glover admitted that Brexit had posed a problem but then criticized the EU for behaving in a ‘bloody-minded way’. He also slated Picardo for going along with ‘this charade’. This illustrates two points: First, the widespread cognitive dissonance on the part of those who strongly argued for Brexit but can never bring themselves to admit the real challenges the decision caused and that pragmatic compromises are needed to resolve them. Second, the paternalist view towards Gibraltar—the local government was centrally involved in the negotiations and felt that on balance the deal was the right one. If UK politicians and commentators say they support the BOTs, they also need to accept the autonomy of the territories to make their own decisions. The removal of the border infrastructure will undoubtedly bring new challenges, but many opportunities—and it is this effective functional cooperation that is most important and may well lessen the centrality of formal sovereignty. Caribbean BOTs. Then there is the Caricom (Caribbean Community) Reparations Commission, which has recently called on the UK to ‘decolonize’ its remaining territories in the region—the Caribbean BOTs. The Commission focused particularly on the BVI. Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the commission, argued: ‘We object to the fact that in the Virgin Islands, our people cannot make fundamental decisions because they have to consult with the British governor and consult with Downing Street to make decisions’. This is to an extent true, but the BVI has significant autonomy, though it has not always used that power in the best way (see for example, Commission of Inquiry Report). The focus on the BVI by the Commission coincides with the beginning of constitutional review talks between the territory and the UK. The House of Assembly of the Virgin Islands is asking for a significant reduction in the power of the Governor and greater devolved responsibilities to the local government. It will be interesting to see what is negotiated, but it is unlikely the BVI will get everything it wants and there is little appetite for independence. Thus, the Caricom Reparations Commission intervention is timely, but does not fully acknowledge the nuances of relations between the BVI (and other Caribbean BOTs) and the UK—that independence is not an option and while that remains the case the UK believes it should have certain powers to intervene, if necessary, to ensure its international obligations are upheld. Finally, there is the situation in the Chagos Islands, also known as the British Indian Ocean Territory. I have written previously on the issue, and the handover has been paused because of opposition from the Trump administration despite earlier support. This is because US agreement is needed due to the UK/US military base on Diego Garcia. There is recognition from the UK that there will be a delay, and this was recently illustrated by the renewal of an agreement with another BOT, St Helena—that any migrants arriving in the Chagos Islands will be sent to St Helena (St Helena will receive £9 million from the UK as part of the deal). Notwithstanding, it seems that Burnham will stick to the original agreement and push it through once the US is again supportive. The decision was criticized by many on the right but as has been the case throughout this saga there remains a failure to recognize the real international legal pressures that will lead to the return of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius. In conclusion, while recent events have generated an unusual degree of attention for the BOTs, it would be mistaken to view them as evidence of an imminent unravelling of the UK’s relationships with its remaining territories. One of the most important points is that the BOTs are too often discussed as though they constitute a single category with common interests and identical political aspirations. In reality, big differences exist between territories such as the Falkland Islands, Gibraltar, the BVI, and the Chagos Islands. These distinctions are not always recognized in public debate, yet such nuance is essential if recent developments are to be properly understood. There are undoubtedly pressures on UK relations with the BOTs, but few of these are entirely new. Questions of sovereignty, self-determination, constitutional reform, international law, and decolonization have shaped these ties for decades. Such pressures may have become more acute in the current geopolitical environment, but they are not fundamentally different in character. Indeed, the Chagos agreement is an attempt to address colonial legacies, any new constitutional settlement with the BVI is likely to mitigate similar concerns, and Gibraltar has largely resolved one of the most difficult practical consequences of Brexit. Arguably, the Labour government is achieving a considerable amount in this policy space. Nevertheless, because the BOTs are deeply connected to questions of history, empire, war, and national identity, they will continue to provoke strong opinions and intense political debate. (*) Peter Clegg is Professor of Politics and Head of Social Sciences at University Western England, UWE Bristol. He has written extensively on the political economy of the Caribbean and non-independent territories. Recent publications have focused on the Falkland Islands, the impact of Brexit, and COVID-19.

World.title: Burnham's first moves as UK PM: new chancellor, Miliband to foreign office and a social turn
World.content:
Burnham's first moves as UK PM: new chancellor, Miliband to foreign office and a social turn

20th Monday, July 2026 - 20:52 UTC Full article

Burnham, 56, acknowledged the fragility of his position and said politicians “need to be better” to restore stability

The United Kingdom's new prime minister, Labour's Andy Burnham, began shaping his government with a cabinet reshuffle and a series of socially oriented announcements, hours after taking office in place of Keir Starmer. The former mayor of Greater Manchester, who reached Downing Street without a general election after winning the Labour leadership, is Britain's seventh prime minister in a decade.

Among the cabinet changes, the appointment of John Healey as Chancellor of the Exchequer, in charge of finances, stood out as a move that surprised Westminster, after Rachel Reeves confirmed her departure. Former Energy Secretary Ed Miliband was promoted to foreign secretary, while Shabana Mahmood was reappointed home secretary. Louise Haigh, a close ally who coordinated his preparations for office, was placed in charge of the Cabinet Office as first secretary of state. Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Secretary David Lammy tendered his resignation. Further appointments are expected in the coming hours.

In his first speech outside Downing Street, delivered without a lectern or notes, Burnham promised to “end rough sleeping” among homeless people, a goal backed by an official announcement of an additional £340 million over five years. He proposed a “circuit breaker” for a system that, he said, had taken wrong turns since the 1980s, and previewed a ten-year plan, the construction of more council housing, and changes to the education system. Announcements on the cost of living will begin on Tuesday.

Burnham, 56, acknowledged the fragility of his position and said politicians “need to be better” to restore stability, alluding to the succession of governments in recent years. He pledged to honor defense-spending commitments and to respect the country's fiscal rules. The next general election is not expected for about three years.

Internationally, US President Donald Trump held a phone call with Burnham on Monday, according to the White House. Trump praised on his social network the new prime minister's intention to expand North Sea oil production, having earlier attributed Starmer's downfall to alleged failures on immigration and energy. The change of government also places British foreign policy in Miliband's hands, including the position on the Falklands, which the outgoing Starmer government had reaffirmed in recent days amid the controversy over the banner displayed by Argentine players at the World Cup.

Starmer, who governed for two years after his 2024 victory, bid farewell saying he leaves the country “stronger and fairer.” “I go with good grace, I go with a smile,” he said.

World.title: Petro calls for 'general and indefinite strike' if successor repeals his reforms
World.content:
Petro calls for 'general and indefinite strike' if successor repeals his reforms

20th Monday, July 2026 - 20:12 UTC Full article

Petro warned that a repeal of the labor reform, approved in June last year, would in his view represent a setback for workers' rights

Colombia's outgoing president, Gustavo Petro, called on Monday for a “general and indefinite strike” should the government of his successor, Abelardo de la Espriella, repeal his administration's labor reform or reverse the land reform. De la Espriella, elected in the June 21 runoff, will take office on August 7.

“The opposition is exercised in the streets, with resistance and with peace, but it must be forceful,” Petro said during his last public address in southern Bogotá, delivered to mark Independence Day. He argued that social mobilization should become the main mechanism of opposition to the incoming government and encouraged unions and peasant, Indigenous and grassroots organizations to peacefully defend the reforms passed during his four-year term.

Petro warned that a repeal of the labor reform, approved in June last year, would in his view represent a setback for workers' rights. “If they are going to tear down the job stability and working conditions won under this government, there will be a general and indefinite strike in Colombia,” he said. He added that if the incoming government alters land-access policies, “there will be a national agrarian strike.”

The president-elect, a right-wing leader of the Defensores de la Patria movement, has announced that he will review several of the current government's main reforms, including the labor reform, arguing they harm job creation and the country's competitiveness. De la Espriella has not so far proposed an immediate repeal, but a review.

Petro does not recognize his successor's election, alleging fraud —a claim he has not substantiated and that runs counter to the official validation of the result. The National Electoral Council proclaimed De la Espriella president-elect on June 24, after completing the runoff count, in which he obtained 49.66% of the vote against 48.70% for the leftist Iván Cepeda. Cepeda himself accepted the defeat and announced he would take a seat in Congress under the opposition statute.

Monday's speech was Petro's final address to the public as president. He indicated he would continue to take part in political life from the opposition once he hands over power on August 7. That same Monday he was due to speak again at the seat of Congress, for the installation of the new legislative session.

World.title: Argentina's June trade surplus rises 149% year-on-year on stronger exports
World.content:
Argentina's June trade surplus rises 149% year-on-year on stronger exports

20th Monday, July 2026 - 20:05 UTC Full article

The June surplus, however, marked a 36.4% drop from May's figure, which had been a record $3.450 billion

Argentina posted a trade surplus of $2.194 billion in June, a 149.6% increase from the same month in 2025, driven by growth in exports, the National Institute of Statistics and Census (Indec) reported on Monday.

The June surplus, however, marked a 36.4% drop from May's figure, which had been a record $3.450 billion. With this result, the country strung together 31 consecutive months of surplus in its trade balance.

Trade flows —the sum of exports and imports— grew 16.4% year-on-year in June, to $15.916 billion. Exports totaled $9.055 billion, up 24.5% from June 2025, while imports reached $6.861 billion, a 7.3% year-on-year rise.

In the first half of the year, Argentina accumulated a trade surplus of $13.923 billion, with exports of $49.454 billion and imports of $35.531 billion. The surplus accumulated through June already exceeds that of all of 2025, which had stood at $11.320 billion.

Economy Minister Luis Caputo highlighted that first-half goods exports set “a new all-time record,” with growth of 24.4% compared with the same period the previous year. In a message on social media, Caputo said first-half foreign sales of fuels and energy rose 42.5% year-on-year, industrial manufactures 27.5%, primary products 24.4%, and agricultural manufactures 15.1%. According to the minister, exports of industrial manufactures, fuels and energy, and primary products recorded the highest value in the historical series.

Export performance in recent months has been underpinned largely by the energy sector, whose foreign sales had been showing strong year-on-year increases, partly linked to better international prices. Argentina's trade balance has posted uninterrupted positive results since late 2023.

World.title: Ortega says Nicaragua will hold no more elections
World.content:
Ortega says Nicaragua will hold no more elections

20th Monday, July 2026 - 20:03 UTC Full article

The president announced during the commemoration of the Sandinista revolution that he will pursue legal reforms to prevent the opposition from contesting power through the ballot box

Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega said on Sunday that the country will no longer hold elections as a mechanism for the opposition to reach power. “There will be no more elections here for them to try to seize the government, to seize power,” he declared during the event marking the 47th anniversary of the Sandinista uprising that overthrew Anastasio Somoza Debayle in 1979, held in Managua.

Ortega, 80, has governed Nicaragua since 2007 and since 2017 has shared power with his wife, Rosario Murillo, named co-president in February 2025 following a constitutional reform pushed by the executive. That amendment extended the presidential term from five to six years and reorganized the structure of the state, meaning the next general elections would in theory be scheduled for November 2027. The reform was criticized by the UN, the Organization of American States, the European Union and the United States.

In his speech, Ortega announced that he would work with the National Assembly —controlled by his party— to pass laws that would “put up a wall” against parties seeking to reach the government through elections. He did not specify how the change would take shape.

While the statement does not immediately alter a known situation —international observers have for years reported the absence of real competition in Nicaraguan elections— it does mark an explicit shift in official rhetoric. In the 2021 presidential election, Ortega and Murillo jailed the main opposition candidates and claimed close to 76% of the vote, in a contest the United States and other governments did not recognize.

Opposition figures in exile interpreted Ortega's words as confirmation of a dominant-party model. Juan Sebastián Chamorro, one of the presidential hopefuls jailed before the 2021 election, said the president aspires to a single-party system inspired by models such as China's. The Costa Rica-based group Nicaragua Nunca Más said the Sandinista Front has become a party with no real opposition within the country, and pointed to the closure of thousands of civil organizations, the cancellation of parties and the shuttering of media outlets.

The announcement runs counter to Washington's policy, which since the 2018 crisis has conditioned any resolution on the restoration of democracy and free elections with international observation. In January, the State Department accused Murillo of having assumed the co-presidency without a mandate or legitimacy. Since 2018, the United States has imposed sanctions on dozens of officials and entities linked to Ortega's government.

World.title: Rubio says talks on Venezuela's democratic transition will begin in early August
World.content:
Rubio says talks on Venezuela's democratic transition will begin in early August

20th Monday, July 2026 - 19:51 UTC Full article

“I believe the first official conversations will begin the first week of August,” Rubio said at a news conference at Andrews Air Force Base

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that talks to begin a democratic transition in Venezuela will start in early August. Rubio, who leads Washington's relationship with Caracas, said a group representing the National Assembly elected in 2015 —the last one the United States recognizes as legitimate— met with the interim government and agreed to establish a forum for reconciliation talks and to begin the transition process.

“I believe the first official conversations will begin the first week of August,” Rubio said at a news conference at Andrews Air Force Base, before traveling to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit. The announcement coincides with a State Department statement last week backing a joint agenda set to begin on August 1, aimed at stability, democracy and national recovery, with the interim government's endorsement.

The United States has maintained a close relationship with Caracas since January 3, when it launched a military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro and flew him to New York to face criminal charges. Delcy Rodríguez, until then vice president, took over as interim president. Since then, Rubio has laid out a three-phase plan: stabilization, economic recovery and transition.

The process is advancing amid divisions within the opposition. The agenda does not include María Corina Machado, whose supporters have pressed for her role after arguing she won the 2024 election. Instead, representation falls to Dinorah Figuera, who holds —in a post disputed with Jorge Rodríguez— the presidency of the 2015 Assembly and returned to Caracas last month after years in exile. Figuera met with the U.S. chargé d'affaires and with Jorge Rodríguez, president of the Assembly that exercises effective control in the country and brother of the interim president, to agree on a technical and political working group.

The negotiations come during reconstruction work following the late-June earthquakes, which struck the north of the country. According to still-provisional official figures, the quakes left more than 5,200 dead and tens of thousands injured in La Guaira and Caracas, with hundreds of buildings and numerous public facilities collapsed.

On aid, Rubio said the United States had already contributed more than $180 million of the $300 million pledged. “We've already surpassed $180 million and we're looking for more; we'll do more,” he said, adding that Washington is working to help Venezuela access international financing for reconstruction, whose total cost is still being calculated.

World.title: Argentina players spark brawl and snub trophy ceremony after World Cup final defeat
World.content:
Argentina players spark brawl and snub trophy ceremony after World Cup final defeat

20th Monday, July 2026 - 19:17 UTC Full article

The tension, built up over a physical and stop-start match, boiled over after the whistle

The 2026 World Cup final between Spain and Argentina ended on Sunday with Spain champions by 1-0 after extra time, but the sporting outcome was overshadowed by a brawl between players from both sides moments after the final whistle at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, and by the decision of Argentina's players to turn their backs on the trophy ceremony.

The decisive goal came from substitute Ferran Torres in the 106th minute, in the second period of extra time, after 120 minutes in which Spain dominated possession without finding the net. Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez turned in a standout performance with eleven saves, a record for a World Cup final. Argentina, the defending champions, played much of the second half a man down after the sending-off of Enzo Fernández, the sixth player ever shown a red card in a World Cup final.

Lo que la no mostró: la brutal pelea de Paredes y Gavi tras la final del partido pic.twitter.com/T6xeCFWMyp — Carlos Montero (@CMonteroOficial) July 20, 2026

The tension, built up over a physical and stop-start match, boiled over after the whistle. According to television footage and international news agency accounts, defender Nahuel Molina struck Spain captain Rodri as he ran to celebrate. In the ensuing scuffle, Leandro Paredes grabbed Eric García by the throat and, together with Thiago Almada, knocked Gavi to the ground when the midfielder came to defend his teammate. Players and coaching staff from both sides stepped in to separate those involved; Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni was among the first to try to defuse the situation.

Paredes was initially reported to have been shown a red card for violent conduct in the incident after the match, though, according to the BBC, that sanction was later removed from the official record, leaving Enzo Fernández as the only player dismissed in the game.

The Argentine players' conduct led FIFA to open a disciplinary investigation. The governing body will review the reports of Slovenian referee Slavko Vinčić and the match delegates, together with video footage, before deciding whether sanctions are warranted. Those under scrutiny include Paredes, Molina and assistant coach Roberto Ayala, a former Valencia and Zaragoza player, who television footage places in a clash with Spain's Dani Olmo. The case was opened days after FIFA began separate proceedings against the Argentine Football Association over a banner asserting a sovereignty claim over the Falklands displayed after the 2-1 semifinal win against England.

TANTO VA EL CÁNTARO A LA FUENTE, QUE AL FINAL... ¡AMARILLA! #DAZNMundial pic.twitter.com/7nILZ7JNsN — DAZN España (@DAZN_ES) July 19, 2026

Minutes later, as Spain's players filed up to collect their medals and lift the trophy, Argentina's players chose not to witness the ceremony: they turned their backs on the stage and faced one of the stands occupied by their supporters.

The incidents also included verbal exchanges. Broadcast cameras caught Nicolás Otamendi confronting Rodri over Spain's earlier complaints about the officiating, in an exchange the Spain captain met with looks of surprise.

The win is Spain's second world title and brings a frustrating close to what may be Lionel Messi's last World Cup appearance. The post-match confrontations raise the prospect of disciplinary action, a finish at odds with the magnitude of the title at stake.

World.title: Mexico’s hosting of World Cup wins praise all around
World.content:
During the FIFA men’s World Cup final in New Jersey on Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Spanish King Felipe VI praised Mexico as a host of the quadrennial soccer tournament and spoke glowingly about the Mexican team, according to President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Sheinbaum, who attended the match between Spain and Argentina at MetLife Stadium near New York City after receiving an invitation from Trump, said that everyone she had the opportunity to speak to at the final, “from President Trump to [Prime] Minister Carney to the King of Spain,” spoke “wonders of la selección nacional.”

The Mexican World Cup team won all three of its group stage matches, and its round of 32 clash against Ecuador, before losing 3-2 to England in a pulsating, nail-biting round of 16 game in Mexico City. El Tri’s four victories sparked jubilant — and very large — celebrations in Mexican towns and cities, especially the capital.

Sheinbaum said that world leaders and other officials she interacted with on Sunday — among whom were also Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, First Lady Melania Trump and FIFA President Gianni Infantino — also spoke wonders of Mexico as a co-host of the World Cup along with the United States, where the majority of the tournament’s 104 matches were played, and Canada.

“[They spoke about] how well Mexico did hosting the World Cup. Everyone was congratulating the fans [in Mexico],” she said, adding that her interlocutors at MetLife Stadium also mentioned “the happiness” with which the World Cup in Mexico was experienced.

Sheinbaum — who has asserted that Mexico had the best World Cup atmosphere of the three co-hosts — also said that Trump, Carney, King Felipe and others spoke about the warm way in which Mexico welcomed World Cup teams and tourists.

South Africa, Spain, Uruguay, Czechia, South Korea, Japan, Colombia, the Netherlands, Morocco, England and Sweden were among the teams that played matches in Mexico during the June 11-July 19 tournament. Another team, Iran, set up its base camp in Tijuana even though it played its three World Cup matches in the United States. The Iranian team received a very warm welcome from Tijuana locals. For his part, King Felipe watched Spain take on Uruguay in Guadalajara after meeting with Sheinbaum at the National Palace in Mexico City on June 25.

Sheinbaum reiterated at her Monday press conference that “everyone” at the stadium on Sunday congratulated her on the job Mexico did hosting the World Cup and spoke about “how well the Mexican team played.”

The president watched Spain defeat Argentina 1-0 in extra time from a glass-fronted stadium box filled with dignitaries. Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco attended the final with Sheinbaum, who presented the Golden Ball award to Spanish captain Rodri (Rodrigo Hernández), who was deemed the best player of the 2026 World Cup.

FIFA official: Mexico ‘was ready’ to host the World Cup; Mexican security team did an ‘excellent job’

Rodrigo Martínez-Celis, FIFA’s executive director for safety and security in Mexico, told the news agency EFE earlier this month that Mexico had “more than proven” that it was ready to host the World Cup despite a “narrative” of insecurity.

Before and during the tournament, Sheinbaum maintained that security in Mexico during the World Cup was guaranteed, and asserted that there was “no risk” for tourists who came to the country to attend matches in Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey. In late February, Infantino expressed his support for Mexico continuing as a co-host of the World Cup, despite the outbreak of violence on Feb. 22 after Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera was fatally shot in an army operation in Jalisco.

None of the 13 matches played in Mexico was disrupted by security concerns, leading Martínez-Celis to say that “we can say that Mexico was indeed ready to host” the World Cup.

“The best indicator for us is that today the world is talking about how well the matches were organized in Mexico,” the FIFA official told EFE in Mexico City.

He also said that Jalisco — where the violence in late February was concentrated — proved itself to be a worthy World Cup host. Four matches were played in Guadalajara, the state capital.

Martínez-Celis said that the federal government’s security cabinet, which was responsible for executing Mexico’s World Cup security plan, did an “excellent job.” Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said last week that Mexico had demonstrated its “capacity to organize global events with professionalism, hospitality and close coordination between the three levels of government.”

“The organization of the tournament strengthened Mexico’s image around the world and confirmed that the institutions of the Mexican state have the capacities needed to plan and carry out large-scale security arrangements in a coordinated and effective way,” he said.

Martínez-Celis said that “the World Cup for Mexico was an issue of national security and an issue of national pride.” He highlighted that the opening ceremony and match of the tournament in Mexico City went off well despite “additional pressure” from things such as transport concerns and protests.

Turning his focus to a World Cup tragedy, Martínez-Celis acknowledged the deaths of four people in Mexico City in a crowd crush during celebrations following Mexico’s June 30 win over Ecuador. He described the deaths as “terrible” and said that FIFA would review and analyze what happened.

Despite that calamity, the FIFA official made it clear that soccer’s international governing body considered the World Cup in Mexico a success. Most Mexican fans — who bonded over an optimistic (but ultimately unfulfilled) dream that El Tri could go all the way in 2026 — would probably agree, although the vast majority of them were unable to afford a ticket to watch a match live.

With reports from EFE

World.title: Feds and Jalisco state are joining forces to tackle water contamination in greater Guadalajara
World.content:
The federal and Jalisco state governments are embarking on a joint effort to clean up the region’s rivers, improve wastewater treatment and fix the water distribution system in a long-awaited effort to end the water pollution crisis affecting millions of residents in the Guadalajara metropolitan area.

With federal technical support, the project will rehabilitate the antiquated Chapala aqueduct in Guadalajara, clean up the Lerma-Santiago river basin, increase enforcement against industrial polluters and increase investment under the National Water Plan.

At President Sheinbaum’s morning press conference Thursday, head of the National Water Commission (Conagua) Efraín Morales confirmed federal collaboration with Jalisco’s government to address the water quality crisis.

“We are doing our part from the Federation to provide technical support so that the project is a real solution to the problems experienced in the city of Guadalajara as well as its metropolitan area,” Morales said.

Morales attributed Jalisco’s water issues to the deterioration of the original Chapala aqueduct, which has long lacked adequate maintenance.

The Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct carries water from Lake Chapala — the main source of supply for the Guadalajara metropolitan zone (ZMG) — to the city. The original pipeline is in a critical state, with leaks, internal corrosion and loss of capacity, which increases the risk of failures and leads to sediments and contaminants in the water that reaches the network.

Simultaneous with the pipeline rehabilitation will be an increased cleanup effort for the region’s rivers. Mexico’s Environment Ministry (Semarnat) said that the ZMG’s water issues are also linked to industrial contamination, with discharges from industries polluting the Lerma River.

“Industrial discharge is crucial as that’s where heavy metals and truly toxic products come from, and Lerma is one of the rivers presenting such a problem,” Semarnat Minister Alicia Bárcena said.

She added that companies thought to be responsible for discharging industrial waste have been identified and that inspections are underway that could lead to penalizing any proven to have violated environmental regulations.

She also explained that the federal government is implementing the 2024–2030 National Water Plan, a 20-billion-peso (US $1.15 billion) initiative that includes river cleanup programs and new wastewater treatment plants in the Atoyac, Lerma–Santiago and Tula river basins, Mexico’s most polluted rivers.

Although the federal government pledged technical support for the river cleanup efforts, experts argue that addressing Guadalajara’s water crisis will also require a stronger local strategy.

With reports from Zona Franca

World.title: Is iceberg lettuce from Mexico safe to eat?
World.content:
Yes, at least according to available evidence.

So far, authorities in Mexico and the United States say there is no confirmed evidence that iceberg lettuce sourced in central Mexico was contaminated with Cyclospora cayetanensis, the parasite responsible for a multi-state outbreak of Cyclospora infections in the U.S. that is widely known for its unpleasant side effect of “explosive diarrhea.”

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported Saturday that a lettuce sample obtained during border surveillance of products from Taylor Farms in Mexico had tested positive for the Cyclospora parasite. However, it said Sunday the test produced a “false positive.”

The false positive was revealed after the agency’s laboratory specialists reviewed the sample again and concluded that the initial result was incorrect.

The latest news does not change Taylor Farms Mexico’s earlier voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce produced in central Mexico, which was served at Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia.

Taco Bell also reported that it recalled lettuce sourced from Taylor Farms de Mexico starting on July 17.

In a statement Sunday, Taylor Farms de Mexico echoed the FDA’s statement and acknowledged its correction.

“To be clear, at this moment, FDA has not identified a single positive product test result for Cyclospora,” the company said.

Mexico became the center of public attention after the FDA identified a common lettuce supplier through epidemiological tracing: Taylor Farms de Mexico, located in the central state of Guanajuato.

In response to the accusations, the Mexican Ministries of Health and Agriculture activated an inter-institutional technical group led by the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) and the General Directorate of Epidemiology (DGE) to collaborate with the U.S. in the investigation of the outbreak.

From the outset, the Mexican government clarified that the reference to the country of origin was a traceability measure, not conclusive proof that the contamination had occurred within Mexican territory.

Authorities in Mexico said they will continue working in coordination with the U.S. to determine the source of the outbreak and protect the population of both countries.

With reports from Bloomberg and El País

World.title: Nuevo León leads all Mexican states in announced investments so far this year
World.content:
Nuevo León ranks No. 1 in investment expectations this year, accumulating 12% of all investment announcements recorded by Mexico’s Finance Ministry through June.

The northern state received pledges for US $5.58 billion of the cumulative US $46.96 billion committed to Mexico through the first six months of 2026.

The official data recognizes Nuevo León as the state with the highest expectations, followed by Chihuahua, Sinaloa, Hidalgo and México state.

According to information from the state and federal governments, the projects announced in Nuevo León will include the creation of 6,120 new jobs, primarily in advanced manufacturing, electromobility, technology, logistics, energy and innovation.

While acknowledging that the results reflect the joint effort of the state and federal governments, the business sector and universities, Nuevo León Economy Minister Betsabé Rocha Nieto said they also demonstrate the reputation the state enjoys.

“There is no doubt about the strength and confidence of national and international companies in Nuevo León as a primary destination to develop new productive projects,” she said.

Every new project “represents more opportunities for development, quality jobs and heightened welfare for Nuevo León families,” she said.

Recently, the national statistics institute INEGI reported that Nuevo León had also received the most investment in construction projects over the previous 20-month period.

In last week’s investment update, the Finance Ministry revealed that manufacturing remained the top recipient of announced investments during the first six months of the year.

Pharmaceutical companies — among them, Laboratorios Kener, Liomont, Bayer and Grupo Neolpharma — were among the leading investors, while automotive companies, as well as logistics and infrastructure companies, were also well represented.

Investment expectations in Mexico’s automotive sector surpassed US $2 billion, heavily focused on electromobility, supply chain integration and regional production.

In early June, e-commerce and financial services platform Mercado Libre announced an investment of US $4.6 billion with a particular focus on logistics, development and technological innovation.

As for infrastructure investments, Vinci Airports provided US $800 million to modernize and expand the network of airports managed by Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte.

With reports from El Economista, MVS Noticias and Mexico Business News

World.title: 6 celebrities who you might not realize are (kind of) Mexican
World.content:
What does it mean to be Mexican? It’s a complicated question — since not only are there more than 130 million native-born citizens, but a Mexican diaspora numbering over 40 million around the globe — making it nearly an impossible task to come up with a completely satisfying definition.

One thing is clear: Mexico is a very warm country, especially when it comes to welcoming those who embrace it with love. There’s even a popular saying that captures this idea: “Los Mexicanos nacemos donde se nos pega la gana,” which means that a Mexican can be born wherever they choose.

The nation is also a melting pot, having welcomed significant populations of Italians, Germans, Lebanese, Argentinians, Venezuelans, Japanese and Koreans into the country as immigrants since the late 19th century. President Claudia Sheinbaum comes from a family of European Jews who settled in Mexico, for example, and the many examples like this make the question of Mexican identity even more nuanced.

If we consider Mexican identity not only in the traditional sense (native-born citizens), but also more inclusively to include those with Mexican roots or heritage, there are more international Mexican celebrities than you might think. In fact, a few of the names on this list even surprised us.

Alan Cleland

A professional surfer who competed in the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and won gold at the 2023 International Surfing Association (ISA) World Surfing Games, Alan has been making his mark in extreme sports. But with sandy blonde hair and a surfboard on him at all times, the average person may think he’s just another Californian who grew up near the beach.

Born to a Mexican mother and an American ex-pro surfer father in Boca de Pascuales, Colima, Alan learned to surf before he even learned to speak English. He later moved to San Diego to further develop his surfing skills and began competing in the World Surf League when he was only 13.

After he won gold in 2023, there was even a video of him carrying the Mexican flag and chanting “Viva Mexico” as any proud Mexican would in the same position. He completed the 2025 season ranked 19th in the World Surf League (WSL) tour.

Wee Man

Best known for his role in the “Jackass” movie franchise, Wee Man has made a name for himself by performing stunts on film that the average viewer should never try at home. In addition, he’s a pro skateboarder and was a host on the Fox Sports Net television show “54321.” Despite his impressive resume, his background is more diverse than most people would assume.

Wee Man’s legal name is Jason Shannon Acuña, and he is of Mexican and German descent. He’s spoken openly in the past about growing up eating tacos and menudo. The “Jackass” actor, idolized for getting into cages with bulls, bungee jumping and funny pranks, also has an entrepreneurial side, having been a long-time investor in the popular Mexican-American franchise Chronic Tacos.

Kat Von D

A well-known public figure in her niche, Kat Von D may look like the reincarnation of Amy Winehouse, yet is actually a Mexican-born tattoo artist from Nuevo León.

She’s most recognized for her work on the TLC reality show “LA Ink.” On the show, she set the record for the most tattoos done in 24 hours at 400 and was named to the Guinness Book of World Records for that milestone — a record that has since been surpassed.

In addition, Von D has also released a makeup collection with Sephora in 2008, released two studio albums and written two New York Times bestselling books.

Anthony Quinn

If you’re a fan of old movies and love trivia, Anthony Quinn could be defined as a legend of Hollywood. In the 1950s, he cleaned up at the Oscars — winning two Best Supporting Actor awards, one in 1952 for “Viva Zapata!” and another in 1956 for “Lust for Life.” What many U.S. audiences didn’t know at the time, however, was that he was also Mexican.

His legal name was Manuel Antonio Rodolfo Quinn Oaxaca. What’s also intriguing is the fact that he was born in Chihuahua at the midpoint of the Mexican Revolution in 1915. It’s said his father was Irish and his mother was from Mexico, yet in his biography, “The Original Sin: A Self-Portrait,” he claimed his Irish father was just a story made up by Hollywood publicists. In other words, he was as proud to be Mexican as they come. That alone deserves to be celebrated as much as his Oscars.

Hubertus von Hohenlohe-Langenburg

Most people know a famous Mexican soccer player or boxer, but what about one who’s a well-known skier? Hubertus Hohenlohe-Langenburg is a pioneer in niche sports in Mexico, having competed in six Winter Olympics as an alpine skier and founded the Mexican Ski Federation in 1981.

His family story is also one that could be turned into a scripted television series. Hohenlohe is a descendant of German royalty, being the son of Prince Alfonso of Hohenlohe-Langenburg and Princess Ira von Fürstenberg. He was born in Mexico City, moved to Spain and then eventually settled in Austria.

In addition, Hohenlohe is a photographer and businessman and was even a pop singer who went by the stage names Andy Himalaya and Royal Disaster.

Lupita Nyong’o

Having won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress in the film “12 Years a Slave” in 2014, Lupita Nyong’o has gone on to be one of Hollywood’s brightest stars, appearing in “Black Panther” and “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” But the most intriguing thing about her is her cultural background. Not only does she hold U.S. and Kenyan citizenship, but she also carries Mexican citizenship.

Her father is a Kenyan politician who was teaching in Mexico City when she was born. Although she grew up in Kenya and later came over to the United States to study at Yale University, she has always maintained that she is Kenyan-Mexican.

So who else should have been mentioned on our list? Let us know in the comments below.

Ian Ostroff is an indie author, journalist, and copywriter from Montreal, Canada. You can find his work in various outlets, including Map Happy and The Suburban. When he’s not writing, you can find Ian at the gym, a café, or anywhere within Mexico visiting family and friends.

World.title: Zacatecas AG: Multihomicide of 10, including officials, may be linked to extortion and collusion
World.content:
The murders of 10 men whose bodies were found in three different municipalities in the state of Zacatecas on Saturday could be linked to extortion and collusion between criminals and public officials, the Zacatecas attorney general said Sunday.

The bodies — including that of Ignacio Castrejón Valdez, a former mayor of Sombrerete, Zacatecas — were found in the municipalities of Morelos, Pánuco and Saín Alto, all located north of Zacatecas City. Five of the bodies were found hanging from a bridge in Pánuco.

Among the other victims were Fidel Alvarado de la Torre, an official with the Fresnillo municipal government, and Andrés Vázquez Gurrola, an ex-councilor in the municipality of Canatlán, Durango.

In a video message on Sunday, Zacatecas Attorney General Cristian Paul Camacho said that “various pieces of evidence have been collected, which indicate that the main lines of investigation involve possible acts of extortion and collusion by public officials.”

“This investigation must be carried out in a very exhaustive and very professional way,” he said, adding that a financial probe could be part of it.

Camacho said that authorities had obtained video footage that allowed them to establish the vehicles that were used in “the criminal events” — i.e., those used to dump the bodies in public places.

“It is necessary to inform that at this time a search warrant is being executed at a property in the municipality of Fresnillo, where it has been determined at least two of the victims were there before they were killed,” he said.

“… At a different place, a vehicle related to the events was seized.”

Camacho said that eight of the victims were from Zacatecas and two were from the neighboring state of Durango.

“Among the victims is the ex-mayor of Sombrerete, Ignacio Castrejón Valdez, and two officials from the municipality of Fresnillo. One of them worked as the director of social development and one was a Civil Protection member,” he said.

Referring to ex-municipal councilor Andrés Vázquez Gurrola, Camacho said that another victim was a lawyer and former police officer from Durango. Six others were businessmen in various fields including agriculture, entertainment and construction. One of the businessmen owned a bar.

Camacho said that eight of the victims were strangled to death, while two others, including Alvarado, the social development director in Fresnillo, were shot. He said that bullet casings recovered by authorities were being subjected to an “exhaustive analysis” in order to establish whether perpetrators of the murders had used the same weapons in other crimes.

According to the attorney general, four of the victims stopped communicating with their families last Thursday, while five ceased communication last Friday. The other victim ceased contact with his family on Saturday.

Camacho said that the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office didn’t receive any reports that the victims had been abducted.

Citing the results of toxicology tests, Camacho said that five of the victims, including the two municipal officials from Fresnillo, had recently consumed drugs.

In the same video message, Rodrigo Reyes Mugüerza, general secretary of the Zacatecas government, said that it had been a “weekend of uncertainty … fear and concern” for residents of the northern state.

Homicides declined by more than 60% annually in Zacatecas in the first six months of 2026, according to government data, but Reyes said that “days like Saturday … remind us that the process of pacification is a complex and continuous process.”

He said that state authorities were carrying out an operation aimed at detaining those responsible for the murders and were committed to “minimizing the possibility of these events being repeated.”

“From the state government, we once again confirm our commitment to peace, to security and above all to solidarity with all the people of Zacatecas,” Reyes said.

At a press conference on Monday, Governor David Monreal Ávila conveyed his condolences to the victims’ families and declared that there will be no impunity for the murders.

“Far from intimidating us, expressions of barbarity like those of last Saturday force us to redouble efforts. They oblige us not to let our guard down, not to take a backward step or fear groups that violate peace,” he said.

The Morena party governor said that his government is supported by the federal government, and stressed that the state of Zacatecas has sufficient technology, equipment and trained security personnel.

“We’ll put all this capacity in play to shed light on the events of Saturday and, above all, to guarantee that they are not repeated and to ensure that whoever committed this atrocity receives the appropriate punishment,” Monreal said.

With reports from Aristegui Noticias, Reforma, El Financiero and El Sol de Zacatecas

World.title: Pre-Columbian skeletal remains discovered in Playa del Carmen cenote
World.content:
Deep in the underground waters of a cenote in Quintana Roo, divers have documented the skeletal remains of a young woman who may have lived in pre-Columbian times, Mexican authorities revealed last week.

Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) said custodians of the Yaakun cenote near Playa del Carmen reported the find after technical divers spotted submerged materials in late 2025.

Within months, underwater archaeologist Gustavo García García led a five-day survey, conducted at depths of 42 to 53 meters (138 to 174 feet), that confirmed a cluster of human bones and, about 30 meters away, ceramic vessels.

Preliminary analysis indicates the individual — who has been named Yatzil — was between 18 and 25 years old, based on skeletal features and limited dental wear.

Researchers have identified long bones, the pelvis, a cranium and part of a mandible with three molars.

Her remains, still submerged in a sloping chamber about 45 meters below the surface, are considered well preserved due to stable underwater conditions, including low light and temperature.

The ceramics — mostly globular pots likely used domestically in the eastern Maya region — may date to the Late Postclassic period (1200–1521 AD), according to INAH.

However, researchers are being cautious about assigning a precise date or cultural affiliation to Yatzil’s remains, noting that her chronology is still unknown despite the ceramics likely dating to the pre-Columbian period (before the Spanish conquest in the early 1500s).

INAH specialists say they will wait for DNA from a tooth scheduled to be removed in a second field session in 2027 before drawing firmer conclusions.

Authorities have launched the Cenote Yaakun Research Project to document and protect the site. A perimeter has been established, and divers are urged not to disturb the materials.

Culture Minister Claudia Curiel de Icaza emphasized the importance of working with the local communities on discoveries such as this one.

“Each archaeological find that we manage to protect,” she said in a press release, “strengthens our knowledge about the cultures that inhabited this territory and reaffirms that heritage is a shared responsibility.”

The Yaakun project is the latest underwater discovery on Mexico’s Caribbean coast, where at least 11 prehistoric skeletons were found in flooded caves and cenotes between Playa del Carmen and Tulum in recent decades. One of them, reported earlier this year, may be around 8,000 years old.

With reports from Infobae and Informador

World.title: MND Local: Two art exhibits, a global diving competition and a comedy show in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week, we take a look at two thought-provoking art exhibits now showing at the Museum of Art in Zapopan, an international diving competition and a comedian who brings joy and irreverence in wine drinking to the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA).

Two exhibits at the Museum of Art Zapopan tackle timely themes

The current exhibition “Unlevel Playing Fields” (“Canchas Desiguales” in Spanish) by Costa Rican conceptual artist Priscilla Monge uses soccer to convey a deeper message about the human condition.

Monge’s transformation of a traditional soccer field into a sloped, irregular surface is meant to highlight that not everyone in Latin America and the world starts on a level playing field.

The exhibition arrives at a time when Mexico is beset by enormous economic inequality, something that’s readily apparent with the World Cup currently underway. While the matches are attracting the attention of millions, the live experience in Mexico was restricted to the wealthy, who could afford to pay prices that often exceeded the average monthly salary of ordinary Mexicans.

This interactive work will tour each of Mexico’s 2026 World Cup host cities: Guadalajara, Monterrey and Mexico City. Despite the differences among the venues, the exhibition poses the same questions to all: How do we play, participate and share a space when the conditions of the game are not the same for everyone?

Priscilla Monge is known for her thought-provoking, interactive art installations. Her work explores the power struggles and inequality embedded in modern societies with a mixture of humor and cynicism. Previously, her art has been exhibited at the Rufino Tamayo Museum in Mexico City, the Venice Biennale and the Tate Modern in London.

Yukinori Yanagi exhibit at Estación MAZ

Two blocks away in the brand-new Estación MAZ building across from the Line 3 light rail station, a new exhibit by Japanese artist Yukinori Yanagi, “The Pacific Ocean,” explores identity, nationalism and global conflict.

The Pacific Ocean’s name suggests peace and tranquility, but its history has been anything but. This vast sea has been the scene of some of the greatest violence of the twentieth century, from Japan’s imperial expansion across Asia to the Second World War, and the first use of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

A core part of Yanagi’s work consists of revisiting these human tragedies that changed the course of history. Works like “Absolute Dud” (2007-2016) and “From the Sky” (2024) serve as symbolic recollections of the dire consequences of the Second World War. At the same time, he incorporates reflections on the limits of international boundaries and the dangers of excess nationalism.

Dates and locations: “Unlevel Playing Fields” runs through July 31 at the Museum of Art Zapopan (MAZ), Andador 20 de Noviembre, Zapopan Center.

“The Pacific Ocean” runs through Aug. 9 at Estación MAZ, Avenida de las Américas, Zapopan Center.

Cost: The MAZ in Zapopan is always free. Check the website to plan your visit.

Laugh about wine? Innovative stand-up comedy plus wine tasting in Zapopan

Who hasn’t had a good laugh about the pretentiousness of wine at some point in their life? Now, there’s a show where it’s safe to laugh and learn without fear of committing a social faux pas.

The brainchild of Australian comedian Merrick Watts, a certified wine taster, “An Idiot’s Guide to Wine: Comedy between Drinks” is a show that’s appeared at festivals, wineries and bars across Australia to sold-out crowds.

In Guadalajara, a new iteration of the show will feature a local comedian (and performed in Spanish), but the concept remains the same. During the set, the audience will enjoy wines from around the world, while learning about aromas, grape varieties and winemaking styles.

Your biggest challenge at this show won’t be trying to seem knowledgeable about wine but not spilling your glass while laughing. So don’t worry if you can distinguish between a Malbec and a Merlot. The point is no-pressure learning while having a good time.

For those who don’t wish to imbibe, non-alcoholic drinks will be available for an extra charge.

Date: Saturday, Oct. 10 and Saturday, Nov. 14 at 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.

Location: A 70-minute set at Escenik Teatro Bar in Zapopan.

Cost: Available now from Feverup, starting from 570 pesos.

World.title: Mexico Fighter Jets: Air Force Eyes F-16s to Replace 1982 Fleet
World.content:
Mexico · Defense

Key Facts —Current fleet. Mexico operates only three aging Northrop F-5E/F Tiger II fighters, in service since 1982. —Program goal. The Air Force aims to buy about 12 new jets to restore air defense and ground-attack capabilities. —Frontrunner. The U.S.-made F-16 Block 70/72 Viper is considered the leading candidate despite its higher cost. —Budget status. No official budget figure has been released by Mexican defense officials as of July 2026. —Timeline. A potential deal could be finalized by late 2026, with first aircraft arriving by 2028.

Mexico fighter jets are under formal evaluation as the country’s Air Force launches its first major combat aircraft acquisition in decades, aiming to replace a tiny fleet of planes that first flew in the early 1980s.
