World.title: Hungary’s big week: New constitutional rules, AI ambitions and billion-euro investments explained
World.content:
Hungary’s Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán has outlined a packed week of political, economic and diplomatic developments, highlighting constitutional reforms, new government programmes and efforts to strengthen the country’s position within Central Europe.

In a Facebook post reviewing last week’s events, Orbán described a series of decisions aimed at reinforcing Hungary’s institutions, boosting economic development and expanding regional cooperation.

Constitutional amendment enters into force

According to Orbán, Parliament approved the 17th amendment to the country’s Fundamental Law on Monday, with the changes taking effect immediately.

The amendment introduces a 12-year limit on the time members of Parliament may serve, strengthens the independence of the Constitutional Court and the judiciary, and establishes the constitutional basis for a new office responsible for recovering unlawfully used public assets.

The constitutional reform forms part of the government’s broader programme of institutional changes following this year’s political transition.

France ties and economic cooperation in focus

On Tuesday, Orbán represented Hungary as Deputy Prime Minister during celebrations marking France’s National Day. She highlighted the strong economic relationship between the two countries, noting that nearly 500 French companies employ around 45,000 people in Hungary, while bilateral trade approached EUR 10.2 billion in 2024.

According to the foreign minister, renewed momentum in Hungarian-French relations could encourage further investment, support secure jobs and strengthen Hungary’s ability to represent its interests within Europe.

New development programmes approved

Wednesday’s all-day cabinet meeting resulted in several major government decisions. Orbán said the government is launching the Saint Stephen Programme, designed to help rural communities retain their population while creating new employment opportunities.

The cabinet also approved Hungary’s participation in the European AI Gigafactory initiative and the IRIS² satellite programme, alongside adopting the Baross Gábor Programme, a comprehensive strategy aimed at modernising the country’s railway network.

Regional cooperation and Hungarian communities abroad

On Thursday, Orbán held her first meeting with Franco Dal Mas, Secretary General of the Central European Initiative, to discuss closer regional cooperation. She said stronger cooperation among Central European countries would improve Hungary’s energy security, infrastructure and economic competitiveness.

Later the same day, Orbán attended a meeting of Parliament’s Committee on Hungarian Communities Abroad, stressing that foreign policy and national policy cannot be separated. She said protecting the security, language rights, educational opportunities and community rights of ethnic Hungarian communities beyond Hungary’s borders remains a priority in both bilateral and European negotiations.

Baden-Württemberg visit highlights investment links

The minister also welcomed Thomas Strobl, President of the Parliament of Germany’s Baden-Württemberg state, whose first official foreign visit was to Hungary. Orbán described Baden-Württemberg as one of Hungary’s key economic partners, pointing to the recent inauguration of Mercedes-Benz’s EUR 1 billion expansion in Kecskemét, announced earlier last week.

If you missed it: Germany’s Baden-Württemberg seeks closer ties with Hungary as top officials meet in Budapest

Busy week of reforms and diplomacy

Summing up the week, Orbán described it as one marked by constitutional reform, significant government decisions and important Central European diplomatic meetings, presenting the developments as part of the government’s efforts to strengthen Hungary’s domestic institutions while expanding its international partnerships.

World.title: Heatwave returns to Hungary: temperatures could soar to 38°C next week
World.content:
After a brief spell of cooler-than-average weather, the heatwave in Hungary is set to return, with temperatures expected to climb back above 30°C by the weekend and potentially reach 38°C early next week.

According to 24.hu, meteorologists say the current respite will be short-lived, although there is growing optimism that August could finally bring more regular rainfall after months of severe drought.

Cooler weather only temporary

A cold front swept across Hungary on Sunday, bringing a noticeable drop in temperatures across the country.

Maximum temperatures on Monday reached 26–31°C (79–88°F), while Tuesday is expected to be even cooler, with highs between 24–30°C (75–86°F). Scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible in some areas, but widespread rainfall is still not expected.

Another cold front is forecast to arrive on Wednesday, keeping daytime temperatures between 23–28°C (73–82°F) through the second half of the week.

Although these values may feel refreshingly cool after recent extremes, meteorologists note that they are actually close to the long-term average for late July.

Heatwave to return this weekend

The cooler conditions will begin to disappear over the weekend as warmer air spreads back into the Carpathian Basin.

According to meteorologist László Molnár, temperatures will rise steadily from 26–27 July, with much of Hungary once again exceeding 30°C (86°F).

By next Monday, afternoon highs are expected to reach 30–35°C (86–95°F), while some of the hottest parts of the country could experience temperatures of 33–38°C (91–100°F) during the first half of next week.

Why is the weather changing again?

The latest heatwave will develop under different atmospheric conditions from the previous one.

The persistent high-pressure “omega block” that contributed to exceptional heat across western Europe is expected to break down. The region will instead be influenced by a low-pressure system positioned between two high-pressure areas over the Atlantic and Russia.

For Hungary, this setup is forecast to draw very warm air northwards from southwestern Europe, triggering another spell of intense summer heat.

Western Europe, meanwhile, is expected to receive some relief after experiencing one of its most remarkable early-summer heat episodes in decades.

Read Hungary’s most important news in English every evening in one place: 

Better news could arrive in August

There may finally be encouraging news for Hungary’s drought-stricken countryside.

Current forecasts suggest that the high-pressure system over Russia could weaken towards the end of July or the beginning of August. If that happens, prevailing westerly winds would become more dominant over Central Europe.

This weather pattern typically brings more regular Atlantic weather systems and increased rainfall to Hungary.

While forecasts this far ahead remain uncertain, meteorologists say the shift could help ease the country’s prolonged drought during August after one of the driest periods in recent years.

This article will show you how to reach this affluent demographic through high-authority English-language media that readers trust. You will also learn how to capitalize on the current 0% advertising tax rate to maximize your brand visibility without overextending your budget.

Key Takeaways

Identify specific segments within the international community, including digital nomads and business travelers, to ensure your messaging resonates with the right demographic.

Evaluate the “noise problem” in unmoderated social media groups and why high-authority news platforms provide a more credible environment for your brand.

Master the five-step process to advertise to international community Budapest audiences effectively by prioritizing brand awareness and native storytelling over generic ads.

Understanding the International Demographic in Hungary

Hungary’s international landscape has evolved rapidly. As of 2026, there are over 252,000 foreign nationals residing in the country. This group isn’t a monolith; it includes corporate expats, digital nomads, international students, and frequent business travelers. World.title: Hungary’s OTP Bank signs agreement to acquire Luminor Bank
World.content:
Hungary’s OTP Bank has signed a share purchase agreement to acquire Luminor Bank’s parent company, giving the Hungarian banking group a route into all three Baltic markets. The transaction covers 100% of Luminor Holding, although its financial terms have not been disclosed.

OTP Bank announced the agreement on Monday, 20 July, saying it would acquire the shares from a consortium of private equity funds managed by US investment firm Blackstone and from Norway’s DNB Bank.

The deal remains subject to the approval of the relevant regulatory authorities. Until those approvals are secured and the transaction is completed, Luminor will remain under its existing ownership.

OTP Bank to take full control of Luminor

Under the agreement, OTP Bank will acquire 100% of Luminor Holding, the parent company of Luminor Bank.

Blackstone-managed funds currently own just over 80% of the Baltic lender, while DNB holds the remaining stake. The sellers have agreed to transfer their entire shareholdings, meaning OTP would become Luminor’s sole owner after closing.

No purchase price, expected completion date or financing structure was included in the announcements published by the companies.

Luminor recorded total assets of EUR 15.9 billion and a profit after tax of EUR 158 million in 2025. OTP described the target as a stable, strongly capitalised and significant universal bank in the Baltic region.

The lender operates in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, providing services to private individuals, families and businesses. Luminor describes itself as the third-largest financial services provider in the Baltic region and operates as a pan-Baltic universal bank.

Acquisition would take OTP Bank into three new markets

The transaction represents a major geographical expansion for OTP Bank, which does not currently have banking subsidiaries in the Baltic states, Market Screener said.

OTP Group presently operates in 11 countries across Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia, serving close to 17.5 million customers and employing nearly 40,000 people. Its total assets stood at approximately EUR 124 billion at the end of the first quarter of 2026.

As Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania would all be new markets for the Hungarian group, the acquisition would increase OTP’s presence to 14 countries, provided the transaction receives regulatory approval.

The move also fits OTP’s long-standing strategy of expanding through bank acquisitions and seeking strong market positions in the countries it enters. Over the past two decades, the group has built substantial operations in markets including Bulgaria, Croatia, Serbia and Slovenia.

If you missed it: Hungary’s OTP breaks into world’s top 400 companies!

Luminor expects support for its next growth phase

Luminor said joining OTP Group would support its strategy of strengthening its position as a top-three universal bank in the Baltic states.

The bank highlighted its digital-first operating model, modern IT platform and progress in expanding its customer base. Luminor chief executive Wojciech Sass said the two institutions shared a commitment to customers, long-term value creation and financing the economies of their home markets.

According to Sass, becoming part of OTP would give Luminor the backing of an experienced international banking group with an established presence across Central and Eastern Europe.

Péter Csányi, chief executive of OTP Bank, said the Hungarian group intended to bring capital, liquidity and technological expertise to the acquired institution.

He added that OTP’s objective was to build on Luminor’s existing market position, strengthen its role in the Baltic states and support lending and financial innovation across the region.

Read Hungary’s most important news in English every evening in one place: 

Regulatory approval remains the next major step

As Luminor is a significant bank operating within the European Union, the proposed change of ownership will require scrutiny from the relevant European and national supervisory authorities.

The companies have not said when they expect the approval process to be completed. They have also not announced whether the Luminor name, management structure or customer services will change following the acquisition.

For customers, the agreement does not result in an immediate change. Luminor will continue its existing operations while the parties seek the permissions required to close the transaction.

Should the deal be completed, OTP Bank would gain an established platform across all three Baltic states and Luminor would become part of one of the largest independent banking groups based in Central and Eastern Europe.

World.title: Trump warns Iran over US troop deaths
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said Monday that Iran will pay “many times over” for any American troops killed amid ongoing hostilities in the Middle East.

Pentagon: three US deaths over the weekend

“Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

This directive has been passed on to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Daniel Caine, and “every Leader in the Military,” Trump added.

The statement came as the US continued to carry out airstrikes against Iran, with the attacks largely focused on southern Iran. Tehran retaliated with strikes targeting facilities and bases that it says are used by the US military in several regional countries, Anadolu said.

The Pentagon confirmed three US deaths over the weekend, including two at a military base in Jordan and one in northern Iraq.

The exchange of fire between the two countries comes despite a Pakistani-brokered memorandum of understanding signed in June to end the war and reach a lasting peace deal.​​​​​​​

According to a report by CNN, the US and Iran have considered a 10-day ceasefire to halt hostilities in an effort to prompt a return to negotiations, with the cessation in violence also including lifting restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz.

The White House said that diplomacy was proceeding along with efforts to make Iran “pay” for the recent deaths of US soldiers.

“Right now, President Trump is focused on making Iran pay for their violations of the MOU (memorandum of understanding) and their continued acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz,” a US official said.

“In addition, the president will make Iran pay for the recent deaths of U.S. soldiers,” the official said. “These devastating blows will continue until the president deems otherwise, but talks between our countries are continuing.”

If you missed it: Hungary lobbies Washington to avoid possible 100% US tariffs over Russian energy imports

Trump says Netanyahu ‘will not be arrested’ in US

In a separate post, Trump said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America.”

“He is fighting against the Islamic Republic of Iran, which recently killed 52,000 innocent protestors, and has spent the last 47 years killing American Soldiers, and others,” Trump added.

“The only ones that should be arrested are the people that led Iran into this unprecedented spiral of death and destruction, something that should have been dealt with years ago, by previous Presidents.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has told The New York Times that his administration’s legal department is actively discussing the potential arrest of Netanyahu.

“I believe that Prime Minister Netanyahu belongs in The Hague,” Mamdani said. “He’s a war criminal who has been charged by the International Criminal Court. And what you will find is that is an opinion that is held by many purely because of what his actions have wrought over these last many years.”

Netanyahu recently postponed a US visit originally set for this month to September.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar regrets Judit Polgár’s decision but accepts it ‘with respect’
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said he regretted Judit Polgár’s decision not to accept a potential presidential nomination but would respectfully acknowledge it. He also took personal responsibility for communication mistakes surrounding the selection process.

Magyar published a video statement on Facebook on Monday evening after holding talks with Polgár, whom he described as “a living legend of Hungary”.

According to the prime minister, the chess grandmaster told him that, considering the circumstances surrounding the proposed nomination, she would not stand for the presidency.

“I am sorry, but I respectfully acknowledge her decision,” Magyar said.

He added that millions of Hungarians would probably agree that the country would have gained an exceptional opportunity had Judit Polgár agreed to serve as head of state.

Magyar praised her knowledge, international reputation, humanity and patriotism, arguing that these qualities could have made her an outstanding president.

Magyar says Judit Polgár acted responsibly

The prime minister said Polgár’s refusal itself demonstrated that she would have been suitable for the position.

In his assessment, she had carefully considered the weight of the office, including its personal and public consequences, before reaching a clear and honest decision.

Magyar thanked Polgár for taking the proposal seriously and praised the openness, directness and dignity with which she handled the situation.

Following their conversation, he said he respected her even more because she had shown responsibility, restraint, humanity and commitment to Hungary.

“Judit Polgár’s life, achievements and service to Hungary are an example to all of us,” the prime minister said.

Polgár, widely regarded as the strongest female chess player in history, announced earlier on Monday that she did not feel she had sufficient strength to assume the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation. She nevertheless promised to support a future independent and respected president.

Prime minister accepts responsibility for communication mistakes

Magyar also addressed the criticism surrounding the speed and handling of the attempted nomination.

He apologised if communication errors caused by his enthusiasm and complete confidence in Polgár had contributed to the situation or influenced her decision.

“The responsibility lies solely with me,” he said.

The proposed nomination had prompted criticism from politicians, analysts and civil society organisations. Some argued that the process appeared rushed and did not provide enough time for meaningful public discussion.

Magyar acknowledged that events had not unfolded in a manner everyone would regard as correct or ideal. However, he argued that no selection process could gain the support of every citizen.

He said the government and the governing Tisza Party would learn from both their mistakes and the experience.

Read Hungary’s most important news in English every evening in one place: 

Tisza to continue searching for Hungary’s next president

Magyar insisted that the government had requested recommendations from political parties, public figures, civil organisations and private citizens from the beginning of the process.

He said Polgár had been proposed by respected representatives of Hungary’s cultural, scientific and sporting communities, while several other public and confidential recommendations had also been received.

The prime minister contrasted this process with previous presidential selections, which he claimed had been decided through agreements between political parties. This was Magyar’s political characterisation of the earlier procedure.

Under the current transitional rules, Hungary’s National Assembly will elect a president to serve until a new constitution is adopted. Magyar said the Tisza parliamentary group was expected to meet several times during the week to assess the proposed candidates before submitting its nomination to parliament.

According to the prime minister, Tisza will support a candidate who can represent the entire nation, possesses authority based on personal achievement and remains independent of party-political conflicts.

He said the party would not back anyone who had played a prominent role as an MP, minister or senior partisan figure during the divisive political decades preceding the 2026 change of government.

Magyar concluded that Hungary needed a president capable of bringing estranged social groups closer together after decades of political confrontation.

The search will therefore continue for a candidate whose integrity, judgement, patriotism and public service are recognised across political divisions.

World.title: French group Syclef takes over Romanian industrial refrigeration player Horeco
World.content:
Syclef, which specializes in commercial refrigeration, industrial refrigeration, and HVAC (heating, ventilation, air conditioning), has taken over Horeco Holding, a Romanian group specializing in industrial refrigeration.

The transaction remains subject to obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals from the Romanian Competition Council and the Commission for the Examination of Foreign Direct Investments (CEISD).

Founded in 1995 and based in Buzău, in eastern Romania, Horeco Holding brings together two companies: Horeco Impex and Frigoclima. The group employs more than 90 people and reported revenue of over EUR 20 million.

Florin Niculescu, the current CEO, remains a shareholder and will continue to lead the company's management and strategic development.

The partnership with Horeco is the second transaction in Romania announced by Syclef this month. In early July, the group announced that Unicool, a Romanian group specializing in commercial refrigeration, was joining it.

Headquartered in Cluj county, Unicool was founded in 2011. The group gathers two companies: Unicool Instalatii Frig and Acsa Coolteam. The founders will remain shareholders in both companies and will continue to manage operations.

Syclef is present in France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Belgium, the Netherlands, Ireland, Poland, Africa, the Indian Ocean region, and Romania. It designs, installs, and maintains custom technical solutions for a wide range of sectors.

World.title: President greenlights law establishing 2026 as Year of US in Romania
World.content:
President Nicușor Dan promulgated the law establishing 2026 as the Year of the United States of America in Romania on Monday, July 20. The bill was initiated by several lawmakers from the far-right, Eurosceptic but pro-Trump Alliance for the Union of Romanians party, or AUR.

According to the law set to be implemented, 2026 is the Year of the United States of America in Romania. As such, events may be organized to strengthen the Romanian-American strategic relationship and reaffirm Romania's commitment to the values of the free world, freedom of expression, and genuine democracy, according to the law cited by Digi24.

To mark the celebration, central and local public administration authorities may organize or provide material or logistical support, within the limits of the approved budget allocations, for the organization and holding of conferences and public debates; cultural, academic and educational events dedicated to American history and values; Romanian-American public diplomacy and communication activities; any other activities promoting Romanian-American cooperation and democratic values.

In addition, the Romanian Public Radio Broadcasting Company and the Romanian Public Television Company may broadcast thematic materials produced on the occasion of the Year of the United States of America in Romania.

The AUR bill was passed by the plenary of the Chamber of Deputies on June 30, with 283 votes in favor, 8 against and 4 abstentions.

World.title: Romanian drone maker BraveX Aero, Romaero expand UAV production capacity
World.content:
Romanian aerospace company BraveX Aero and state-owned Romaero are developing an industrial capacity to produce up to 17 unmanned aircraft per month as they seek to meet growing demand from the defense sector. BraveX Aero also announced a EUR 4 million funding round to support the expansion of its production capabilities.

Under the plan, BraveX Aero will expand production at its own facility to a capacity of up to seven aircraft per month, while Romaero will add the capacity to manufacture up to 10 aircraft airframes per month. The companies aim to increase the joint production capacity to 30 airframes per month from 2028.

“We are deliberately building a two-tier industrial model. Our own production capacity gives us direct control over technology, quality, and the pace of development, while our collaboration with Romaero allows us to prepare a genuine industrial reserve in advance. In the defense and security sectors, the ability to scale production rapidly should not be improvised when the need arises; it must be designed and planned in advance,” said Răzvan Costea-Bărluțiu, CEO of BraveX Aero.

The company's new production facility, expected to become fully operational in August, will manufacture composite airframes and support output of up to seven aircraft per month. BraveX Aero said it is also investing in equipment and expanding its workforce from 23 to 28 employees by the end of 2026, with plans to reach around 50 employees by the end of 2028.

“The new facility allows us to integrate the production of composite airframes more efficiently with our mechatronics, integration, and testing activities. Together with the new equipment and the expansion of the team, this organisation enables us to support a production capacity of up to seven aircraft per month while maintaining direct control over critical processes and the quality of every platform," explained Rareș Racoțean, CTO and Founder of BraveX Aero.

The partnership with Romaero is expected to enter the production phase in September, when the first BraveX-1 aircraft structure manufactured under the collaboration is scheduled to be completed. The companies also plan to begin preparing production of the new BraveX-Delta unmanned platform in the fourth quarter of 2026.

“The collaboration with BraveX Aero leverages Romaero’s infrastructure and expertise in the production and inspection of aircraft airframes. We are preparing an additional capacity of up to 10 airframes per month in the first stage, supported by quality control processes and non-destructive testing (NDT). Our shared objective is for this capacity to be capable of being activated rapidly, based on clear industrial planning and a well-controlled technology transfer,” added Speranța Munteanu, Special Administrator Romaero.

BraveX Aero said the additional production capacity at Romaero could be activated within one week in response to large commercial orders or national security requirements. The company added that the EUR 4 million funding round will support production expansion, the industrialization of new unmanned aircraft platforms, and its growth in the European defense market.

This year, BraveX Aero completed the validation campaign for the Vimana Jet platform and began customer deliveries. The company also developed and tested the Vimana Life Saver platform for long-endurance search and rescue missions and continues the development programmes for the BraveX-Delta and VTOL platforms.

World.title: Program to build angel investment capacity launches in Moldova, Romanian investors among backers
World.content:
TechAngels Romania, Business Angels Europe, META Group and the Moldovan Technology Transfer Network (MTTN) have jointly launched ESIL Moldova, a two-year program designed to build business angel investment capacity in Moldova.

While Moldova continues to produce highly skilled graduates, technology professionals, and promising startups, access to early-stage investment remains limited, a challenge ESIL Moldova aims to address.

The program will provide aspiring and existing business angels with training, mentoring, peer-to-peer learning, pitching opportunities and access to experienced investor communities across Europe. Activities will take place both in Chișinău and online and will cover startup evaluation, deal flow, syndication and cross-border investing.

The project is funded by the European Union and co-funded by the French Government through Expertise France as part of the EU4Innovation East program.

As part of the consortium, TechAngels will contribute practical experience accumulated through its work with early-stage technology companies and its community of more than 130 entrepreneurs, investors and senior executives. Its involvement will also support stronger connections between investors in Moldova, Romania and the wider European ecosystem, the organization said.

“Moldova has talented entrepreneurs with strong innovation potential, but successful startup ecosystems also need investors willing to share their experience, mentor founders and take informed risks. ESIL Moldova aims to help build a more active, connected and internationally engaged investment community,” Charles Mathiaux, Deputy Project Director of EU4Innovation East, said.

“Angel investing is best understood through practical experience, real investment decisions and interaction with experienced peers. We want to help investors in Moldova build the confidence, discipline and networks needed to support promising founders over the long term,” Cosmin Curticăpean, TechAngels Vice President and coordinator on behalf of TechAngels of the ESIL Moldova program, said.

ESIL Moldova builds on the experience of the Early Stage Investing Launchpad, which has worked since 2017 to strengthen business angel ecosystems across Europe, particularly in countries where organized early-stage investment remains underdeveloped.

TechAngels Romania brings together more than 130 entrepreneurs, investors and senior executives. Its members invest in and support early-stage technology companies with capital, operational experience, sector expertise, mentorship and access to business networks. In the past 13 years, the group has contributed over EUR 47 million to the development of local tech startups and has more than 270 startups in its aggregated portfolio.

World.title: PPC Blue installs ultra-fast EV charging stations at Bucharest's Henri Coandă Airport
World.content:
PPC Blue Romania announced that it put into operation seven ultra-fast electric vehicle charging stations at Bucharest’s Henri Coandă International Airport, expanding charging infrastructure at Romania's largest airport. The stations are located in the North parking area and are now available to electric vehicle users.

The new infrastructure consists of seven 200 kW charging stations, providing a total of 14 charging points with a combined installed capacity of 1.4 MW.

Located near the Departures Terminal, the stations are designed to reduce charging times and accommodate a high number of users, the company said.

“We are happy to announce that the 7 ultra-fast stations at Henri Coandă Airport are operational and available to electric car users. Otopeni Airport is one of the most dynamic transit points in the country, and our presence here is a clear signal that charging infrastructure must be where people need it,” said Andreea-Dana Popescu, General Manager of PPC Blue Romania.

The company installed the charging infrastructure after winning a five-year contract awarded through a tender organized by the National Company Bucharest Airports.

With the addition of the airport charging hub, PPC Blue's network now exceeds 1,400 charging points across all Romanian counties, up about 27% from the end of last year. The network has a total installed capacity of more than 46 MW, making it one of the country's largest electric vehicle charging networks.

The company said it plans to continue expanding its charging infrastructure in retail areas, business districts, residential neighborhoods, industrial parks, tourist destinations, and along transit routes, while also integrating charging stations with renewable energy and storage solutions.

World.title: Romania’s first female supercentenarian celebrates 111th birthday
World.content:
The oldest person in Romania, a woman from the city of Cugir, central Romania, born in 1915, was celebrated on Monday, July 20, on the occasion of her 111th birthday.

Noja Paladia, who ranks 124th in the world among the longest-living people, holds the official status of the oldest living person in Romania. On her birthday, she was visited by Cugir mayor Adrian Teban. During the visit, the mayor presented the celebrant with a certificate of appreciation, a bouquet and a symbolic amount of money, “as a sign of deep respect and public recognition from the entire local community for a life that has crossed, with exemplary dignity, a century and more than a decade,” according to the Orașul Cugir Facebook page.

The woman lives in her own home together with her 76-year-old daughter, who takes care of her permanently, while the entire extended family is involved in ensuring all the necessary conditions for a peaceful old age, the same source stated.

“The case of Mrs Noja Paladia (born Bâldea) has received international recognition. On April 16, 2026, the international organization Gerontology Research Group (GRG) officially confirmed and validated her supercentenarian status following rigorous demographic checks: 124th place in the official global ranking of the longest-living people currently alive on the planet,” representatives of the local administration said.

According to them, Noja Paladia is also the oldest person in the Balkan region and, at the same time, the oldest woman who has ever lived in Romania, becoming the first female supercentenarian in the documented history of the country.

Paladia is close to reaching the title of the longest-lived person in the entire documented history of Romania, a record held by the late World War II veteran Ilie Ciocan, who recently passed away on May 27, 2026, at the astonishing age of 112 years and 351 days.

Paladia’s secret to longevity is a moderate lifestyle. She never smoked, never drank alcohol, and always ate in moderation. She had many stomach problems due to pregnancies and underwent surgery three times. Her diet, simple and natural, was always based on traditional foods grown in her own garden. She grew up with home-cooked meals, fresh vegetables and dairy products, without excesses.

Corporate: experiences move from rewards to retention and loyalty-building



For years, the budget for a team experience sat under the "reward" category: a nice gesture, but an optional one, often among the first to be cut when budgets tightened. Complice.ro's data for the first half of 2026 shows that this logic has changed: more and more companies now treat experiences as a retention tool, both for employees and for partners and clients.



The growth in the corporate segment is mainly driven by Complice.ro's existing clients, which have allocated budgets for experiences dedicated to teams and business partners. This evolution contrasts with the general market trend, as most companies in Romania have reduced or reorganised spending in this area: fewer events, shorter formats, smaller numbers of participants, while some companies have temporarily given up such initiatives altogether.

"The situation is the same for everyone: smaller budgets, uncertainty, pressure on any cost that is not strictly critical. The difference lies in how each company reacts to it. Many of our clients are large companies in IT, retail, real estate or financial services, which feel the crisis less and have chosen to work with fewer suppliers, but trusted ones, instead of spreading the budget across several providers. In practice, we have become their partner for this type of decision, beyond being an experience provider. And I see something very concrete: companies that have already included these experiences in their retention strategy do not cut them from the budget at the first sign of pressure, because they know exactly how much it costs to replace a good employee they want to keep close," says Oana Pascu.

At the same time, the type of projects being implemented has also changed. While in previous years most corporate initiatives were one-off projects, linked to an event or a special occasion, in the first half of 2026 companies more often ordered projects integrated into recurring, well-established programmes, rather than isolated events. In practice, the decision to invest in a team experience no longer comes from an events calendar, but from an HR or marketing strategy.



An important part of this growth also comes from projects dedicated to top business partners, such as off-road or sailing events in mixed teams, challenge-based routes or themed treasure hunts, as well as private tastings organised abroad for strategic partners. These projects are on a completely different scale from a classic team building, with considerably higher budgets, and they have remained a priority for companies this year as well.

"This year, we have received many more requests for spectacular experience-based projects dedicated to very important business partners. Companies invest in relationships with strategic partners precisely during difficult periods, because that is where the trust they need to navigate these times more easily is built," says Oana Pascu.

Residential: desire remains, frequency decreases, average order value holds steady



In the individual customer segment, both the number of orders and turnover are slightly below the 2025 level, while the average order value remains stable at around RON 590, similar to the same period last year. High inflation, the depreciation of the leu, the wave of corporate restructuring and political uncertainty directly affect people's purchasing power and their willingness to spend money on things that do not represent an immediate or necessary need.

"Order frequency is decreasing, but the average value of an order placed on the website remains almost constant. In practice, people are not giving up on the idea of offering an experience as a gift; they are simply doing it less often and choosing more carefully. We see this clearly in the growing preference for Flexibox, where you choose the package but leave the exact experience to the person receiving the gift, and for the gift card, which has gained a lot of ground recently. At the same time, the decline in purchasing power is slowing down the tendency for experiences to become part of everyday life. For now, they remain a solution for events and special occasions, such as wedding or relationship anniversaries, wedding gifts, gifts for godparents, civil ceremonies or milestone birthdays," says Oana Pascu.

Among individual experiences, the best-selling ones in the first half of the year remain, to a large extent, those with a strong track record in the Complice.ro portfolio. A stay at a manor house in Prahova, with a wine tasting experience, and the similar winery option confirm the steady appetite for one-day or weekend escapes focused on wine and gastronomy. The 30-minute flight in a light aircraft near Bucharest and the Boeing flight simulator experience remain constant choices for those looking for a memorable moment with controlled adrenaline, while the hot rod ride and floating therapy, designed for deep relaxation, complete the top, confirming that interest in both thrill-based and wellbeing experiences remains just as strong.

*This is a press release.

World.title: Romanian president Nicușor Dan congratulates new UK prime minister Andy Burnham for appointment
World.content:
Romanian president Nicușor Dan congratulated Labour leader Andy Burnham on his appointment as prime minister of the United Kingdom on Monday, July 20.

The Romanian official said he was confident that under Burnham's leadership, the United Kingdom would continue to actively contribute to strengthening peace, security and international cooperation.

"I am delighted to extend to Andy Burnham my warmest congratulations and best wishes on his appointment as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. I am confident that, under his leadership, the UK will continue to actively contribute to strengthening peace, security and international cooperation, and that we will further deepen Romanian-British collaboration bilaterally and within NATO, in the spirit of allied solidarity,” Dan said on X.

He also reaffirmed Romania’s commitment to its partnership with the United Kingdom. “The over one million Romanians living in the UK remain an essential bridge between our two societies,” he added.

The new leader of Britain's Labour Party, Andy Burnham, accompanied by his Dutch-born wife, Marie-France van Heel, was received by King Charles III at Buckingham Palace at midday on Monday. He was appointed prime minister and asked to form a government the same day.

The former mayor of the Greater Manchester urban area, Andy Burnham, aged 56, gave his inaugural speech outside the government headquarters at 10 Downing Street. He promised a "ten-year plan" to restore the United Kingdom and said the country must "regain its stability." He also pledged to act "now to give people a little breathing space and help them cope with the cost of living," according to the BBC.

In the longer term, Burnham said the government would help more young people into work by changing the education system and providing them with more support, including greater mental health support. He also promised that more social housing would be built.

Andy Burnham is already King Charles III's fourth prime minister since his accession to the throne in September 2022, and the seventh prime minister the kingdom has had in ten years. The country’s executive became more unstable following the Brexit vote in 2016, despite the 2024 change in power between the Labour Party and the Conservatives.

The UK’s last prime minister, Keir Starmer, announced his resignation on June 22 after becoming unpopular in the country and facing strong opposition within his own party following ill-judged decisions, controversies and electoral defeats at the local level.

The new prime minister, however, faces major challenges. Burnham must first unveil his cabinet and then address a long list of issues, from sluggish economic growth to the cost-of-living crisis and the poor performance of utility companies.

World.title: Tests Show Faeces Contaminated North Macedonia Town’s Water Supply
World.content:
The centre of Gostivar, North Macedonia. Photo: Fazlijah/Wikimedia Commons.

Lab tests have confirmed the presence of faecal contamination in the drinking water supplied to the western North Macedonian town of Gostivar, local prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

The findings, disclosed by the Gostivar Basic Prosecutor’s Office, appear to prove that the town’s water supply is linked to an epidemic of gastrointestinal illness that has overwhelmed local health services since last week.

On Monday, police detained the head of the local public water utility, Artana Asani, and two other managers over the outbreak that has made more than 3,000 people sick so far.

The Gostivar Prosecutor’s Office said three officials are suspected of committing “serious crimes against the environment and nature through the pollution of drinking water.

“The suspects, acting together in their official capacities … made the drinking water in the overflow chamber of the system supplying Gostivar municipality and several surrounding villages unusable by introducing a harmful substance into it,” the Prosecution said.

The probe suspects the water supply became contaminated when the water company, in a presumed attempt to increase the water supply last month, connected additional pumps to the existing system that drew in water from an unhealthy surface-level source.

According to the prosecution, laboratory tests conducted by the Institute of Public Health detected faecal contamination in the water supply, including extremely high concentrations of coliform bacteria and the presence of Escherichia coli (E. coli), indicating contamination with human or animal faecal matter and rendering the water unsafe to drink.

Before his arrest, water utility head Asani last week insisted the outbreak of illness in the town was not caused by water but food poisoning. But authorities pinpointed drinking water as the most likely culprit, given the sheer scale of the outbreak.

The outbreak has sent more than 3,000 people to hospitals and clinics with symptoms including severe stomach pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and nausea, making it one of the largest recorded waterborne health incidents in North Macedonia in decades.

The Health Ministry has warned that the flow of new patients is not subsiding yet and is running at about 200 to 300 new patients per day.

Meanwhile, tap water in the town of roughly 80,000 people, some 65 kilometres west of the capital, Skopje, is unusable, and the municipal and state authorities have sent trucks with bottled water for residents’ use.

The Health Ministry on Monday said some of the contaminants found in the system are not easy to deal with, so the ban on drinking tap water will likely stay in place for some time.

The incident has triggered widespread public anger, with residents questioning how contamination on this scale could have gone undetected until thousands of people had already become ill.

Gostivar Mayor Valbon Limani on Monday denied any responsibility for the crisis himself, saying he had no role in the water company.

“I do not feel any moral responsibility because the public utility company Komunalec is a separate legal entity that manages and operates the water supply system. Otherwise, the citizens who know me are aware that, had the situation been different, I would certainly have been the first to resign,” Limani said.

World.title: Hungarian PM’s Presidential Gambit Fails as Polgar Declines Nomination
World.content:
“The responsibility is entirely mine,” Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar admitted on Monday night, after he had failed to convince the world’s greatest female chess player of all time, Judit Polgar, to accept the nomination to be the country’s next president.

“I don’t feel the strength to take on the historic responsibility, therefore I am unable to accept the invitation,” Polgar, 49, posted last night, ending a day of intense speculation in Hungary and abroad.

Nominating a grandmaster as Hungary’s next president was just the latest in a series of unconventional moves by the government headed by Magyar’s Tisza party. It was a hasty decision by a government that seems to be under constant time pressure to deliver on the numerous promises it made during the campaign for the April 12 election, which it won by a landslide.

“The selection of Hungary’s next president should not be rushed, Peter Magyar is acting as if there were no time for a meaningful public debate about the country’s next head of state,” the human rights watchdog Amnesty International said in a statement.

Tamas Sulyok was regarded as an ideological presidential appointee of former prime minister Viktor Orban. According to Sulyok’s critics, he stood by as the previous government weakened democratic institutions and undermined the rule of law. As a result, voters had lost confidence in him, Magyar argued during the campaign, and his removal would be an essential step in rebuilding democracy and the system of checks of balances in Hungary.

Sulyok refused to budge for weeks until a constitutional amendment was passed on July 13 by the Tisza-dominated parliament which, among other measures, term-limited MPs to 12 years, pensioned off constitutional court judges at 70 and, in a single sentence, terminated the president’s mandate with immediate effect. Sulyok announced on Saturday he would sign the constitutional amendment, “fulfilling my obligation under the Fundamental Law [Hungary’s constitution] after carefully weighing my legal options and my conscience”.

In a lengthy video posted on Facebook, the outgoing president lamented the “end of constitutionalism” and warned that the Tisza government posed a threat to Hungarian democracy. The president has a largely ceremonial role but can block some legislation and delay appointments.

Hungary’s parliament now has 30 days to elect a new head of state, who will be in office until a new constitution is drawn up and adopted, but no longer than five years.

Magyar had promised broad public consultation in choosing the next president, saying he wanted a person capable of uniting Hungary’s deeply polarised society and representing the country abroad. But on Sunday, only hours after Sulyok had stepped down, a group of Hungarian intellectuals, athletes and public figures – mainly critics of the former Fidesz government but also some more aligned with it – published an open letter on Facebook endorsing Polgar for the presidency.

Magyar replied in a Facebook post that he would discuss the matter on Monday with Polgar, who he saw as the most suitable candidate. Tisza’s parliamentary group leader Andrea Bujdoso also described Polgar as the party’s preferred candidate for the presidency.

Some sensed a stitch-up after evidence emerged showing Magyar meeting with Polgar two weeks earlier at the US embassy’s Fourth of July reception in Budapest, where she quickly defeated the prime minister in a chess match. It remains unclear whether they discussed a possible political role before or after the event.

Polgar and her two older sisters were born into a Hungarian Jewish family and educated by their father, Laszlo Polgar, who developed an unconventional method aimed at proving that geniuses are made rather than born. The sisters did not attend school in Communist Hungary but instead spent eight to ten hours a day playing chess. The family travelled extensively around the world at a time when few Hungarians enjoyed such opportunities.

Polgar won her first championship at the age of nine and became the world’s highest-ranked female player at just 12. Throughout her career she played in the men’s league, and defeated several world champions, including Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov. “They thought I was this little girl with a cute ponytail, but I wasn’t that cute when I played,” she once said in an interview.

At the age of 15, she became the youngest grandmaster in history at the time, breaking Bobby Fischer’s longstanding record. A documentary of her life, Queen of Chess, was released earlier this year and became an instant hit on Netflix. Since retiring from competitive chess in 2014, Polgar has focused on educational initiatives and promoting chess among children. She is married to a veterinarian, has two children, and lives in Budapest.

Her potential nomination prompted a variety of reactions. Critics argued that Polgar has never shown any interest in politics and was never publicly critical of Orban’s government. Supporters argued it is an advantage that she has never been affiliated with any political party or movement, but is admired across the political spectrum as one of Hungary’s most accomplished and internationally respected public figures.

But most criticism was focused on the speed with which Tisza tried to rush through the nomination process, arguing that there had been little genuine public consultation despite the lack of urgency.

Fidesz politicians maintain that whoever is elected under the current circumstances will lack democratic legitimacy because of the manner in which the previous president was removed.

World.title: It’s Time NATO Stopped Ignoring Bosnia’s Ammunition Industry
World.content:
When NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned Allied defense ministers that Russia produces in three months what the entire Alliance produces in a year, Europe quickly moved.

Germany’s Rheinmetall accelerated artillery production across two countries. The US Army drove toward 100,000 155mm shells per month. Billions of euros poured into the EU’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production. Summits convened. A strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation was adopted. Commitments were signed.

What largely escaped notice in all those urgent conversations was a pair of factories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only country currently in NATO’s Membership Action Plan.

Pretis d.d., located in Vogosca, near Sarajevo, and Binas d.d., in Bugojno, have operated quietly for decades, largely overlooked by NATO. Pretis is among the few facilities in Europe producing 155mm artillery shells to full NATO standards – the exact caliber at the center of the Alliance’s ammunition crisis.

World.title: ‘Obviously Dangerous’: Unlicensed Jet Skis Pose Growing Hazard on Albania’s Coast
World.content:
On September 11 last year, 18-year-old David’s holiday in Albania took an harrowing turn. The Czech teenager was riding a jet ski in Saranda Bay when there was an accident.

While returning to shore at low speed to pick up his mother, who was waiting to join him as a passenger, he was hit by another watercraft operated by tourists from France.

The impact left him unconscious in the water. His mother, who was filming from the pier, was shocked to see her son floating motionless on the surface, kept afloat only by his life jacket.

“My son fell into the water, remaining motionless and unconscious,” she told BIRN. David and his mother, who asked to remain anonymous, provided BIRN with the full case file, including footage showing the moment of the collision.

World.title: Serbia’s Media Regulator Resumes Work After EU Prompting
World.content:
Serbia’s new Council of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media, REM, held its first constitutive session on Monday but failed to elect a president. The Council is still not composed completely as its ninth member has not been elected yet.

The previous REM Council’s mandate expired in November 2024. Since then, Serbia’s parliament has failed to appoint a new Council. The selection process was marked by numerous allegations of irregularities. Establishing a fully operational REM Council was one of the European Union’s key demands for Serbia as part of its rule-of-law obligations in its EU accession process.

The establishment of the new Council was enabled after four members who had previously resigned agreed to assume their positions earlier in July.

Eight members of the new REM Council were elected in November 2025. However, the ruling majority in parliament did not vote for the ninth member, who was to be chosen from representatives of national minorities. Claiming that the ruling majority had sabotaged the election because their preferred candidate would not be chosen, four of the elected members resigned in December last year.

However, on July 10, parliament adopted an interpretation of the Law on Electronic Media clarifying that the resignations had no legal effect. Following this, the four members agreed to take up their seats on the REM Council, paving the way for it to be formally constituted.

On Monday, two candidates for the president’s position, Mileva Malesic and Milos Garic, won the same number of votes. Malesic was among the candidates who had resigned in December 2025.

Afterwards, Dubravka Valic Nedeljkovic, who chaired the meeting, said consultations would continue and a new session would be held soon.

“Until a president or chairperson is elected, the oldest member of the Council, which is me, will preside until a consensus is reached,” Valic Nedeljkovic said, adding that a president must be elected before the Council can begin to address the important issues concerning the REM.

EU reports on Serbia have repeatedly urged the REM Council to be established and start operating. The latest Rule of Law Report, published in July, said: “Serbia’s audiovisual market continued to face serious challenges in the absence of a functioning decision-making body of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media.”

Some of the problems that the Commission noted in the absence of a regulatory authority is that the competition for the allocation of the fifth frequency for national broadcasting, launched in 2022, has not yet concluded.

Some TV channels have started broadcasting on Telekom Srbija cable without the require licence, and have also received public funding, and public officials have appeared on them.

World.title: Bulgaria to Greenlight US Use of Air Base as Long-Term Hub
World.content:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev stated on Monday that parliament will likely authorise the presence of US aircraft at the Bezmer military base near Sofia.

Approval is likely to allow US aircraft passing through Sofia to refuel in relation to US operations in the Middle East to use the base long-term. On Tuesday, parliament’s defence committee will meet to kickstart the approval process.

Previously, in May, Radev criticised the presence of US aircraft at Sofia’s main Vassil Levski airport.

Radev had tried to hatch a deal with US President Donald Trump and allow a US presence at Sofia airport in exchange for the US lifting visa requirements on Bulgarian citizens. He eventually said he had “not received a positive answer” from Trump.

The Bezmer base is located around 260 kilometres from Sofia near the town of Yambol and is currently used by the Bulgarian Air Force – with which, before entering politics, Radev was a Major General and Commander. Bezmer had been previously used by US military in line with the Defence Cooperation Agreement between Bulgaria and the US signed in 2006.

The latest move fits Radev’s recent political manoeuvering between Washington, Brussels and Moscow.

Back in January he quit as President to successfully enter the race for parliament and assumed office as Prime Minister with his Progressive Bulgaria party, following a landslide win.

The foreign policy of Radev and Progressive Bulgaria is widely seen as being at odds with EU partners, but has also been flexible in practice. His government opposed the recent package of fresh EU sanctions on Russia, for example, but eventually decided not to veto them.

Earlier this month, Radev declined French President Emmanuel Macron’s invitation to attend the summit of the “Coalition of the Willing” aiding the defence of Ukraine. Radev said he did not see Bulgaria attending a summit that “insists on continuing financial and military aid to Ukraine”; however, on July 15, Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova took part in the 5th Ukraine-Southeast Europe Summit in Kyiv.

In a separate development, the Radev government was recently criticised for moves to close the commission that identifies people’s ties to communist-era security services.

World.title: Kosovo Prosecutorial Council Rejects Serb Prosecutors’ Return to Old Posts
World.content:
The Kosovo Prosecutorial Council meeting on July 20, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Prosecutorial System/Facebook Live/Screenshot.

The Kosovo Prosecutorial Council, KPC, on Monday denied the requests of several Serb prosecutors to return to their posts, nearly four years after Kosovo Serbs staged a mass resignation from Kosovo institutions in 2022.

Chief State Prosecutor Zejnullah Gashi told the KPC meeting on Monday that while he supported prosecutors from the Serb community being part of the system, he had not had time yet to familiarise himself with the matter.

“I stand by the position … that colleagues from the Serb community should also be part of the prosecutorial system. Regarding this topic or issue, I must honestly say that I was not informed in time, as I have only just assumed the role of Chief Prosecutor,” he said.

Media in Kosovo have reported that five prosecutors and 15 administrative staff members have asked to return.

KPC member Arlinda Muqa said the return of Serb prosecutors should not be treated as a political matter but solely as a legal issue.

“Kosovo has fulfilled all obligations arising from the agreements on the integration of the judiciary and the prosecution service. It provided them [Serbs] with the opportunity to become part of the constitutional system, enjoying all associated rights and professional guarantees. In 2022, they chose to resign; this constitutes a personal and legal act, the consequences of which are clearly defined by law,” she said.

Another KPC member, Visar Krasniqi, said: “As things stand, I cannot find grounds to support their return. I am convinced that the failure to verify their integrity is a serious issue, and I do not feel able to vote in favour of their return until time reveals whether these individuals were involved in activities that our own legislation does not recognise.”

Most Serbs in Kosovo’s four Serb-majority northern municipalities resigned on November 5, 2022, from their state posts, claiming that EU-mediated agreements between Serbia and Kosovo were being breached.

The resignations followed a meeting in the town of Zvecan organised by the Belgrade-backed party representing Kosovo Serbs, Srpska Lista.

Srpska Lista said the mayors of the Serb-majority municipalities, councillors, MPs, judges, prosecutors, judicial staff and Kosovo Police officers had all quit their jobs. During the meeting in Zvecan, Serb police officers symbolically took off their Kosovo police uniforms to applause from the participants.

The then leader of Srpska Lista, Goran Rakic, announcing the boycott of Kosovo’s institutions, said these decisions would remain in effect until an Association of Serb-Majority Municipalities, as agreed in the EU-facilitated Kosovo-Serbia dialogue, was established.

The move came two days after then regional director of the Kosovo Police for the Serb-majority north, Nenad Djuric, was suspended after he claimed that police in the north would not implement the government’s decision to issue reprimands to drivers of vehicles with licence plates issued by Serbia, which are considered illegal by the Kosovo authorities.

Sources told BIRN that the Kosovo Judicial Council has also received requests to return to work from several Serb judges. The exact number is not known.

After the 2022 boycott took effect, ethnic Albanians were elected as mayors in the north in extraordinary local elections in April 2023, on very low turnouts, after Serbs stayed away from the polls.

After these new mayors took office, the security situation in the north deteriorated. Clashes between protesters and NATO peacekeeping forces led to around 93 NATO personnel being injured, with one having a leg amputated.

Kosovo authorities also shut down a series of so-called “parallel” Serb institutions – services run outside government control – in the north of the country.

The European Union imposed some sanctions on Kosovo in June 2023 in response to the worsening security situation. These measures were lifted in March 2026.

Serb mayors retook power in the four Serb-majority municipalities in December 2025. During the election campaign, Srpska Lista admitted it had made a mistake in urging Serbs to abandon Kosovo institutions in 2022 – but said the decision had at least attracted the attention of the international community.

World.title: Croatian Clubs Discover Potential European Draws
World.content:
Croatia’s European hopefuls found out their possible third qualifying round opponents on Monday, with draws confirmed across the Europa League, Champions League, and Conference League paths.

Hajduk could face Salzburg

Should Hajduk get past Cypriot side Pafos in the second qualifying round of the Europa League, their reward will be a third-round clash with Austria’s Salzburg. Hajduk host Pafos in the first leg on Thursday in Split, with the return fixture in Cyprus the following Thursday. Should they progress, Hajduk would again have home advantage in the first leg of the third round, with the second leg to follow in Salzburg. Third qualifying round ties are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

Should Hajduk instead lose against Pafos, they would drop into the Conference League third qualifying round, where they’d face the winner of the tie between Georgia’s Dinamo Tbilisi and Lithuania’s Žalgiris, with the first leg played away from home.

Dinamo await Vikingur or Hapoel

Champions Dinamo Zagreb have also learned their potential path forward. Should they be eliminated by Switzerland’s Thun in the Champions League second qualifying round, Dinamo would drop into the Europa League third qualifying round to face either Iceland’s Vikingur or Israel’s Hapoel Beer Sheva.

Should Dinamo instead get past Thun and reach the Champions League third qualifying round itself, Mario Kovačević’s side would face the winner of the tie between Faroese side Klaksvik and Lithuania’s Kauno Žalgiris, coached by Željko Sopić. First legs in that round are set for August 4/5, with second legs on August 11.

UEFA has scrapped the previous system of forming subgroups ahead of the “champions’ path” draw this season, meaning Dinamo faced a considerably wider pool of possible opponents than in previous years.

Before turning their attention to the third qualifying round, Dinamo first face Thun in the first leg of the second qualifying round on Tuesday in Switzerland, kicking off at 8 pm, with the return leg set for Tuesday, July 28.

Rijeka and Varaždin could head to Iceland

Rijeka and Varaždin also discovered their potential third qualifying round opponents in the Conference League on Monday. Rijeka, if they eliminate Ireland’s Derry City in the second round, would face the winner of the tie between Iceland’s Stjarnan and Finland’s Ilves. Varaždin, if they see off Czech side Jablonec, would take on the winner between Latvia’s RFS and Iceland’s Vestri.

Third qualifying round fixtures in the Conference League are scheduled for August 6 and 13.

World.title: Croatia vs Spain, Greece & Italy: Which Destination Comes Out on Top?
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – Croatia has become one of Europe’s most sought-after summer destinations, but how does it compare to the longtime tourism giants Spain, Greece and Italy?

As Vedran Salvia reports for Index, each country offers something unique, from world-famous beaches to ancient cities and exceptional cuisine. Despite the constantly evolving competition, Croatia appears to very successfully continue carving out its own niche, attracting travellers looking for crystal-clear waters, historic towns and a more relaxed coastal experience.

the croatian coast needs very little help in attracting attention

Croatia’s greatest strength remains its spectacular Adriatic coast. Stretching for more than 1,700 kilometres and dotted with over 1,200 islands, islets and reefs, it offers endless opportunities for sailing, island hopping and discovering secluded beaches. Unlike many Mediterranean destinations where development unfortunately totally dominates the coastline, much of Croatia’s shore remains remarkably well preserved, with national parks, hidden coves and picturesque, ancient fishing villages sitting alongside popular tourist hotspots like Dubrovnik, Split and Makarska.

how does that compare with spain?

Tourism heavyweight Spain continues to attract visitors with its vast array of long, sandy beaches, lively nightlife and major cities such as Barcelona, Valencia and Málaga. It also offers year-round sunshine in many regions. Croatia, however, appeals to travellers seeking a more intimate experience. While destinations like Dubrovnik can become crowded during peak season, much of the coastline remains quieter than Spain’s busiest resorts, particularly away from the best-known locations.

greece – the home of influencer islands

Nearby Greece is globally renowned for iconic, entirely different islands such as Santorini, Mykonos and Crete, along with its ancient history and rich Mediterranean cuisine. Croatia, located just up north, offers a different style of island holiday. Rather than focusing on a handful of internationally famous islands which have become totally swamped by influencers over more recent years (see Mykonos, for example), visitors can choose from hundreds of inhabited and uninhabited islands. Each of them has its very own character, from the lavender fields of Hvar’s interior and the vineyards of Korčula to the untouched nature of Mljet and Lastovo.

the home of the romans is hard to contend with, yet croatia manages to do so

Neighbouring Italy remains one of the world’s most visited countries thanks to remarkable cities such as Rome, Venice and Florence, alongside the Amalfi Coast and Sicily. The country that gave the world the Romans would be difficult to compete with for anyone, and yet Croatia, in its own way, still manages. Naturally, Croatia cannot match Italy’s sheer number of globally recognised cultural landmarks or its geographical size, but it often provides a similar Adriatic atmosphere at a more accessible price point. This is particularly true for sailing holidays, waterfront accommodation and seafood dining outside the very height of the summer season.

croatian prices – a gap that is narrowing (and quickly)

One of Croatia’s traditional advantages has always been affordability, although that gap has greatly narrowed in recent years. Since the country’s accession to the Eurozone, prices for accommodation, restaurants and tourism services have spiked noticeably, especially in popular coastal destinations. During the peak summer months, visitors may find Croatia approaching the prices of parts of Italy or Greece, particularly down in Dubrovnik, as well as in central Dalmatian destinations such as Hvar and Split. Despite that being the case, many lesser-known destinations continue to offer excellent value, particularly along the Kvarner coast, northern Dalmatia and of course away from the sea entirely in inland Croatia.

croatia is so much more than “just beaches”

Croatia’s appeal extends well beyond the coastline and 1,000+ islands. Visitors can explore the marvellous Plitvice Lakes National Park, hike through the imposing mountains of Velebit, discover a great many Roman monuments in Zadar, Pula and Split, sample world-class wines up in Istria and down Pelješac, or experience vibrant festivals and cultural events throughout the entire summer. Combined with its strong reputation as one of Europe’s safest destinations by far, these experiences continue to attract travellers looking for far more than a traditional beach holiday.

the verdict – croatia is the small country that could (and very much has)

Spain offers energy and variety, Italy delivers world-famous culture, and Greece remains synonymous with idyllic island escapes. Croatia, meanwhile, combines elements of all three: spectacular islands, historic towns, exceptional natural beauty and a coastline that remains one of the cleanest and most diverse in Europe. For travellers seeking a Mediterranean holiday that balances relaxation, adventure and history, Croatia continues to prove that it deserves its place alongside the region’s biggest tourism giants.

World.title: Europe’s Smallest Bible Is Hidden in Croatia, And It Fits in the Palm of Your Hand
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – You don’t have to be religious to appreciate the wonder of religious architecture and items, and one of the most fascinating (and tiny) items can be found in Croatia. Europe’s smallest Bible is actually hidden in a relatively overlooked part of Croatia.

Croatia is home to countless historical treasures, but few are as surprising as the smallest Bible in all of Europe, a tiny masterpiece that can fit comfortably in the palm of your hand. Putni kofer writes that this truly remarkable miniature Bible is kept in the town of Ludbreg, widely known as “the centre of the world” in northern Croatia, where it has become one of the area’s most unusual cultural attractions.

ludbreg – full of surprises

Despite its incredibly small dimensions, the Bible contains both the Old and New Testaments, printed in microscopic text and bound with exceptional craftsmanship. Its pages are so small that visitors are often astonished that an entire Bible could be produced in such a compact format, making it as much a feat of printing as it is an object of religious significance.

The miniature Bible forms part of Ludbreg’s exceptionally rich cultural and religious heritage. The town is already well known as one of Croatia’s most important pilgrimage destinations thanks to the Sanctuary of the Precious Blood of Christ, which attracts thousands of visitors each year, but this tiny book offers another fascinating reason to visit.

Visitors to Ludbreg are often surprised to discover that such a unique artefact is housed in a small Croatian town rather than in one of Europe’s larger museums.

more than a mere religious object

While the Bible’s size makes it an instant conversation piece, it also reflects the extraordinary skill of the printers and bookbinders who created it. Miniature books have long fascinated collectors around the world, but examples containing the complete biblical text are exceptionally rare, making Ludbreg’s specimen one of the continent’s most unusual literary treasures.

As touched on above, Ludbred is known as the “Centre of the World” thanks to a local legend. This small, humble northern Croatian continues to surprise visitors with attractions that extend far beyond its famous pilgrimage traditions. From its historic streets and castle to one of Europe’s tiniest Bibles, the town proves that some of Croatia’s most remarkable stories are found in places many international visitors have yet to discover.

World.title: Croatia Tightens Online Alcohol Sales With e-Citizens Age Verification
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – Croatia is continuing to fight its apparent war on alcohol sales from all angles, with mandatory e-Citizens age verification looming.

Purchasing alcohol online in Croatia is set to become significantly more secure after new rules introduced by the government require customers to verify their age through the e-Citizens (e-Građani) digital identity system before buying it. Poslovni reports that this latest measure is designed to prevent minors from buying alcoholic beverages online by introducing a reliable electronic age verification process, replacing the self-declaration methods commonly used by many online retailers today.

the age of digital id

Under the new rules, customers purchasing alcoholic drinks online will have to confirm they are of legal drinking age using Croatia’s e-Citizens platform. The digital verification system will allow retailers to confirm whether a customer is an adult without relying solely on manually entered dates of birth or simple tick-box declarations, which have long been criticised as ineffective.

In traditional shops, retailers are obviously already required to refuse alcohol sales to minors and can ask customers to present identification if they doubt their age. The new system aims to bring online alcohol sales closer to those same standards by ensuring age verification takes place before the transaction is completed. Officials say the change reflects the growing importance of digital commerce and the need to apply the same consumer protection rules regardless of whether alcohol is purchased in person or online.

online retailers should have the exact same level of responsibility

Businesses selling alcoholic beverages over the internet will now need to integrate the e-Citizens verification process into their online stores. The move is expected to improve legal certainty for retailers while making it considerably more difficult for underage users to bypass age restrictions through false declarations.

The introduction of mandatory digital age verification is another example of Croatia expanding the use of its e-Citizens platform beyond mere public administration into everyday commercial services. Over the past decade, the platform has become a central gateway for accessing government services, digital documents and official records. Its use for online age verification reflects a broader shift towards secure digital identity solutions that are becoming increasingly common across Europe.

For consumers, the biggest change will be simple: anyone buying alcohol online in Croatia should expect to log in through e-Citizens before placing an order for alcohol, adding an extra step designed to ensure that alcohol is sold only to adults.

World.title: Zagreb Bus Station Set for Major Renovation as First Phase Gets Underway
World.content:
July the 21st, 2026 – The now quite dated and dilapidated Zagreb bus station is set to undergo a major renovation as the first phase finally gets underway.

Zagreb bus station is set to undergo a long-awaited modernisation, with the first phase of renovation focusing on improving passenger facilities and upgrading key parts of one of Croatia’s busiest transport hubs.

AKZ.hr reports that this significant investment marks the beginning of a broader effort to revitalise the station, which has served millions of passengers for decades and remains the country’s largest hub for domestic and international bus travel.

The initial phase of works will prioritise improvements that passengers use every day, including the station’s waiting areas, sanitary facilities and other public spaces that have shown signs of age after years of heavy use. Station management has claimed that the primary goal is to improve comfort, accessibility and the overall travel experience while ensuring the terminal remains fully operational throughout the renovation process.

modernising a crucial national transport hub

Opened back in 1987, Zagreb bus station handles thousands of passengers each day and connects the Croatian capital with destinations across Croatia and Europe. Despite its importance, much of the complex has remained largely unchanged for decades, prompting growing calls for refurbishment as passenger expectations and transport standards have evolved. The planned upgrades are expected to improve both the appearance and functionality of the station while extending the lifespan of the existing infrastructure.

The renovation is being presented as the first stage of a wider modernisation programme that could eventually include additional commercial spaces, energy-efficiency improvements and further infrastructure upgrades. By carrying out the work in phases, operators aim to minimise disruption while gradually bringing the station up to modern standards.

As Croatia continues investing in transport infrastructure as a whole, from railways and airports to roads and public transport, the refurbishment of Zagreb bus station represents yet another concerted effort to modernise the country’s key mobility hubs. For the millions of passengers who pass through the station each and every year, the first phase of works is expected to deliver noticeable improvements while laying the groundwork for a more comprehensive transformation in the years ahead.
